docs.title: The Core Skill: Explicit vs. Inference
docs.text:
• Explicit — You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.

docs.title: How to Use This Series
docs.text:
Each study has four files:

File Level Contains Answers? beginner-questions.md Beginner No — questions only beginner-answers.md Beginner Yes — full answer key advanced-questions.md Advanced No — questions only advanced-answers.md Advanced Yes — full answer key

All 20 study folders follow this four-file structure (80 study files + this README = 81 files total).

Beginner level focuses on reading Scripture and observing what the text says. No prior knowledge of Hebrew, Greek, or theology is needed.

Advanced level includes original-language word studies, cross-referencing, counter-arguments, and evidence classification exercises.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
This series is based on the etc6 research series, which investigated every relevant biblical passage using a rigorous evidence classification system. The studies present evidence from all sides — both conditionalist and eternal conscious torment (ECT) positions — and classify each piece of evidence by what the text actually says.

The approach is investigative, not advocacy. The goal is to let the reader see what the text says and draw their own conclusions from the evidence.

docs.text: Each study guide is derived from a detailed research study with full evidence tables, word studies, and cross-references. The source studies are located in the bible-studies/etc6-* directories.

docs.title: Study 1: What Is Man? — Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Biblical Anthropology: Hebrew and Greek Word Studies

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) — The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) — No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed — every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) — Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: The Hebrew Word for "Soul" — Nephesh (H5315)
docs.text:
1. Nephesh appears approximately 780 times in the Old Testament and is translated over 40 different ways. Using a concordance, find at least five different English words used to translate nephesh. What does this range tell you about whether nephesh simply means "immortal soul"?

Nephesh is translated: soul, life, creature, person, body, dead body, self, desire, appetite, heart, mind, among many others. With 780 occurrences and 214 distinct translations in the KJV, the word covers a vast semantic range. It clearly does not mean "immortal soul" — it refers to the whole living being, life itself, or even a dead body. The assumption that nephesh = "immortal soul" imports a concept the word itself does not carry.

2. In Genesis 2:7, the Hebrew verb is hayah (Qal Wayyiqtol 3ms) — "became." Does the grammar support "man received a soul" or "man became a soul"?

The grammar supports "man became a living soul." The verb hayah means "to become" or "to be." The construction is: God formed man, breathed into him, and man became (hayah) a nephesh chayyah. There is no grammatical basis for reading this as receiving a soul as a separate component placed into a body. The soul is what the whole person is.

3. In Genesis 1:20-21, 24, 30, and 2:19, animals are called nephesh chayyah. In Genesis 2:7, man is called nephesh chayyah. The KJV translates the animal occurrences as "living creature" and the human occurrence as "living soul." What does the identical Hebrew tell you?

The Hebrew is identical in both cases: nephesh chayyah. The difference in English translation obscures this fact. Both animals and humans are nephesh chayyah — living beings animated by the breath of life. The term nephesh does not distinguish humans from animals. What distinguishes humans is the imago Dei (image of God) — Genesis 1:26-27, 9:6.

4. In Leviticus 21:11 and Numbers 6:6, the Hebrew says nephesh meth — literally "dead soul." How does this usage affect the claim that the soul is immortal?

Scripture itself uses the phrase "dead soul" (nephesh meth), translated "dead body" in English. If the soul were inherently immortal and could not die, the phrase "dead soul" would be self-contradictory. The Bible does not treat it as contradictory — it uses the phrase naturally because nephesh refers to the whole being, which can die.

5. In Leviticus 17:11, 14, Scripture says "the nephesh of the flesh is in the blood." What does this tell you about whether nephesh refers to an immaterial, immortal entity?

The nephesh is identified with the blood — a physical substance. This is a biological, material identification. An immaterial, immortal entity cannot be "in the blood." This confirms that nephesh refers to the life or vitality of the creature, not to a separable immortal component.

docs.title: Section B: The Hebrew Words for "Spirit" and "Breath" — Ruach (H7307) and Neshamah (H5397)
docs.text:
6. Ruach appears 434 times and is translated "spirit," "wind," and "breath" among other ways. In Ecclesiastes 3:19, the text says humans and animals have "one ruach" (breath/spirit). If ruach meant an immortal conscious entity unique to humans, what problem would this create?

If ruach meant an immortal conscious entity, then animals would also possess one, since Ecclesiastes 3:19 says humans and animals have "one ruach" (ruach echad). The text explicitly states man "has no preeminence above a beast" regarding this ruach. Either ruach is an immortal soul (in which case animals also have one), or it is the breath of life shared by all creatures. The latter reading is consistent with the text.

7. Neshamah appears 25 times. Compare Genesis 2:7 (God breathed neshamah into man) with Genesis 7:22 (all creatures with neshamah in their nostrils). Do animals also have neshamah?

Yes. Genesis 7:22 says "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life (neshamah)" — referring to all air-breathing creatures that died in the flood. The neshamah that God breathed into man is also attributed to animals. It is the breath of life, not a uniquely human immortal component.

8. Read Isaiah 42:5, Acts 17:25, and Zechariah 12:1. Who is the source of breath and spirit? Is it inherent to humans, or given by God?

Every passage identifies God as the source: - Isaiah 42:5: God "giveth breath to the people upon [the earth], and spirit to them that walk therein." - Acts 17:25: God "giveth to all life, and breath, and all things." - Zechariah 12:1: The LORD "formeth the spirit of man within him."

Breath and spirit are given by God, not inherent to humans. At death, they return to God who gave them (Ecc 12:7). They were never "ours" — they are on loan.

9. In the Septuagint (Greek OT), neshamah is typically translated pnoe (G4157) and ruach is translated pneuma (G4151). Both are breath/wind words. What does this mapping suggest about whether the translators understood these as conscious, immortal entities?

The LXX translators chose breath/wind words to render both neshamah and ruach. Pnoe means "a blowing, breath." Pneuma means "wind, breath, spirit." The Greek-speaking translators did not use vocabulary suggesting a conscious, immortal soul — they used vocabulary consistent with the breath-of-life reading. This is significant because the LXX translators consistently used breath/wind vocabulary rather than terminology suggesting a conscious, immortal entity.

docs.title: Section C: Death as Reversal of Creation
docs.text:
10. Construct the creation/death reversal from the text:

  • Creation (Gen 2:7): dust + breath of life = living soul
  • Death (Ecc 12:7): dust returns to earth + spirit returns to God
  • Result: The living soul ceases.

The formula works in one direction (creation) and reverses in the other (death). No third component — an immortal soul that continues — is mentioned in either process.

11. Read Psalm 146:4 carefully. The Hebrew word for "thoughts" is eshtonot and the verb is abad (perish). What is the timing? Does the text say thoughts perish gradually, or "in that very day"?

"In that very day" (bayom hahu) — the cessation is immediate. When the breath departs, thoughts perish that same day. The text does not describe a gradual fading or a transition to a different mode of thinking. It describes the end of all cognitive activity at the point of death.

12. Read Job 34:14-15. What happens if God withdraws his ruach and neshamah? Does this apply only to humans or to "all flesh"?

"All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust." Both ruach and neshamah are mentioned, and the effect of their withdrawal is universal — "all flesh" perishes. Elihu describes the same process as Ecclesiastes 12:7 and Psalm 104:29.

13. Read Psalm 104:29. Compare with Job 34:14-15 and Ecclesiastes 12:7. How many authors describe the same death process?

At least three authors — the Psalmist (Ps 104:29), Elihu/Job (Job 34:14-15), and Solomon (Ecc 12:7) — describe the identical process: God withdraws breath/spirit, the creature dies and returns to dust. This consistent testimony across multiple authors and books strengthens the classification of these as reliable descriptions of what death is.

docs.title: Section D: Immortality — Three Greek Words
docs.text:
14. Look up the following Greek words and their occurrences:

  • Athanasia (G110) — "deathlessness." 3 NT occurrences. 1 Timothy 6:16: God "only [monos] hath immortality [athanasia]." 1 Corinthians 15:53-54: mortals "must put on" athanasia at the resurrection. Athanasia belongs to God alone and is given to believers at the resurrection — not at birth and not at death.

  • Aphtharsia (G861) — "incorruptibility." 8 NT occurrences. Romans 2:7: believers "seek for" aphtharsia. 2 Timothy 1:10: Christ "brought life and immortality [aphtharsia] to light through the gospel." Something that must be sought and was brought to light by Christ is not an inherent human possession.

  • Thnetos (G2349) — "mortal." 6 NT occurrences. Romans 6:12: "your mortal [thnetos] body." 1 Corinthians 15:53: "this mortal [thnetos] must put on immortality." The human body is explicitly called mortal. The transformation to immortality is future, not present.

15. Read Genesis 3:22-24. If man already possessed an immortal soul, why would God need to bar him from the tree of life to prevent him from "living forever"?

The action would be pointless. If man already had an immortal component that could not die, barring him from the tree of life to prevent him from "living forever" (chay le-olam) accomplishes nothing — he would already live forever regardless. God's action only makes sense if man is wholly mortal and the tree of life was the means by which he could have sustained life indefinitely.

docs.title: Section E: The Intermediate State — Competing Passages
docs.text:
16. Read 2 Corinthians 5:1-8.

Paul's desire is to be "clothed upon" (ependysasthai) — to receive the new body over the old — not to be "unclothed" (ekdysasthai) or disembodied (v.4). He wants "mortality swallowed up of life." This exact phrase appears in 1 Corinthians 15:54, where it describes the resurrection. Paul is not describing an intermediate disembodied state — he is describing his preference to be alive at the Second Coming and transformed without dying.

17. Read Philippians 1:23.

Paul desires "to depart and be with Christ." But in the same letter (Phil 3:11), his stated hope is "if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead." And in Phil 3:20-21, he awaits a Savior who "shall change our vile body." Paul's own writings consistently tie being with Christ to the resurrection. From the perspective of the sleeper, departing (death) and being with Christ (resurrection) are experienced as immediate — with no subjective awareness of the time between.

18. Read Luke 23:43.

Greek manuscripts had no punctuation. "I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise" is as grammatically valid as "I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." John 20:17 states that on Sunday morning — two days after the crucifixion — Jesus said "I am not yet ascended to my Father." If Jesus was not in paradise on Friday, neither was the thief. The reading "I say to you today" is consistent with all other explicit statements; the other reading creates a contradiction with John 20:17.

19. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17.

Paul explicitly describes the sequence: "The dead in Christ shall rise first: then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them... and so shall we ever be with the Lord." Being with the Lord happens after the resurrection and at the Second Coming — not at death. This is Paul's own didactic teaching on the subject.

docs.title: Section F: Anthropological Models
docs.text:
20. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Mark 12:30.

1 Thessalonians 5:23 lists three terms (spirit, soul, body). Mark 12:30 lists four (heart, soul, mind, strength). Deuteronomy 6:5 lists three different ones (heart, soul, might). No passage prescribes a specific number of human components as a doctrinal teaching. These passages use overlapping terms to describe the whole person comprehensively. Reading any of them as a technical anatomy lesson requires importing a framework the text does not provide.

21. Read Isaiah 26:9 and Luke 1:46-47.

In both passages, "soul" and "spirit" are used in synonymous parallelism — a Hebrew poetic device where two lines say the same thing in different words. "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour" (Luke 1:46-47). Mary is not describing two separate components of herself; she is expressing one reality in two parallel phrases.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise — Answers
docs.text:
1. "Man became a living soul" (Gen 2:7) - Explicit (E). Genesis 2:7 directly states this in the text.

2. "The same term (nephesh chayyah) is used for both humans and animals, so the term does not distinguish humans from animals." - Necessary Implication (N). The fact that both humans (Gen 2:7) and animals (Gen 1:20-21,24) receive the same designation is explicitly stated. The conclusion that a shared term cannot serve as a distinguishing marker follows unavoidably — no interpretation or framework is needed.

3. "The human soul is inherently immortal and survives death as a conscious entity." - Inference (I) — specifically I-D (Counter-Evidence External). No verse states this. It requires: - Adding the concept "immortal soul" (no verse uses this phrase) - Redefining "only" in 1 Tim 6:16 to exclude a type of immortality - Redefining "die" in Ezek 18:4 to mean something other than death - Redefining "destroy" in Matt 10:28 to mean something other than destruction - Applying a Platonic philosophical framework not found in Scripture - This is the weakest type of inference because it requires overriding what the text explicitly states.

4. "Man does not inherently possess immortality." - Necessary Implication (N). God only has immortality (1 Tim 6:16 — explicit). Immortality must be sought (Rom 2:7 — explicit). It must be put on at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53 — explicit). Together, these leave no room for humans already possessing immortality. Every reader, regardless of theological position, must acknowledge what "only," "seek," and "must put on" mean.

5. "Death involves the cessation of cognitive activity." - Necessary Implication (N). Seven explicit statements from five authors state the dead lack thoughts (Ps 146:4), knowledge (Ecc 9:5), remembrance (Ps 6:5), work or wisdom (Ecc 9:10), perception (Job 14:21), and praise (Ps 115:17). The cumulative, unanimous testimony leaves no alternative reading of what these texts say. (Note: one could infer these are limited in scope — but the limitation itself would be an inference, since no verse states it.)

6. "Paul's desire to 'depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23) proves a conscious intermediate state between death and resurrection." - Inference (I) — specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). Phil 1:23 expresses Paul's desire (explicit). But Paul's own teaching in 1 Thess 4:16-17 ties being with the Lord to the resurrection (explicit). The claim that Phil 1:23 proves a conscious intermediate state must be chosen over Paul's didactic teaching in 1 Thessalonians. It is an inference with competing textual evidence on both sides, and the clearer passage (didactic instruction) interprets the less clear (personal expression of desire).

7. "The spirit (ruach) that returns to God at death (Ecc 12:7) carries the person's consciousness." - Inference (I) — specifically I-C (Compatible External). Ecclesiastes 12:7 says the ruach returns to God (explicit). The text does not say it carries consciousness, identity, or personality. Psalm 146:4 says thoughts perish when the ruach departs. The claim that the returning ruach is conscious adds a concept the text does not contain. It does not directly contradict Ecc 12:7 (it's compatible with it), but it requires importing information from outside the text.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said — Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. Man was formed from dust and God breathed the breath of life into him; man became a living soul (Gen 2:7).
  2. The same term nephesh chayyah applies to both humans and animals; it does not distinguish them.
  3. Animals and humans share the same ruach/breath (Ecc 3:19; Gen 7:22).
  4. At death, dust returns to earth and ruach returns to God (Ecc 12:7). Thoughts perish that same day (Ps 146:4).
  5. The dead know nothing, have no remembrance, no work, no knowledge, no wisdom (Ecc 9:5,10; Ps 6:5; 115:17).
  6. The soul (nephesh) can die (Ezek 18:4) and be destroyed (Matt 10:28).
  7. God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). Humans must seek it (Rom 2:7) and put it on at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53).
  8. Man was barred from the tree of life to prevent him from living forever (Gen 3:22-24).
  9. Death is called "sleep" by seven or more biblical authors.
  10. Being with the Lord is tied to the resurrection (1 Thess 4:16-17).

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied — requires adding something):

  1. That humans have an "immortal soul." The phrase never appears in Scripture. The claim requires overriding multiple explicit statements.
  2. That the ruach/spirit carries consciousness after death. Psalm 146:4 says thoughts perish when it departs.
  3. That a conscious intermediate state exists between death and resurrection. Paul ties being with the Lord to the resurrection, not to death.
  4. That nephesh distinguishes humans from animals. The same term applies to both.
  5. That Scripture prescribes a specific anthropological model (dichotomy or trichotomy). Terms are used flexibly, not technically.
  6. That Ecclesiastes' death statements are limited to an "earthly perspective." No verse states this limitation, and the "under the sun" phrase appears in Ecc 9:6, not in 9:5, 9:10, Ps 146:4, or Ps 6:5.
  7. That 2 Corinthians 5:8 describes a disembodied intermediate existence. Paul expressly says he does not desire to be "unclothed" (v.4).

docs.title: Section C: Death as Reversal of Creation
docs.text:
1. Construct the creation/death reversal from the text:

    • Creation (Gen 2:7): _ + = __
    • Death (Ecc 12:7): _ returns to + __ returns to _____
    • Result: The _ ___ ceases.

  2. Read Psalm 146:4 carefully. The Hebrew word for "thoughts" is eshtonot and the verb is abad (perish). What is the timing? Does the text say thoughts perish gradually, or "in that very day"?

docs.title: Section D: Immortality — Three Greek Words
docs.text:
1. Look up the following Greek words and their occurrences:

    • Athanasia (G110) — deathlessness: how many NT occurrences? Who does 1 Timothy 6:16 say possesses it?
    • Aphtharsia (G861) — incorruptibility: what does Romans 2:7 say about it? What does 2 Timothy 1:10 say?
    • Thnetos (G2349) — mortal: how does Romans 6:12 describe the human body? What does 1 Corinthians 15:53 say must happen to it?

  2. Read Genesis 3:22-24. If man already possessed an immortal soul, why would God need to bar him from the tree of life to prevent him from "living forever"?

docs.title: Section E: The Intermediate State — Competing Passages
docs.text:
1. Read 2 Corinthians 5:1-8. Paul says he desires to be "clothed upon" (v.4), not "unclothed." What does Paul want — to be disembodied, or to receive the resurrection body? Compare 2 Corinthians 5:4 with 1 Corinthians 15:54 — both use the phrase "mortality swallowed up."

  2. Read Philippians 1:23. Paul desires "to depart and be with Christ." Now read Philippians 3:11, 20-21. What does Paul say his hope is? Does Paul elsewhere describe being with Christ as happening at death or at resurrection?

  3. Read Luke 23:43. The Greek text has no punctuation. Two possible readings:

    • "I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise."
    • "I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise." Now read John 20:17, where Jesus says on Sunday morning: "I am not yet ascended to my Father." Which reading of Luke 23:43 is consistent with John 20:17?

  4. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17. When does Paul say believers will "ever be with the Lord" — at death, or at the resurrection?

docs.title: Section F: Anthropological Models
docs.text:
1. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:23 (spirit, soul, body) and Mark 12:30 (heart, soul, mind, strength). Does either passage prescribe a specific number of human components as doctrine, or are these terms used flexibly?

  2. Read Isaiah 26:9 and Luke 1:46-47. In these poetic passages, are "soul" and "spirit" used as synonyms, or as distinct components?

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise

Classify each claim below as Explicit (E), Necessary Implication (N), or Inference (I). For each inference, identify what must be added beyond what the text says.

docs.title: Study 1: What Is Man? — Answer Key
docs.text:
Biblical Anthropology and Human Nature

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we will learn to distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion — possibly a good one, possibly not — but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction matters more than you might think. Many beliefs people hold about the Bible are inferences, not explicit statements. Learning to tell the difference is one of the most important Bible study skills you can develop.

docs.title: Section A: How Was Man Created?
docs.text:
1. Read Genesis 2:7. What two things did God use to create man? What was the result?

God used (1) the dust of the ground and (2) the breath of life (neshamah). The result: "man became a living soul (nephesh chayyah)." The formula is: dust + breath of life = living soul.

"And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." — Genesis 2:7

2. Did man receive a soul, or did man become a soul? What does the text say?

Man became a living soul. The Hebrew word hayah means "became." The text does not say God placed a soul inside a body — it says the combination of dust and breath resulted in a living soul. The soul is what man is, not something he has.

3. Read Genesis 1:20-21, 24. What does God call the animals?

Animals are called nephesh chayyah — the exact same Hebrew phrase translated "living soul" for man in Genesis 2:7. English Bibles typically translate it as "living creature" for animals and "living soul" for humans, but the Hebrew is identical.

4. If animals and humans are both called nephesh chayyah, what makes humans different? Read Genesis 1:26-27.

What distinguishes humans is the image of God (imago Dei), not the possession of a soul. Both humans and animals are nephesh chayyah. Only humans are made "in the image of God."

"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him." — Genesis 1:27

docs.title: Section B: What Happens at Death?
docs.text:
5. Read Ecclesiastes 12:7. What happens to the body at death? What happens to the spirit?

The dust (body) returns to the earth, and the spirit (ruach) returns to God who gave it.

"Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." — Ecclesiastes 12:7

6. Compare Ecclesiastes 12:7 with Genesis 2:7. If creation was dust + breath = living soul, what is death?

Death is the reversal of creation. At creation: dust + breath = living soul. At death: dust returns to earth + spirit returns to God = the living soul ceases. What God assembled, death disassembles.

7. Read Psalm 146:4. When a person's breath leaves, what happens to their thoughts?

Their thoughts perish — "in that very day." The cessation of thought is immediate upon death.

"His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish." — Psalm 146:4

8. Read Ecclesiastes 9:5. What do the dead know?

Nothing. "The dead know not any thing."

"For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten." — Ecclesiastes 9:5

9. Read Ecclesiastes 9:10. What work, knowledge, or wisdom exists in the grave?

None. "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave."

10. Read Psalm 115:17 and Psalm 6:5. Do the dead praise God? Is there remembrance of God in death?

No. "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Ps 115:17). "In death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?" (Ps 6:5). Multiple authors — David, Solomon, Hezekiah (Isa 38:18-19) — all say the same thing.

docs.title: Section C: Can a Soul Die?
docs.text:
11. Read Ezekiel 18:4, 20. What happens to the soul that sins?

It dies. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die." The Hebrew word mut means to die. God directly says the nephesh (soul) is subject to death.

12. Read Matthew 10:28. What is God able to do to "both soul and body"?

Destroy them. "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell [gehenna]." The Greek word apollymi means to destroy. Jesus says the soul can be destroyed.

13. Read Leviticus 21:11 and Numbers 6:6. The Hebrew here literally says nephesh meth — "dead soul." What does this tell you about whether a soul can die?

The Bible itself uses the phrase "dead soul" (translated "dead body" in English). A soul is not inherently immortal — Scripture applies the word "dead" directly to nephesh.

docs.title: Section D: Who Has Immortality?
docs.text:
14. Read 1 Timothy 6:16. Who has immortality? Does the text say "God and humans" or "God only"?

God only. The Greek word monos means "alone" or "only." "Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto."

15. Read Romans 2:7. Must immortality be sought, or do we already have it?

It must be sought. "To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality [aphtharsia], eternal life."

16. Read 1 Corinthians 15:53-54. When do believers receive immortality — at death, or at the resurrection?

At the resurrection. "This mortal must put on immortality." The language "must put on" indicates we do not currently possess it.

17. Read Genesis 3:22-24. Why was Adam barred from the tree of life? What would it have given him?

God barred Adam "lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever." If man already had an immortal soul, barring him from the tree of life to prevent him from living forever would be meaningless.

docs.title: Section E: What Does the Bible Call Death?
docs.text:
18. Read John 11:11-14. What did Jesus call Lazarus' death? Then what did He clarify?

Jesus said "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth" — then clarified plainly: "Lazarus is dead." Jesus equated death with sleep.

19. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14 and Acts 7:60. What term did Paul and Luke use for death?

Both use the language of sleep. Paul: "them which are asleep." Luke: Stephen "fell asleep." At least seven biblical authors use this metaphor for death.

20. Read James 2:26. What is the body without the spirit?

Dead. "The body without the spirit is dead." The spirit is what animates the body — when it departs, the person is dead. The verse does not say the spirit is conscious after leaving; it says the body is dead without it.

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? — Answers
docs.text:
A. "Man became a living soul." - Explicit. Genesis 2:7 directly states this.

B. "The human soul is immortal and cannot die." - Inference. No verse says this. In fact, Ezekiel 18:4 says "the soul that sinneth, it shall die," and Matthew 10:28 says God can "destroy both soul and body." The claim of an immortal soul requires adding a concept that Scripture does not state — and overriding verses that say the opposite.

C. "The dead know not any thing." - Explicit. Ecclesiastes 9:5 directly states this.

D. "When a person dies, their spirit goes to heaven as a conscious being." - Inference. Ecclesiastes 12:7 says the spirit returns to God, but Psalm 146:4 says thoughts perish at death. No verse says the returning spirit is conscious. The claim requires adding the concept of consciousness to a text that does not mention it.

E. "God only hath immortality." - Explicit. 1 Timothy 6:16 directly states this.

docs.title: Study 2: Who Has Immortality? — Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Immortality Vocabulary, Word Studies, and Evidence Classification

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) — The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) — No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed — every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) — Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: The Greek Word for "Immortality" — Athanasia (G110)
docs.text:
1. Athanasia appears only 3 times in the entire New Testament. Look up all three occurrences: 1 Timothy 6:16, 1 Corinthians 15:53, and 1 Corinthians 15:54. In each case, who possesses athanasia?

  • 1 Timothy 6:16: God "only hath" athanasia — it is God's present, exclusive possession.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:53: "This mortal must put on" athanasia — believers will receive it at the resurrection. They do not have it now.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:54: "When this mortal shall have put on" athanasia — the same future event described as accomplished.

In all three occurrences, athanasia is either (a) God's present exclusive possession or (b) a future acquisition for believers at the resurrection. Zero occurrences apply it to humans as a present possession.

2. In 1 Timothy 6:16, the word monos modifies who has athanasia. The same word monos appears in 1 Timothy 1:17 and John 17:3. In those cases, does monos carry a qualified or absolute sense?

In 1 Timothy 1:17 ("the only wise God") and John 17:3 ("the only true God"), monos is understood absolutely — God is not "the only self-existent wise God" with room for other wise gods, nor "the only true God in a special sense." Monos marks exclusivity. The same word governing "hath immortality" in 1 Timothy 6:16 should be read with the same absolute force: God alone has it.

3. In 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, the verb is enduo. Paul uses the same verb elsewhere. In every case, does enduo describe acquiring something one already has?

No. Enduo always describes putting on something not currently possessed or worn: - Romans 13:14: "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ" — from a state of not being clothed with Christ. - Galatians 3:27: "Put on Christ" — at baptism, a new state. - Ephesians 6:11: "Put on the whole armour of God" — from unarmed to armed. - Colossians 3:10: "Put on the new man" — from old to new.

The mortal "putting on" immortality describes a transition from not having it to having it — not the reaffirmation of something already possessed.

docs.title: Section B: Incorruptibility — Aphtharsia (G861) and Aphthartos (G862)
docs.text:
4. Look up all 8 NT occurrences of aphtharsia. In how many is it described as a present human possession?

  • Romans 2:7: Must be sought — not a present possession.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:42: The body is raised in incorruption — future event.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:50: Corruption cannot inherit incorruption — the two are mutually exclusive states.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:53: The corruptible must put on incorruption — future transformation.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:54: "When this corruptible shall have put on" incorruption — future event.
  • Ephesians 6:24: Grace to those who love Christ "in sincerity/incorruption" — modifies the love, not the person's nature.
  • 2 Timothy 1:10: Christ brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel — revealed, not inherent.
  • Titus 2:7: "In doctrine showing incorruptness" — integrity of teaching.

Zero occurrences describe aphtharsia as an inherent present human possession. It is consistently something to seek, something that will be put on, or something Christ revealed.

5. Look up all 7 NT occurrences of aphthartos. To whom or what is it applied? Is it ever applied to the human soul?

  • Romans 1:23: Describes God — "the uncorruptible God."
  • 1 Corinthians 9:25: An "incorruptible crown" — the believer's future reward.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:52: "The dead shall be raised incorruptible" — future transformation.
  • 1 Timothy 1:17: Describes God — "immortal, invisible."
  • 1 Peter 1:4: An "incorruptible inheritance" reserved in heaven — a future possession.
  • 1 Peter 1:23: "Incorruptible seed" — the word of God, not the human soul.
  • 1 Peter 3:4: "That which is not corruptible" — the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit (describing a quality of character, not asserting ontological immortality of the soul).

Aphthartos is never applied to the human soul as an inherent attribute. It describes God (2x), future rewards/inheritance (2x), the resurrection state (1x), the word of God (1x), and a quality of spirit (1x).

6. In Romans 1:23, aphthartos describes God and phthartos describes man — in the same verse. What interpretive move is required to maintain that humans possess an incorruptible component?

One must argue that Paul is describing only the body as corruptible while an unstated, unmentioned soul is incorruptible. This requires adding a body/soul distinction that Paul does not make in the verse. Paul's contrast is between God and man — not between God and the human body. The interpretive move is an inference that imports a framework (body-soul dualism) not present in the text.

docs.title: Section C: Mortality — Thnetos (G2349) and Corruption — Phthora (G5356)
docs.text:
7. Look up all 6 NT occurrences of thnetos. In each passage, what is described as mortal?

  • Romans 6:12: "Your mortal body (soma)."
  • Romans 8:11: "Your mortal bodies."
  • 2 Corinthians 4:11: "Our mortal flesh (sarx)."
  • 2 Corinthians 5:4: "Mortality" (to thneton) — used absolutely, no noun specified.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:53: "This mortal" (touto to thneton) — used absolutely.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:54: "This mortal" — used absolutely.

In three passages, thnetos modifies "body" or "flesh." In three passages, it is used absolutely — "this mortal" or "mortality" — without restricting the referent to the body alone.

8. In 1 Corinthians 15:53, Paul writes "this mortal" without the noun "body." Compare with Romans 6:12 where he writes "your mortal body." What is the significance?

When Paul wants to specify the body, he does so explicitly (Rom 6:12: "mortal body"; Rom 8:11: "mortal bodies"; 2 Cor 4:11: "mortal flesh"). In 1 Corinthians 15:53, he uses the absolute form — "this mortal" (touto to thneton) — without specifying "body." The absolute form describes the whole mortal entity, not a specific part. Paul's own usage shows he is capable of restricting the referent to the body when he intends to. Here he does not.

9. Look up key occurrences of phthora. In Galatians 6:8, what is the alternative to "reaping corruption"?

"He that soweth to the flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption (phthora); but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting." — Galatians 6:8

The alternative to corruption is "life everlasting." The contrast is exhaustive and mutually exclusive — corruption or everlasting life. There is no third option of "corruption plus continued conscious existence." This parallels Romans 6:23 (death vs. eternal life) and John 3:16 (perish vs. everlasting life).

10. Read 2 Peter 2:12. How many destruction-related words does Peter use? What does the comparison to animals suggest?

Peter uses three destruction terms in a single verse: phtheiro ("destroyed"), kataphtheiro ("utterly perish"), and phthora ("corruption"). He compares false teachers to "natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed." The comparison to animals — whose destruction is physical and final — suggests the same kind of destruction: cessation, not ongoing conscious torment.

docs.title: Section D: The Conditional Structure of Eternal Life
docs.text:
11. Read John 3:16, 3:36, 5:40, 6:53, 10:28, and 1 John 5:11-12. What is the common condition? What happens without it?

The common condition is relationship with Christ — believing in him, coming to him, having him. Without it: - John 3:16: the person perishes (apollymi). - John 3:36: "shall not see life." - John 5:40: they lack life — "that ye might have life" (implying they do not). - John 6:53: "ye have no life in you." - John 10:28: perishing is the negated alternative — "they shall never perish" (implying perishing is the default without Christ). - 1 John 5:12: "he that hath not the Son of God hath not life."

Six explicit statements from two authors (Jesus and John) present the same pattern: life is through Christ; without Christ, the person does not have life. None of these texts describes the alternative as continued conscious existence.

12. Read Romans 6:23 and Galatians 6:8 side by side. List both pairs of outcomes.

  • Romans 6:23: death vs. eternal life.
  • Galatians 6:8: corruption vs. everlasting life.

In neither text is a third option mentioned. The contrasts are exhaustive: one or the other. Both pairs present the same structure — the outcome of sin is cessation/decay; the gift of God through Christ is life.

13. Read 2 Thessalonians 1:9. Does the text describe unending conscious existence, or unending destruction?

The text says "everlasting destruction" (olethros aionios). The noun olethros means ruin or destruction. The adjective aionios modifies the destruction, not the consciousness. The text does not say "everlasting conscious torment" or "everlasting punishing" — it says "everlasting destruction." (This passage receives more detailed study in a later etc6 study.)

14. Read John 5:26. What does this suggest about whether humans have life inherently?

The Father "hath life in himself" and "hath given to the Son to have life in himself." The phrase "life in himself" describes self-existent life — life that is not derived from another source. Even the Son receives this by the Father's gift. If self-existent life belongs to God and is given to Christ by special act, there is no basis for claiming humans possess it by nature.

docs.title: Section E: The Absence of "Immortal Soul"
docs.text:
15. Search a concordance for "immortal soul." How many occurrences exist?

Zero. The phrase "immortal soul" does not appear anywhere in the Old or New Testament. No verse states "the soul is immortal," "the soul cannot die," or "the soul lives forever." The concept must be constructed entirely from inference — and the inferences required conflict with verses that directly state the soul can die (Ezek 18:4) and be destroyed (Matt 10:28).

16. Read Ezekiel 18:4 and Matthew 10:28. What must be done to "die" and "destroy" to maintain the immortal-soul claim?

  • Ezekiel 18:4: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" — mut in Hebrew. To maintain that the soul is immortal, "die" must be redefined to mean something other than death (typically "spiritual death" or "separation from God").
  • Matthew 10:28: "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" — apollymi in Greek. To maintain the soul is indestructible, "destroy" must be redefined to mean something other than destruction (typically "ruin without cessation" or "make miserable").

Both redefinitions require overriding the plain lexical meaning of the words. This is why the claim of an immortal soul is classified as I-D (counter-evidence inference) — it requires the text to mean something other than what it says.

17. Read Psalm 49:7-9, 12, 15, 20. How does the psalmist describe the fate of "man that is in honour"?

The psalmist says "man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts that perish" (v.12, 20). The comparison to animals that perish equates the human fate with animal death. However, the psalmist also states an exception: "But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave" (v.15). Redemption from death is divine intervention, not inherent survival. The natural state of man is to perish like the beasts; God's redemption is what saves the soul from that fate.

docs.title: Section F: Counter-Arguments and Competing Readings
docs.text:
18. "God only hath immortality" means God alone has self-existent immortality — leaving room for humans to have derived immortality. Does the text make this distinction?

No. 1 Timothy 6:16 says "who only (monos) hath immortality (athanasia)." The text does not say "who only hath self-existent immortality" or "who only hath underived immortality." The derived/underived distinction is not present in the passage. It must be imported from an external theological framework. This is classified as an I-C inference (compatible external) — it does not directly override the text, but it qualifies it by adding a distinction the text does not make.

19. Does Paul name an immortal counterpart to the mortal body?

No. Paul calls the body mortal (Rom 6:12; 8:11; 2 Cor 4:11), and he says "this mortal must put on immortality" (1 Cor 15:53). But he never states that while the body is mortal, the soul or spirit is immortal. The claim that thnetos applies only to the body while the soul is exempt requires adding information Paul never provides. Paul never names an immortal counterpart to the mortal body anywhere in his letters.

20. Can John's "life" concept be separated from Paul's "immortality" concept?

John does use "has eternal life" in the present tense (John 3:36; 5:24; 6:47), indicating a present dimension to zoe aionios. However, Jesus also connects eternal life to the future resurrection repeatedly: "I will raise him up at the last day" (John 6:40, 44, 54). The attempt to separate John's "life" concept from Paul's "immortality" concept — so that "hath not life" does not bear on the immortality question — requires imposing a hermeneutical framework that the text does not prescribe. Jesus himself ties eternal life to both the present relationship and the future resurrection.

21. Read Luke 20:37-38. Is Jesus arguing for the resurrection, or for a conscious intermediate state?

Jesus is arguing for the resurrection. His explicit point is stated in v.37: "Now that the dead ARE RAISED, even Moses shewed at the bush." The statement "all live unto him" (v.38) functions as the theological ground for why God will raise them — God regards them as living because their resurrection is certain. The passage is not about the patriarchs' current conscious state; it is about whether the dead will be raised. Reading it as proof of present consciousness requires importing a framework Jesus does not invoke.

docs.title: Section G: Cross-Study Connections
docs.text:
22. How does the immortality word study reinforce or challenge the Study 1 findings?

It reinforces them completely. Study 1 found that nephesh (soul) can die (Ezek 18:4), be destroyed (Matt 10:28), and applies to both animals and humans. Study 2 adds that all 18 NT occurrences of immortality vocabulary (athanasia, aphtharsia, aphthartos) describe either God's nature or the future resurrection state — zero describe the human soul as presently immortal. The soul's mortality (Study 1) is confirmed by the total absence of immortality vocabulary applied to it (Study 2).

23. Read 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and Romans 5:12, 17. How did death enter?

"By man came death" (1 Cor 15:21). "By one man's offence death reigned" (Rom 5:17). "By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin" (Rom 5:12). Death is the result of sin, entering through Adam. Before sin, man had access to the tree of life (Gen 2:9; 3:22). After sin, he was barred from it. The human condition before the Fall included access to life; after the Fall, death reigns. This confirms that mortality is the post-Fall human condition, not the original design.

24. Read Acts 17:18, 32. Why would the resurrection provoke mockery if Greek culture accepted the immortality of the soul?

The Greek philosophers at Athens already accepted that the soul survived death — Platonic immortality of the soul was common in Hellenistic thought. Yet when Paul preached the resurrection, they mocked him (Acts 17:32). If the apostolic message had been "the soul is immortal and goes to heaven at death," it would have been unremarkable to Greek ears. The resurrection provoked mockery precisely because it was a different message — life after death through bodily resurrection, not through inherent soul immortality. This confirms that the apostolic message was resurrection-centered, not inherent-immortality-centered.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise — Answers
docs.text:
1. "God only hath immortality" (1 Tim 6:16) - Explicit (E). Paul directly states this in the text.

2. "Man does not inherently possess immortality." - Necessary Implication (N). God only has immortality (1 Tim 6:16 — E). Immortality must be sought (Rom 2:7 — E). It must be put on at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53 — E). Three explicit statements converge: "only" means exclusively; "seek" means pursue what is not yet held; "must put on" means does not currently have. Every reader, regardless of theological position, must acknowledge what these words mean. The conclusion is unavoidable.

3. "The human soul is inherently immortal and survives death as a conscious entity." - Inference (I-D: Counter-Evidence External). No verse states this. It requires: - Adding the concept "immortal soul" (absent from Scripture). - Redefining "only" in 1 Tim 6:16 to mean "only in a special sense." - Redefining "die" in Ezek 18:4 to mean something other than death. - Redefining "destroy" in Matt 10:28 to mean something other than destruction. - Importing a Platonic philosophical framework not found in Scripture. - This is the weakest type of inference because it requires overriding what the text explicitly states.

4. "This mortal must put on immortality" (1 Cor 15:53) - Explicit (E). Paul directly states this in the text.

5. "Immortality is acquired at the resurrection, not before." - Necessary Implication (N). 1 Cor 15:52: "The dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed" — at "the last trump." 1 Cor 15:53-54: "This mortal must put on immortality" — in the same resurrection context. Luke 20:36: The resurrected "can die no more" (ouketi — "no longer") — implying they previously could die. The timing is explicitly placed at the resurrection. No interpretation is needed.

6. "'God only hath immortality' means only self-existent immortality; humans may still possess a derived form." - Inference (I-C: Compatible External). The text does not say "self-existent immortality" — it says "immortality." The derived/underived distinction is not present in the passage. It must be imported from an external theological framework. It is I-C rather than I-D because it qualifies the text rather than directly overriding it — but it still adds a concept the text does not contain.

7. "The wages of sin is death; the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom 6:23) - Explicit (E). Paul directly states this in the text.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said — Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. God alone (monos) possesses immortality (athanasia) (1 Tim 6:16).
  2. God is incorruptible (aphthartos); man is corruptible (phthartos) — explicitly contrasted in the same verse (Rom 1:23).
  3. The human body/flesh is mortal (thnetos) (Rom 6:12; 8:11; 2 Cor 4:11; 5:4).
  4. Mortals must "put on" immortality (athanasia) at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54).
  5. Immortality (aphtharsia) must be sought (Rom 2:7) and was brought to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10).
  6. Eternal life is a gift (Rom 6:23), a promise (Tit 1:2; 1 John 2:25), conditional on relationship with Christ (1 John 5:11-12; John 3:16, 36).
  7. Man does not inherently possess immortality (N — from 1 Tim 6:16 + Rom 2:7 + 1 Cor 15:53).
  8. The alternatives to eternal life are perishing (John 3:16), death (Rom 6:23), corruption (Gal 6:8), destruction (2 Thess 1:9), and absence of life (John 3:36; 6:53; 1 John 5:12). (Note: this is an I-A inference — it systematizes what individual texts say into a composite claim. Each individual text is explicit, but the comprehensive statement requires combining them.)

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied — requires adding something):

  1. It cannot be said that Scripture teaches humans have an "immortal soul." The phrase does not appear in the Bible. No NT passage applies athanasia, aphtharsia, or aphthartos to the human soul as an inherent, present possession. The claim requires overriding Ezekiel 18:4, Matthew 10:28, and 1 Timothy 6:16.
  2. It cannot be said that 1 Timothy 6:16 means only "self-existent" immortality. The text does not qualify monos. The derived/underived distinction must be imported from outside.
  3. It cannot be said that "mortal" applies only to the body while the soul is immortal. Paul never names an immortal counterpart to the mortal body. In 1 Cor 15:53, "this mortal" is used absolutely.
  4. It cannot be said that eternal life is an inherent human possession. Every passage presents it as a gift, promise, hope, or something to seek — never as something humans possess by nature.
  5. It cannot be said that Luke 20:38 describes the patriarchs as presently conscious. Jesus' argument is for the resurrection (v.37), not for a conscious intermediate state.
  6. It cannot be said that any NT passage applies immortality vocabulary to the human soul as an inherent, present possession. All 18 NT occurrences of athanasia, aphtharsia, and aphthartos describe either God's nature, the future resurrection state, spiritual/heavenly qualities, or something to seek. Zero describe the human soul as presently immortal.

docs.title: Study 2: Who Has Immortality? — Advanced Study
docs.text:
Immortality Vocabulary, Word Studies, and Evidence Classification

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) — The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) — No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed — every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) — Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: The Greek Word for "Immortality" — Athanasia (G110)
docs.text:
1. Athanasia appears only 3 times in the entire New Testament. Look up all three occurrences: 1 Timothy 6:16, 1 Corinthians 15:53, and 1 Corinthians 15:54. In each case, who possesses athanasia — God, humans presently, or humans at a future event?

  2. In 1 Timothy 6:16, the word monos ("only, alone") modifies who has athanasia. The same word monos appears in 1 Timothy 1:17 ("the only wise God") and John 17:3 ("the only true God"). In those cases, does monos carry a qualified or absolute sense? What does this tell you about "who only hath immortality"?

  3. In 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, the verb is enduo ("to put on, to clothe oneself with"). Paul uses the same verb in Romans 13:14 ("put on the Lord Jesus Christ"), Galatians 3:27 ("put on Christ"), and Colossians 3:10 ("put on the new man"). In every case, does enduo describe acquiring something one already has, or putting on something new?

docs.title: Section B: Incorruptibility — Aphtharsia (G861) and Aphthartos (G862)
docs.text:
1. Look up all 8 NT occurrences of aphtharsia (incorruptibility/immortality): Romans 2:7; 1 Corinthians 15:42, 50, 53, 54; Ephesians 6:24; 2 Timothy 1:10; Titus 2:7. In how many of these is aphtharsia described as a present human possession?

  2. Look up all 7 NT occurrences of aphthartos (incorruptible/immortal): Romans 1:23; 1 Corinthians 9:25; 15:52; 1 Timothy 1:17; 1 Peter 1:4, 23; 3:4. To whom or what is aphthartos applied in each case? Is it ever applied to the human soul?

  3. In Romans 1:23, aphthartos describes God and phthartos describes man — in the same verse. What interpretive move is required to maintain that humans possess an incorruptible component despite this explicit contrast?

docs.title: Section C: Mortality — Thnetos (G2349) and Corruption — Phthora (G5356)
docs.text:
1. Look up all 6 NT occurrences of thnetos (mortal): Romans 6:12; 8:11; 1 Corinthians 15:53, 54; 2 Corinthians 4:11; 5:4. In each passage, what is described as mortal — the body, the flesh, or the person?

  2. In 1 Corinthians 15:53, Paul writes "this mortal" (touto to thneton) — the word is used absolutely, without the noun "body." Compare this with Romans 6:12 where he writes "your mortal body" (to thneton soma). What is the significance of Paul using the absolute form in 1 Corinthians 15:53?

  3. Look up key occurrences of phthora (corruption/decay): 1 Corinthians 15:42, 50; Galatians 6:8; 2 Peter 1:4; 2:12. In Galatians 6:8, what is the alternative to "reaping corruption"? What does this suggest about what corruption means in contrast to everlasting life?

  4. Read 2 Peter 2:12. Peter compares false teachers to "natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed," and says they "shall utterly perish in their own corruption (phthora)." How many destruction-related words does Peter use in this single verse? What does the comparison to animals suggest about the nature of their destruction?

docs.title: Section D: The Conditional Structure of Eternal Life
docs.text:
1. Read the following passages and note the condition stated in each: John 3:16, John 3:36, John 5:40, John 6:53, John 10:28, 1 John 5:11-12. What is the common condition across all six texts? What happens to those who do not meet it?

  2. Read Romans 6:23 and Galatians 6:8 side by side. Each presents two mutually exclusive outcomes. List both pairs of outcomes. In either text, is a third option (conscious existence without life/incorruption) mentioned?

  3. Read 2 Thessalonians 1:9. The wicked are "punished with everlasting destruction (olethros aionios)." The noun olethros means ruin or destruction. Does the text describe unending conscious existence, or unending destruction?

  4. Read John 5:26. The Father "hath life in himself" and "hath given to the Son to have life in himself." If God has life inherently ("in himself"), what does this suggest about whether humans have life inherently?

docs.title: Section E: The Absence of "Immortal Soul"
docs.text:
1. Search a concordance for the phrase "immortal soul." How many occurrences exist in the Old or New Testament?

  2. Read Ezekiel 18:4 and Matthew 10:28. The first says the soul (nephesh) that sins shall die. The second says God can destroy (apollymi) both soul (psyche) and body in gehenna. If the soul is inherently immortal, what must be done to the plain meaning of "die" and "destroy" in these verses?

  3. Read Psalm 49:7-9, 12, 15, 20. How does the psalmist describe the fate of "man that is in honour"? What comparison does he draw? What exception does he state?

docs.title: Section F: Counter-Arguments and Competing Readings
docs.text:
1. Some argue that "God only hath immortality" (1 Tim 6:16) means God alone has self-existent, underived immortality — leaving room for humans to have a derived form. Does the text make this distinction? What must be added to arrive at this reading?

  2. Some argue that thnetos ("mortal") in Paul applies only to the body, not to the soul or spirit, which is exempt from mortality. Examine 1 Corinthians 15:53 ("this mortal") and 2 Corinthians 5:4 ("mortality"). Does Paul name an immortal counterpart to the mortal body anywhere in his letters?

  3. Some argue that the conditional-life passages in John (3:16, 3:36, 6:53, etc.) refer to a present quality of spiritual life, not to future immortality. Read John 6:39-40, 44, 54 — does Jesus connect "eternal life" with the future resurrection? Can John's "life" concept be separated from Paul's "immortality" concept?

  4. Read Luke 20:37-38. Jesus says "He is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him." Some read this as proving the patriarchs are presently conscious. But what is Jesus arguing for in v.37 — the resurrection, or a conscious intermediate state? What is the function of "all live unto him" in his argument?

docs.title: Section G: Cross-Study Connections
docs.text:
1. In Study 1, you examined nephesh (soul) and found that it can die (Ezek 18:4), be destroyed (Matt 10:28), and is applied to both animals and humans. How does the immortality word study in this study reinforce or challenge those findings?

  2. Read 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and Romans 5:12, 17. How did death enter the human race? If death is the result of sin entering through Adam, was the human condition before the Fall the same as after?

  3. Read Acts 17:18, 32. What was the reaction of the Greek philosophers when Paul preached the resurrection? If Greek culture already accepted the immortality of the soul, why would the resurrection provoke mockery? What does this tell you about whether the apostolic message was about inherent immortality or resurrection?

For inferences, identify the subtype: - I-A: Evidence-extending — uses only the text's own words and concepts, systematized into a broader claim - I-B: Competing evidence — biblical texts on both sides; resolved by Scripture-interprets-Scripture - I-C: Compatible external — adds concepts the text doesn't contain but doesn't contradict it - I-D: Counter-evidence — requires overriding or redefining what the text explicitly says

docs.title: Study 2: Who Has Immortality? — Answer Key
docs.text:
Immortality, Mortality, and Eternal Life in Scripture

Recall from Study 1 the difference between Explicit (the Bible directly says it) and Inference (someone concludes it from the Bible, but no verse states it). Keep that distinction in mind as you work through this study.

docs.title: Section A: Who Possesses Immortality?
docs.text:
1. Read 1 Timothy 6:15-16. Who does Paul say has immortality? Does he say "God and humans" or "God only"?

God only. The Greek word monos means "alone, only." Paul ascribes exclusive attributes to God: "the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; who only hath immortality." The word monos marks exclusivity without qualification — just as "the only true God" (John 17:3) does not mean "true in a special sense."

"Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto." — 1 Timothy 6:16

2. Read 1 Timothy 1:17. What four attributes does Paul give to God? Which one relates to our study?

Paul calls God "the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God." The word "immortal" translates aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible. God's nature is incorruptibility. This is presented as a divine attribute, not a shared human quality.

"Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever." — 1 Timothy 1:17

3. Read Romans 1:23. Paul contrasts "the uncorruptible God" with "corruptible man." According to this verse, which word describes the human condition — corruptible or uncorruptible?

Corruptible. Paul places God and humans on opposite sides of the divide: God is aphthartos (uncorruptible/incorruptible); man is phthartos (corruptible). The contrast is explicit and in the same verse. Man is not described as sharing God's incorruptible nature.

"And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man." — Romans 1:23

4. Read 2 Timothy 1:10. What did Christ bring "to light through the gospel"? If immortality needed to be brought to light, was it already in human possession?

Christ "abolished death, and brought life and immortality (aphtharsia) to light through the gospel." If immortality were already an inherent human possession, there would be nothing to bring to light. The language indicates immortality was revealed and made available through the gospel — not something humans already had.

"Our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel." — 2 Timothy 1:10

docs.title: Section B: Is the Human Body Mortal or Immortal?
docs.text:
5. Read Romans 6:12. What word does Paul use to describe the human body?

"Mortal." The Greek word thnetos (G2349) means "subject to death." Paul says "your mortal body" — directly describing the human body as mortal.

6. Read Romans 8:11. What does Paul say God will do with believers' "mortal bodies"? Is this a present reality or a future promise?

God "shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit." The verb is future — this is a promise of future transformation, not a present reality. The body is mortal now; God will make it alive in the future.

"He that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you." — Romans 8:11

7. Read 2 Corinthians 4:11. What phrase does Paul use for human flesh?

"Mortal flesh" (thnetos sarx). Paul identifies human flesh as mortal — subject to death.

8. Read 2 Corinthians 5:4. What does Paul want to happen to "mortality"?

Paul desires "that mortality might be swallowed up of life." He does not want to be "unclothed" (disembodied) but "clothed upon" — to receive the resurrection body so that mortality is replaced by life. This is the same event described in 1 Corinthians 15:54.

docs.title: Section C: When Is Immortality Received?
docs.text:
9. Read 1 Corinthians 15:53-54. What must "this mortal" put on? When does this happen — now, at death, or at the resurrection?

"This mortal must put on immortality." The context (1 Cor 15:51-52) places this at the resurrection: "the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed." The language "must put on" indicates the mortal does not currently possess immortality — it is something acquired at the resurrection.

"For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." — 1 Corinthians 15:53

10. Read 1 Corinthians 15:52. How does Paul describe the dead after they are raised?

"The dead shall be raised incorruptible" (aphthartos). They are not incorruptible now — they become incorruptible when raised. The transformation happens at the resurrection.

11. Read Luke 20:35-36. Those counted worthy of the resurrection "can die no more." What does this imply about their condition before the resurrection?

The word "no more" (Greek ouketi — "no longer") implies they previously could die. If they were already immortal, saying they "can die no more" would be redundant. The inability to die is a new condition received at the resurrection, not a pre-existing one.

"Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." — Luke 20:36

12. Read Romans 2:7. Is immortality something humans already possess, or something they must seek?

Something they must seek. "To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life." One does not seek what one already possesses.

"To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life." — Romans 2:7

docs.title: Section D: Eternal Life — Gift or Possession?
docs.text:
13. Read Romans 6:23. What is the "gift of God"? What is the alternative?

The gift of God is "eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." The alternative is death: "the wages of sin is death." The contrast is death versus eternal life. Eternal life is a gift, not an inherent possession.

"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." — Romans 6:23

14. Read 1 John 5:11-12. Where is eternal life located? What does the person who does not have the Son possess?

Eternal life is "in his Son" — it resides in Christ. "He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life." The person without Christ does not have life. The text does not say they have a lesser form of life or an immortal existence in torment — it says they do not have life.

"And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life." — 1 John 5:11-12

15. Read John 3:16. What are the two possible outcomes presented? What is the alternative to everlasting life?

The two outcomes are everlasting life or perishing. "Whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." The alternative to everlasting life is not eternal conscious existence in another location — the text says the alternative is perishing.

"For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." — John 3:16

16. Read John 3:36. What does the text say about the person who does not believe?

"He that believeth not the Son shall not see life." Not "shall see a worse form of life" — shall not see life at all.

"He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life." — John 3:36

17. Read Genesis 3:22-24. Why did God bar Adam from the tree of life? What would it have given him?

God barred Adam "lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever." If Adam already possessed an immortal soul that could never die, this action would be meaningless — he would live forever regardless. God's action only makes sense if man is wholly mortal and the tree of life was the means by which he could have sustained life indefinitely.

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? — Answers
docs.text:
A. "God only hath immortality." - Explicit. 1 Timothy 6:16 directly states this.

B. "The human soul is inherently immortal." - Inference. No verse in the Bible says this. No verse uses the phrase "immortal soul." In fact, Ezekiel 18:4 says "the soul that sinneth, it shall die," and Matthew 10:28 says God can "destroy both soul and body." The claim of an inherently immortal soul requires adding a concept the text does not contain and overriding verses that say the opposite.

C. "This mortal must put on immortality." - Explicit. 1 Corinthians 15:53 directly states this.

D. "He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life." - Explicit. 1 John 5:12 directly states this.

E. "All humans are born with an immortal component that can never cease to exist." - Inference. No verse states this. All 18 NT occurrences of immortality vocabulary (athanasia, aphtharsia, aphthartos) describe either God's nature or the future resurrection state. Zero occurrences describe any part of the human being as presently immortal. The claim requires importing a concept from outside Scripture.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... God only has immortality (1 Tim 6:16) All humans possess immortality Man is corruptible; God is uncorruptible (Rom 1:23) Humans have an incorruptible soul This mortal must put on immortality (1 Cor 15:53) Humans already have immortality Immortality must be sought (Rom 2:7) Immortality is inherent The wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23) The wages of sin is eternal torment He that hath not the Son hath not life (1 John 5:12) Everyone has life forever regardless Man was barred from the tree of life lest he live forever (Gen 3:22-24) Man already has eternal existence
