Sheol (H7585) Hebrew ~67 OT All the dead (righteous and wicked) No work, knowledge, wisdom; silence; darkness; rest No — deliverance = resurrection (Hos 13:14) Hades (G86) Greek 11 NT Equivalent to sheol Same as sheol; paired with death No — cast into lake of fire (Rev 20:14) Gehenna (G1067) Greek 12 NT The wicked (eschatological) Destruction (apollumi); fire acting on corpses (Isa 66:24) Final destruction, not ongoing torment Tartaroo (G5020) Greek 1 NT Fallen angels only Chains of darkness; temporary imprisonment No — "reserved unto judgment" (2 Pet 2:4)

docs.title: Study 5: Four "Hell" Words
docs.text:
Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, Tartaroo — What Do They Actually Mean?

A Reminder from Study 1

We are learning to distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion that may or may not be correct — but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction becomes especially important when we examine what the Bible actually says about "hell" — because the English word hides four different words with different meanings.

docs.title: Section A: Sheol — The Old Testament Word
docs.text:
1. The Hebrew word sheol (H7585) appears about 67 times in the OT. The KJV translates it "grave" 31 times and "hell" 27 times. If the same word is translated both ways, what does that tell you about whether sheol inherently means "a place of torment"?

  2. Read Genesis 37:35. Jacob expects to go to sheol mourning for Joseph. Read Psalm 16:10. David trusts God will not leave his soul in sheol. Read Psalm 9:17. The wicked are turned into sheol. If both righteous and wicked go to sheol, is it a punishment venue for the wicked only?

  3. Read Ecclesiastes 9:10. What does this verse say exists in sheol — work, knowledge, wisdom?

  4. Read Psalm 6:5 and Psalm 115:17. Is there remembrance of God in death? Do the dead praise the LORD?

  5. Read Job 10:21-22 and Job 17:13-16. How does Job describe sheol? What imagery does he use — light and activity, or darkness and rest?

docs.title: Section B: Hades — The New Testament Equivalent
docs.text:
1. Read Acts 2:27, 31. Peter quotes Psalm 16:10, which uses sheol in Hebrew. What Greek word does Peter use in its place? What does this tell you about the relationship between the two words?

  2. Read Revelation 20:13-14. What happens to death and hades? Are they permanent or temporary?

  3. Read Revelation 1:18. Who holds the keys of hades and death? What does this suggest about hades — is it a realm under Satan's control, or under Christ's authority?

  4. Read 1 Corinthians 15:55 (compare Hosea 13:14). Paul pairs hades with death in a celebration of victory. What is the "sting" and "victory" that are overcome?

docs.title: Section C: Gehenna — The Place of Destruction
docs.text:
1. Read Joshua 15:8 and 2 Kings 23:10. Gehenna comes from ge-Hinnom (Valley of Hinnom). What happened in this valley historically?

  2. Read Jeremiah 7:31-32 and Jeremiah 19:6. What did Jeremiah rename this valley? What did he say would happen there — ongoing torment or slaughter and burial?

  3. Read Matthew 10:28. What does Jesus say God is able to do to "both soul and body" in gehenna? Does He use a word meaning "torment" or "destroy"?

  4. Read Mark 9:43-48. Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24. Now read Isaiah 66:24 itself. The "worm" and "fire" act on what — living people or "carcases" (dead bodies)?

  5. Read Luke 12:5. What does God do first (kill), and then what does He have power to do (cast into gehenna)? What is the sequence?

docs.title: Section D: Tartaroo — Angels Only
docs.text:
1. Read 2 Peter 2:4. Who is cast into tartaroo — humans or angels? Is this a permanent destination or a temporary holding ("reserved unto judgment")?

  2. Read Jude 1:6. What parallel does Jude give for the same event? Are the angels in their final state or waiting for something?

docs.title: Section E: Comparing the Four Words
docs.text:
1. Based on what you have read: (a) Who goes to sheol/hades — only the wicked, or everyone? (b) What vocabulary does Jesus use for gehenna — "torment" or "destroy"? (c) Who is tartaroo applied to — humans or angels?

  2. The KJV translates all four words as "hell." If a reader only has the English KJV, can they tell these words apart? What problem does this create?

docs.title: Explicit or Inference?
docs.text:
For each statement below, decide: Does the Bible explicitly say this, or is it an inference?

A. "Both righteous and wicked go to sheol." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

B. "In sheol there is no work, no knowledge, no wisdom." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

C. "Gehenna is a place of eternal conscious torment for all the wicked." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

D. "God is able to destroy both soul and body in gehenna." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

E. "The four 'hell' words all describe the same concept — a place of eternal torment." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

docs.title: Study 6: Destruction Vocabulary -- Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Hebrew and Greek Word Studies on the Fate of the Wicked

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Hebrew Destruction Words -- Abad (H6) and Shamad (H8045)
docs.text:
1. Abad (H6) in Psalm 37:20, 68:2, 73:27, 92:9, and Job 20:7.

  • Psalm 37:20: "The wicked shall perish (abad), and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away." Subject: the wicked.
  • Psalm 68:2: "As wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish (abad) at the presence of God." Subject: the wicked.
  • Psalm 73:27: "They that are far from thee shall perish (abad)." Subject: those far from God.
  • Psalm 92:9: "Thine enemies shall perish (abad); all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered." Subject: God's enemies.
  • Job 20:7: "He shall perish (abad) for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where is he?" Subject: the wicked man. Note: "perish for ever" -- permanent destruction.

Collectively, these verses say the wicked will perish, and they use imagery of complete disappearance: consumed into smoke, melted like wax, vanished so that people ask "Where is he?" The word abad consistently describes cessation, not ongoing torment.

2. Shamad (H8045) in Psalm 145:20, 37:38, 92:7, and Isaiah 13:9.

  • Psalm 145:20: "The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy (shamad)." The antithetical parallel is preserve vs. destroy -- continued existence vs. cessation.
  • Psalm 37:38: "The transgressors shall be destroyed (shamad) together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off."
  • Psalm 92:7: "They shall be destroyed (shamad) for ever." Permanent destruction.
  • Isaiah 13:9: "He shall destroy (shamad) the sinners thereof out of it." The day of the LORD brings destruction.

Shamad means "to destroy utterly, to exterminate." In Psalm 145:20, the antithetical parallelism is critical: preserve and shamad are opposites. If shamad meant "ongoing existence in a ruined state," it would not be the opposite of "preserve."

3. LXX translation of abad as apollymi 141 times.

Pre-Christian Jewish translators working on the Septuagint chose apollymi to render abad 141 times -- the overwhelmingly dominant mapping. This establishes a verified lexical chain: when the NT authors used apollymi for the fate of the wicked (Matt 10:28; John 3:16; Luke 13:3; etc.), they were using the same word that the Greek-speaking Jewish world understood as the equivalent of abad. The semantic weight of abad (to perish, to be destroyed) carries directly into the NT through this translation tradition. This is not an inference -- it is an observable textual fact (#4a: SIS-verified cross-testament connection).

4. Isaiah 26:14 -- both shamad and abad together.

"They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed (shamad) them, and made all their memory to perish (abad)."

The verse uses both key destruction words and adds: (1) they shall not live, (2) they shall not rise, (3) their memory perishes. This is triple reinforcement of permanent cessation. Not only are they destroyed, but even the memory of them is obliterated. There is no ongoing existence described here in any form.

docs.title: Section B: Hebrew Destruction Words -- Kalah (H3615) and Shachath (H7843)
docs.text:
5. Kalah (H3615) in Psalm 59:13, 104:35, and 73:19.

  • Psalm 59:13: "Consume (kalah) them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be (ayin)." The stated result of consumption is ayin -- non-existence. David does not pray for their torment; he prays for their consumption to the point of non-existence.
  • Psalm 104:35: "Let the sinners be consumed (kalah) out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more (ayin)." Same result word: ayin.
  • Psalm 73:19: "How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed (kalah) with terrors." Consumption is sudden and complete.

The LXX translates kalah as synteleo (to complete entirely, to consume) 85 times, ekleipo (to cease) 30 times, and pauo (to stop) 15 times. All three Greek renderings convey ending/cessation, not ongoing existence.

6. Shachath (H7843) -- decay/corruption vs. torment.

Shachath means "to corrupt, to decay, to ruin." The LXX renders it as diaphtheiro (to rot thoroughly, to destroy) 48 times and phtheiro (to corrupt, to destroy) 6 times. The semantic field is decay, decomposition, corruption -- the process by which something breaks down and ceases to maintain its form. This is the opposite of preservation. The "torment" semantic field (basanizo, basanismos) describes the experience of pain by a conscious subject. These are entirely different concepts: decay destroys the subject; torment presupposes the subject's continued existence. The destruction vocabulary consistently describes what happens to the subject itself, not what the subject experiences.

7. Psalm 37:20 -- abad + kalah + smoke.

"The wicked shall perish (abad), and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume (kalah); into smoke shall they consume away."

Two destruction verbs reinforce each other: the wicked perish (abad) and consume (kalah). The smoke simile adds a visual: as sacrificial fat burns on the altar, it produces smoke that rises and disappears. The substance is consumed; the smoke dissipates. Nothing remains. The three elements (abad, kalah, smoke) all point in the same direction: the wicked cease to exist.

8. Non-existence language: Psalm 59:13, 104:35, Obadiah 1:16.

The Hebrew word ayin ("there is not" -- non-existence) appears in Psalm 59:13 ("that they may not be") and Psalm 104:35 ("let the wicked be no more"). Obadiah 1:16 uses kelo hayu ("as though they had not been") -- a different construction but the same concept. These are among the most explicit cessation statements in the OT. They do not describe ongoing existence in any form. They describe non-existence: the state of not being.

docs.title: Section C: Greek Destruction Words -- Apollymi (G622), Apoleia (G684), Olethros (G3639)
docs.text:
9. Apollymi (G622) across six NT passages.

  • Matthew 10:28: God destroys (apollymi) soul and body in gehenna. Subject: human soul and body. Direct teaching of Jesus. Didactic genre.
  • John 3:16: Whoever believes should not perish (apollymi) but have everlasting life. Subject: humanity. Contrast: perish vs. life.
  • Luke 13:3: "Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (apollymi)." Subject: Jesus' audience. Warning: repent or perish.
  • Romans 2:12: "Sinned without law shall also perish (apollymi) without law." Subject: sinners. Paul's teaching.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:18: If Christ is not raised, "they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished (apollymi)." Subject: dead believers. Paul's reductio ad absurdum -- without resurrection, the dead have perished.
  • 2 Peter 3:9: "Not willing that any should perish (apollymi), but that all should come to repentance." Subject: all humanity. God's desire.

None of these contexts suggests "ongoing torment." Every usage places apollymi as the opposite of life, salvation, or resurrection. Strong's defines it as "to destroy fully." No lexicon defines it as "torment."

10. Apollymi for wineskins -- Matthew 9:17.

Burst wineskins perish (apollymi). They are not tormented. They burst, lose their form, and cease to function as wineskins. This non-theological usage reveals the word's basic meaning without any eschatological overlay: apollymi describes something that is destroyed and ceases to exist in its prior state. When Jesus uses this same word for the destruction of soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28), the word carries this same meaning.

11. Apoleia (G684) across four NT passages.

  • Matthew 7:13: The broad way leads to destruction (apoleia). The destination is destruction, not torment.
  • Philippians 3:19: "Whose end is destruction (apoleia)." The final outcome (telos) is destruction.
  • 2 Peter 3:7: "Reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition (apoleia) of ungodly men." Fire + destruction.
  • Romans 9:22: "Vessels of wrath fitted to destruction (apoleia)." The vessels are destined for destruction -- not for ongoing existence in a different state.

Strong's defines apoleia as "ruin or loss." It is the noun form of apollymi. No passage defines apoleia as torment. In every case, it describes a terminal outcome.

12. Olethros (G3639) -- "ruin, i.e. death, punishment."

  • 2 Thessalonians 1:9: "Punished with everlasting destruction (olethros) from the presence of the Lord." Olethros means "ruin, death." Paired with aionios (everlasting), it describes a destruction whose result is permanent -- not an ongoing process of being destroyed. Compare: "everlasting salvation" (Heb 5:9) is not an ongoing process of being saved. "Everlasting redemption" (Heb 9:12) is not an ongoing process of being redeemed. The pattern is: aionios + noun = a result that is permanent.
  • 1 Thessalonians 5:3: "Sudden destruction (olethros) cometh upon them, and they shall not escape." Sudden and inescapable.
  • 1 Timothy 6:9: "Drown men in destruction (olethros) and perdition (apoleia)." Two destruction words in parallel.

The OT parallels confirm the result-oriented reading: "destroyed (shamad) for ever" (Psa 92:7) and "perish (abad) for ever" (Job 20:7). Jude 1:7 clinches it: Sodom suffered "the vengeance of eternal fire," yet the cities are not still burning. "Eternal fire" produced a completed destruction whose result is permanent.

13. Olethros + apoleia together in 1 Timothy 6:9.

Paul pairs two destruction words from the same semantic field: olethros (ruin/death) and apoleia (destruction/loss). This double emphasis confirms he is working entirely within the destruction vocabulary, not the torment vocabulary. If Paul meant to describe ongoing torment, the Greek language had perfectly adequate words for that (basanizo, basanismos, kolasis) -- he did not use them. He used two destruction words instead.

docs.title: Section D: The "Perish vs. Life" Contrast Pattern
docs.text:
14. The perish-vs-life contrast table.

Passage Author Outcome A (wicked) Outcome B (righteous) John 3:16 John Perish (apollymi) Everlasting life (zoe aionios) Matthew 7:13-14 Jesus/Matthew Destruction (apoleia) Life (zoe) Romans 6:23 Paul Death (thanatos) Eternal life (zoe aionios) Philippians 3:19 vs. 3:21 Paul Destruction (apoleia) Glorified body Psalm 145:20 David Destroy (shamad) Preserve (shamar) Galatians 6:8 Paul Corruption (phthora) Life everlasting (zoe aionios)

The pattern is consistent across at least four authors (John, Matthew/Jesus, Paul, David). In every case, the two outcomes are antithetical: life vs. death/destruction/perishing. The contrast only works if the two outcomes are genuinely opposite. "Everlasting life vs. everlasting conscious torment" would be two forms of continued existence -- not opposites. "Everlasting life vs. perishing" (cessation) presents genuine opposites. This structural pattern is a Necessary Implication (N028): both sides acknowledge the textual contrast exists; they disagree about what "perish" means.

15. 1 Corinthians 15:18 -- Paul's reductio ad absurdum.

Paul argues: if there is no resurrection, then the dead in Christ "are perished (apollymi)." His argument depends on apollymi meaning cessation -- they are gone, lost forever, no longer existing. If "perished" meant "still existing but in a spiritually ruined state," Paul's argument would collapse: the dead in Christ would still exist (just in a bad state), and the absence of resurrection would not be the catastrophe Paul presents it as. The horror of Paul's reductio is that without resurrection, death is final -- the dead have ceased to exist. This is one of the most revealing uses of apollymi in the NT because the word is applied to believers, not the wicked, showing what the word itself means apart from eschatological context.

docs.title: Section E: Destruction Similes
docs.text:
16. Destruction similes catalog.

Passage Simile What happens to the substance? Psalm 68:2 Wax before fire Melts, loses form, ceases to be wax Psalm 37:20 Fat of lambs / smoke Fat burns away on altar; smoke rises and dissipates Malachi 4:1 Stubble in an oven Burns up completely; "neither root nor branch" remains Malachi 4:3 Ashes Inert residue after complete combustion; walked upon Hosea 13:3 Morning cloud, dew, chaff, smoke Cloud dissipates, dew evaporates, chaff blows away, smoke disperses Nahum 1:10 Stubble fully dry Consumed by fire instantly Isaiah 1:31 Tow (flax fiber) Burns rapidly and completely

Not a single simile depicts a substance that endures indefinitely. Every simile depicts something that ceases to exist through a natural process: melting, burning, evaporating, dissipating, blowing away. This is a Necessary Implication (N029): both sides accept what these substances naturally do. They disagree about whether the similes are meant to depict the actual fate or merely its severity.

17. Isaiah 34:10 and Revelation 14:10-11 -- "smoke ascending forever."

Isaiah 34:10 says of Edom: "the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever." Edom is not still burning. The smoke is not still ascending. The land exists today (modern Jordan). "Smoke ascending forever" is prophetic/apocalyptic imagery for complete, irreversible destruction -- not a literal description of ongoing combustion. This OT precedent (#4a: SIS) governs the reading of Revelation 14:10-11, which uses the same imagery. If "smoke ascending forever" does not mean ongoing burning for Edom, it need not mean ongoing burning for the wicked.

18. Jude 1:7 -- Sodom's "eternal fire."

"Even as Sodom and Gomorrha... are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire."

Sodom and Gomorrah are not still burning. The cities were destroyed -- completely, permanently, irreversibly. "Eternal fire" describes a fire whose result is eternal, not a fire whose process is eternal. This is the biblical example (#4a: SIS) that governs the reading of "everlasting destruction" in 2 Thessalonians 1:9: the destruction is completed; its effect is permanent.

docs.title: Section F: Destruction vs. Torment Vocabulary
docs.text:
19. Destruction vs. torment vocabulary -- frequency and ratio.

The destruction vocabulary (apollymi, apoleia, olethros, plus OT equivalents abad, shamad, kalah, shachath) accounts for approximately 743 combined OT/NT occurrences. The torment vocabulary (basanizo, basanismos, kolasis) is used for the fate of the wicked in a handful of passages, primarily Revelation 14:10-11 (apocalyptic genre), Revelation 20:10 (apocalyptic genre), and Matthew 25:46 (kolasis, which means "punishment," not necessarily torment). The ratio is approximately 30:1 in favor of destruction vocabulary. The Bible's dominant vocabulary for the fate of the wicked is destruction, not torment.

These are distinct word families with different semantic ranges (N030). No lexicon defines any destruction word as "torment," and no lexicon defines any torment word as "destroy." Using passages that employ torment vocabulary (Rev 14:10-11, in apocalyptic genre) to redefine the meaning of passages that employ destruction vocabulary (Matt 10:28, John 3:16, in didactic genre) requires an unverified cross-reference (#4b) between different word families.

20. Revelation 14:10-11 vs. Matthew 10:28 -- vocabulary and genre.

Revelation 14:10-11 uses basanizo (torment) -- torment vocabulary, not destruction vocabulary. It is apocalyptic genre (symbolic vision). Its subjects are specifically "beast-worshippers" within a highly symbolic narrative.

Matthew 10:28 uses apollymi (destroy) -- destruction vocabulary. It is didactic genre (direct teaching of Jesus). It addresses all hearers about the general fate of the wicked.

The more common vocabulary is destruction. The clearer genre is didactic. In the clarity hierarchy, didactic teaching governs apocalyptic imagery, not the other way around. Using the apocalyptic torment passage to redefine the didactic destruction passage inverts the interpretive hierarchy.

Counter-argument -- apollymi in Luke 15 ("lost but still existing"): The ECT position argues that apollymi can mean "lost but still existing" based on the lost sheep, lost coin, and lost son in Luke 15. This commits the illegitimate totality transfer -- importing one sense of a word into all of its occurrences. The active-voice eschatological uses (Matt 10:28: "destroy soul and body"; Matt 2:13: Herod seeking to "destroy" the child Jesus) confirm genuine destruction meaning. The lost son parable itself equates "lost" with "dead" (Luke 15:24, 32: "this my son was dead... was lost"), reinforcing rather than undermining the destruction reading.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise -- Answers
docs.text:
1. "The wicked shall perish" (Psa 37:20; Psa 68:2) - Explicit (E). These verses directly state this using the Hebrew word abad.

2. "The LXX translates abad as apollymi 141 times; the same destruction vocabulary spans both testaments." - Explicit (E). This is an observable textual fact about the Septuagint translation. The data is verifiable.

3. "No lexicon defines abad, shamad, kalah, apollymi, apoleia, or olethros as 'torment' or 'ongoing conscious suffering.'" - Explicit (E). This is a verifiable lexical fact. One can check every major Hebrew and Greek lexicon (BDB, HALOT, BDAG, Thayer, Strong's) and confirm that none of these words is defined as "torment."

4. "The Bible's destruction vocabulary for the wicked means cessation of existence." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-A (Evidence-Extending). This systematizes approximately 40 explicit statements from 15+ biblical authors into a comprehensive claim. Every component is found in the explicit evidence. It is an inference only because it draws a conclusion from the cumulative pattern -- no concept is added beyond what the individual E-items already say. Criteria: #5 (systematizing), #4a (LXX-verified vocabulary chain).

5. "The destruction words are metaphorical: 'perish' means spiritual ruin (continued existence in a ruined state)." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). This claim requires every destruction word to mean something other than its lexical definition. No lexicon defines any of these words as "spiritual ruin" or "continued existence in a ruined state." The FOR evidence comes from torment-vocabulary passages (Rev 14:10-11, using basanizo, in apocalyptic genre) and one parabolic image (Matt 13:42, wailing in furnace). The AGAINST evidence comes from the lexical definitions themselves, from 40+ didactic passages using destruction vocabulary, and from explicit non-existence statements ("shall not be," "be no more," "as though they had not been"). Criteria: #1 (adding a meaning not in lexicons), #2 (choosing between lexical and metaphorical readings).

6. "'Everlasting destruction' means an ongoing process of being destroyed." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). Olethros means "ruin, death" -- a result, not a process. The claim requires "everlasting" to modify the process rather than the result. Compare: "everlasting salvation" (Heb 5:9) is not an ongoing process of being saved. "Everlasting redemption" (Heb 9:12) is not an ongoing process of being redeemed. Jude 1:7's "eternal fire" applied to Sodom demonstrates the result-oriented reading: the destruction was completed; its effect is permanent. The OT parallels "destroyed for ever" (Psa 92:7) and "perish for ever" (Job 20:7) confirm the same pattern. Criteria: #2 (choosing between result-oriented and process-oriented readings).

7. "'Wailing and gnashing of teeth' in a furnace describes eternal conscious torment." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). The furnace passage is parabolic (Matt 13:42, the parable of the tares). The same author, Matthew, uses destruction vocabulary in didactic teaching about the same topic: "destroy soul and body in gehenna" (Matt 10:28) and "the way that leads to destruction" (Matt 7:13). Didactic teaching governs parabolic imagery in the clarity hierarchy. "Wailing and gnashing" could describe the moment of being cast in (anguish at the point of destruction), not an ongoing state. The text does not specify duration. Criteria: #2 (choosing between momentary anguish and ongoing state), #3 (parabolic genre treated as didactic).

docs.title: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said -- Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. The Bible's primary vocabulary for the fate of the wicked consists of destruction/cessation words. Four Hebrew words (abad, shamad, kalah, shachath) totaling approximately 627 occurrences and three Greek words (apollymi, apoleia, olethros) totaling approximately 116 occurrences form the destruction vocabulary. No lexicon defines any of these words as "torment."

  2. The LXX establishes verified cross-testament vocabulary continuity: abad maps to apollymi 141 times, shamad to apollymi 23 times, shachath to diaphtheiro 48 times, kalah to synteleo 85 times. When the NT uses apollymi, it uses the same word the LXX uses for abad.

  3. The "perish vs. life" contrast appears across multiple authors (John 3:16; Matt 7:13-14; Rom 6:23; Phil 3:19; Psa 145:20; Gal 6:8). Life and destruction are presented as opposite outcomes.

  4. All biblical destruction similes depict substances that cease to exist: wax, smoke, chaff, stubble, ashes, dew, morning clouds, fat, tow. Not one simile depicts a substance that endures indefinitely.

  5. Multiple passages state the result of destruction as non-existence: "the wicked shall not be" (Psa 37:10), "that they may not be" (Psa 59:13), "be no more" (Psa 104:35), "as though they had not been" (Oba 1:16).

  6. "Everlasting destruction" (olethros aionios, 2 Thess 1:9) combines "everlasting" with a word meaning "ruin, death." Jude 1:7 demonstrates that "eternal fire" applied to Sodom describes a completed destruction whose result is permanent -- not an ongoing process.

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied -- requires adding something):

  1. It cannot be said that destruction vocabulary means "ongoing conscious torment." No lexicon defines abad, shamad, kalah, shachath, apollymi, apoleia, or olethros as "torment" or "ongoing suffering." Reading these words as "spiritual ruin" requires adding a meaning the text does not contain.

  2. It cannot be said that the destruction similes depict ongoing existence. Chaff, wax, smoke, stubble, ashes, morning clouds, and dew all cease to exist through natural processes. Reading them as depicting something that endures requires them to mean the opposite of what the natural processes illustrate.

  3. It cannot be said that "everlasting destruction" means an ongoing process of being destroyed. Olethros means "ruin/death" (a result, not a process). The biblical example of "eternal fire" applied to Sodom (Jude 1:7) demonstrates the result-oriented reading.

  4. It cannot be said that torment vocabulary defines what destruction vocabulary means. Basanizo (torment) and apollymi (destroy) are different words from different word families. Using Revelation 14:10-11 (basanizo, apocalyptic genre) to define what apollymi means in Matthew 10:28 (didactic genre) requires an unverified cross-reference between different word families.

  5. It cannot be said that "wailing and gnashing of teeth" in a furnace proves eternal conscious torment. The furnace passages are parabolic (Matt 13:42, 50). The same author uses destruction vocabulary in didactic teaching (Matt 10:28; 7:13). Didactic governs parabolic.

  6. It cannot be said that the destruction vocabulary is insignificant or merely metaphorical. Approximately 743 occurrences across both testaments from virtually every biblical author constitute the Bible's dominant vocabulary for the fate of the wicked. This is not a marginal vocabulary set that can be overridden by a few passages from a single genre.

docs.title: Study 6: Destruction Vocabulary -- Advanced Study
docs.text:
Hebrew and Greek Word Studies on the Fate of the Wicked

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Hebrew Destruction Words -- Abad (H6) and Shamad (H8045)
docs.text:
1. Abad (H6) occurs approximately 184 times in the OT and means "to perish, to destroy." Read Psalm 37:20, Psalm 68:2, Psalm 73:27, Psalm 92:9, and Job 20:7. In each verse, what is the subject of abad, and what do these verses collectively say about the fate of the wicked?

  2. Shamad (H8045) occurs approximately 90 times and means "to destroy utterly, to exterminate." Read Psalm 145:20, Psalm 37:38, Psalm 92:7, and Isaiah 13:9. What action does shamad describe? In Psalm 145:20, what is the antithetical parallel to shamad?

  3. The Septuagint (LXX) translates abad as apollymi (G622) 141 times -- a dominant mapping with a PMI score of 30.45. What does this translation pattern tell us about how pre-Christian Jewish scholars understood abad? What does it mean for NT passages that use apollymi for the fate of the wicked?

  4. Read Isaiah 26:14. This verse uses both shamad (destroyed) and abad (perish). What does it say about the dead who have been destroyed? Can they rise? What has happened to their memory?

docs.title: Section B: Hebrew Destruction Words -- Kalah (H3615) and Shachath (H7843)
docs.text:
1. Kalah (H3615) occurs approximately 206 times and means "to consume, to finish, to complete." Read Psalm 59:13, Psalm 104:35, and Psalm 73:19. In Psalm 59:13, what is the stated result of consumption -- what does the psalmist say they should become?

  2. Shachath (H7843) occurs approximately 147 times and means "to corrupt, to decay, to ruin." The LXX translates shachath as diaphtheiro (to rot thoroughly, to destroy) 48 times. How does the "decay/corruption" semantic field differ from the "torment" semantic field?

  3. Read Psalm 37:20. This verse uses both abad (perish) and kalah (consume) together, with the added imagery of smoke. How do the two destruction verbs plus the smoke simile reinforce each other?

  4. Compare Psalm 59:13 ("consume them, that they may not be") with Psalm 104:35 ("let the wicked be no more") and Obadiah 1:16 ("as though they had not been"). All three use non-existence language. What Hebrew word appears in all of these, and what does it mean?

docs.title: Section C: Greek Destruction Words -- Apollymi (G622), Apoleia (G684), Olethros (G3639)
docs.text:
1. Apollymi (G622) is derived from apo + the base of olethros. Strong's defines it as "to destroy fully." It occurs approximately 92 times in the NT. Read Matthew 10:28, John 3:16, Luke 13:3, Romans 2:12, 1 Corinthians 15:18, and 2 Peter 3:9. In each passage, what is the subject, and how is apollymi used? Does any of these contexts suggest "ongoing torment" rather than "destruction"?

  2. In Matthew 9:17, apollymi is used for wineskins that burst -- they "perish." What happens to burst wineskins? Are they tormented, or do they cease to function? What does this non-theological usage reveal about the word's meaning?

  3. Apoleia (G684) is the noun form of apollymi. Strong's defines it as "ruin or loss." Read Matthew 7:13, Philippians 3:19, 2 Peter 3:7, and Romans 9:22. In each passage, what is apoleia the destination or outcome of? Does any passage define apoleia as "torment"?

  4. Olethros (G3639) occurs only 4 times in the NT and is etymologically related to ollymi, the root of apollymi. Strong's defines it as "ruin, i.e. death, punishment." Read 2 Thessalonians 1:9, 1 Thessalonians 5:3, and 1 Timothy 6:9. What does it mean that the word defined as "ruin/death" is paired with "everlasting" (aionios) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9?

  5. In 1 Timothy 6:9, Paul uses olethros (destruction) and apoleia (perdition) together in the same sentence. What does the pairing of two destruction words tell you about the semantic field Paul is working in?

docs.title: Section D: The "Perish vs. Life" Contrast Pattern
docs.text:
1. Examine the following passages and fill in the contrast:

    Passage Author Outcome A (wicked) Outcome B (righteous) John 3:16 John ___ ___ Matthew 7:13-14 Jesus/Matthew ___ ___ Romans 6:23 Paul ___ ___ Philippians 3:19 vs. 3:21 Paul ___ ___ Psalm 145:20 David ___ ___ Galatians 6:8 Paul ___ ___

    Is the pattern consistent across authors? Are the two outcomes presented as antithetical (opposites) or as two forms of continued existence?

  2. Read 1 Corinthians 15:18. Paul argues that if Christ is not raised, "they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished (apollymi)." Paul's reductio ad absurdum depends on apollymi meaning what? If "perished" meant "still existing but in a ruined state," would Paul's argument make sense?

docs.title: Section E: Destruction Similes
docs.text:
1. Catalog the destruction similes from the following passages. For each, identify what the substance does when the described process occurs:

    Passage Simile What happens to the substance? Psalm 68:2 Wax before fire ___ Psalm 37:20 Fat of lambs / smoke ___ Malachi 4:1 Stubble in an oven ___ Malachi 4:3 Ashes ___ Hosea 13:3 Morning cloud, dew, chaff, smoke ___ Nahum 1:10 Stubble fully dry ___ Isaiah 1:31 Tow (flax fiber) ___

    Do any of these similes depict a substance that endures indefinitely?

  2. Read Isaiah 34:10 alongside Revelation 14:10-11. Isaiah 34:10 says of Edom: "the smoke thereof shall go up for ever; from generation to generation it shall lie waste." Is Edom still burning today? What does this tell you about how "smoke ascending forever" functions as biblical imagery?

  3. Read Jude 1:7. Sodom and Gomorrah are said to suffer "the vengeance of eternal fire." Are those cities still burning? What does "eternal fire" describe -- an ongoing process or a completed result?

docs.title: Section F: Destruction vs. Torment Vocabulary
docs.text:
1. The Bible uses two distinct word families when discussing the fate of the wicked:

    • Destruction family: apollymi (G622), apoleia (G684), olethros (G3639)
    • Torment family: basanizo (G928), basanismos (G929), kolasis (G2851)

    These are different Greek words with different definitions. Approximately how many passages use destruction vocabulary for the fate of the wicked, and how many use torment vocabulary? What is the ratio?

  2. Read Revelation 14:10-11 (torment vocabulary, apocalyptic genre) and Matthew 10:28 (destruction vocabulary, didactic genre). Which passage uses the more common vocabulary? Which passage is in the clearer genre (didactic vs. apocalyptic)?

docs.title: Study 6: Destruction Vocabulary -- Answer Key
docs.text:
What Words Does the Bible Use for the Fate of the Wicked?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

In this study, we will look at the actual Hebrew and Greek words the Bible uses when it describes what happens to the wicked. We will ask: what do these words mean in their original languages, and do they match what most people assume the Bible teaches?

docs.title: Section A: The Old Testament Destruction Words
docs.text:
1. Read Psalm 37:20. What two things does this verse say will happen to the wicked? What imagery does it use to describe how they will disappear?

The wicked will (1) perish (abad) and (2) consume away (kalah). The imagery is smoke: "into smoke shall they consume away." The fat of lambs on a sacrifice burns away completely -- it is consumed and gone.

"But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away." -- Psalm 37:20

2. Read Psalm 68:2. What natural substance does the psalmist compare the wicked to? What happens to that substance in the presence of fire?

The wicked are compared to wax. Wax melts before fire -- it dissolves, loses its form, and ceases to exist as wax. The psalmist uses this to describe what happens to the wicked in the presence of God.

"As wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God." -- Psalm 68:2

3. Read Psalm 145:20. What two contrasting actions does God take? What does He do for those who love Him, and what does He do to the wicked?

God preserves those who love Him and destroys (shamad) the wicked. These are opposites: preservation (continued existence) vs. destruction (cessation). The contrast does not say God preserves the righteous in heaven and preserves the wicked in hell -- it says He preserves the one group and destroys the other.

"The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy." -- Psalm 145:20

4. Read Psalm 104:35. After the sinners are "consumed out of the earth," what does the psalmist say they will be?

"No more." The Hebrew word is ayin, meaning "there is not" -- non-existence. The psalmist does not say they will be tormented forever. He says they will be consumed and then they will be no more.

"Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more." -- Psalm 104:35

5. Read Psalm 37:10. What will you find when you look for the wicked? What will happen to "his place"?

You will not find the wicked at all. "The wicked shall not be." Even the place where the wicked person once stood will be empty -- "thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be." The language is that of non-existence, not ongoing suffering.

"For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be." -- Psalm 37:10

docs.title: Section B: The New Testament Destruction Words
docs.text:
6. Read John 3:16. What two outcomes does this verse present? What is the alternative to everlasting life?

The two outcomes are perish (apollymi) and everlasting life. The alternative to everlasting life is not everlasting torment -- it is perishing. The verse presents continued existence (life) vs. cessation (perish) as the two possible outcomes.

"For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." -- John 3:16

7. Read Matthew 10:28. What does Jesus say God is able to do to "both soul and body in hell"? Does He say "torment" or "destroy"?

Jesus says God is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna. The word is "destroy," not "torment." The same word (apollymi) is used for wineskins that burst and are ruined (Matt 9:17) -- they cease to function. Jesus explicitly states that the soul can be destroyed.

"And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." -- Matthew 10:28

8. Read Matthew 7:13-14. What does Jesus call the destination of the broad way? What does He call the destination of the narrow way? What is the contrast?

The broad way leads to destruction (apoleia). The narrow way leads to life. The contrast is destruction vs. life -- not torment vs. life, and not one kind of existence vs. another kind of existence.

"Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life." -- Matthew 7:13-14

9. Read Philippians 3:19. What does Paul say is the "end" (final outcome) of the enemies of the cross?

Their "end" is destruction (apoleia) -- the same Greek word Jesus used in Matthew 7:13. Paul does not say their end is eternal torment. He says their end is destruction.

"Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things." -- Philippians 3:19

10. Read 2 Thessalonians 1:9. What word does Paul use for the punishment of the wicked? Is the word "torment" or "destruction"?

The word is destruction (olethros), not torment. Paul says they will be "punished with everlasting destruction." The Greek word olethros means "ruin, i.e. death, punishment." It is related to the root of apollymi. "Everlasting destruction" means a destruction whose result is permanent -- just as "everlasting salvation" (Heb 5:9) means a salvation whose result is permanent, not an ongoing process of being saved.

"Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power." -- 2 Thessalonians 1:9

docs.title: Section C: Destruction Similes -- What Pictures Does the Bible Use?
docs.text:
11. Read Malachi 4:1, 3. What will the wicked become on the day that burns like an oven? What will be left of them? What will the righteous walk on?

The wicked will be stubble that burns up, leaving "neither root nor branch" -- nothing remains. They will become ashes under the soles of the righteous' feet. Ashes are the inert, lifeless residue left after something has been completely consumed by fire.

"For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch." -- Malachi 4:1

"And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet." -- Malachi 4:3

12. Read Hosea 13:3. List the four things the wicked are compared to. What do all four of these things have in common?

The four similes are: (1) morning cloud, (2) early dew, (3) chaff driven by the whirlwind, and (4) smoke out of a chimney. All four depict things that vanish -- they are present for a moment and then gone. Morning clouds dissipate. Dew evaporates. Chaff blows away. Smoke disperses. Not one depicts something that endures.

"Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney." -- Hosea 13:3

13. Read Nahum 1:10 and Isaiah 1:31. What material are the wicked compared to in both passages? What happens to that material when it meets fire?

Both passages compare the wicked to flammable material that is consumed by fire. Nahum says they will be "devoured as stubble fully dry." Isaiah says "the strong shall be as tow [flax fiber], and the maker of it as a spark, and they shall both burn together." Dry stubble and tow are among the most flammable materials in the ancient world -- they catch fire and are consumed almost instantly.

14. Read Obadiah 1:16. What does this verse say the judged nations will be? In your own words, what does "as though they had not been" mean?

"They shall be as though they had not been." This is one of the most explicit cessation statements in the Old Testament. It means the judged will be returned to the state of non-existence -- as if they had never existed at all. This is not the language of ongoing torment; it is the language of total cessation.

"...they shall be as though they had not been." -- Obadiah 1:16

docs.title: Section D: The "Perish vs. Life" Pattern
docs.text:
15. Look at these five passages together. What pattern do you see? Are the two outcomes presented as two kinds of continued existence, or as opposites?

The pattern is consistent across multiple authors:

Passage Outcome A Outcome B John 3:16 Perish Everlasting life Matthew 7:13-14 Destruction Life Romans 6:23 Death Eternal life Philippians 3:19 Destruction Glory (3:21) Psalm 145:20 Destroy Preserve

In every case, the two outcomes are presented as opposites: one is life/preservation, the other is death/destruction/perishing. None of these passages presents the choice as between two kinds of continued existence. The contrast only works if the two outcomes are genuinely antithetical -- existence vs. non-existence, not heaven vs. hell-as-continued-existence.

16. Read Romans 6:23. If the "gift of God is eternal life," what does that imply about whether eternal life is something humans already possess?

If eternal life is a gift, it is not something humans already possess. A gift must be given -- it is not inherent. This is consistent with 1 Timothy 6:16 (God only has immortality) and Romans 2:7 (immortality must be sought). The opposite of this gift is "the wages of sin is death" -- not ongoing torment, but death.

17. Read Luke 13:3, 5. Jesus gives a warning and a choice. What is the alternative to repentance?

The alternative to repentance is perishing (apollymi): "Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Jesus uses the same word (apollymi) He uses in John 3:16 and that He uses in Matthew 10:28 for the destruction of soul and body. The word means to perish -- to be destroyed.

"I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." -- Luke 13:3, 5

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? -- Answers
docs.text:
A. "The wicked shall perish." - Explicit. Psalm 37:20, Psalm 68:2, Psalm 73:27, and many other verses directly state this using the Hebrew word abad (to perish, to be destroyed).

B. "God is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." - Explicit. Matthew 10:28 directly states this. Jesus uses the word apollymi (to destroy fully).

C. "The destruction words in the Bible really mean ongoing torment, not actual destruction." - Inference. No verse says this. No lexicon defines abad, shamad, kalah, shachath, apollymi, apoleia, or olethros as "torment" or "ongoing conscious suffering." This claim requires adding a meaning that the destruction words do not carry, and overriding their lexical definitions.

D. "The wicked shall be ashes under the soles of your feet." - Explicit. Malachi 4:3 directly states this. Ashes are the inert residue after something has been completely consumed by fire.

E. "When the Bible says 'perish,' it means 'spiritual ruin' -- continued existence in a ruined state." - Inference. No verse defines "perish" this way. The word apollymi means "to destroy fully." When applied to wineskins (Matt 9:17), it clearly means they are ruined and cease to function -- not that they continue to exist in a tormented state. The "spiritual ruin" reading requires adding a concept that no lexicon supports.
