docs.title: Study 11: Smoke Ascending Forever -- Answer Key
docs.text:
Revelation 14:9-11 and 19:3 -- What Does the Imagery Mean?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is critical in this study. Revelation 14:10-11 is one of the most frequently cited passages in the eternal torment debate. Before deciding what it means, we need to examine where its imagery comes from.

docs.title: Section A: The OT Source -- Isaiah 34 on Edom
docs.text:
1. Read Isaiah 34:9-10. What happens to Edom's land? What does the text say about the fire and the smoke?

Edom's streams are turned to pitch and its dust to brimstone. The fire is "not quenched night nor day" and "the smoke thereof shall go up for ever." This is the OT passage that Revelation 14:11 draws its "smoke ascending for ever" formula from.

"And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever." -- Isaiah 34:9-10

2. Now read Isaiah 34:11-14. After the "smoke ascending for ever" and "not quenched night nor day" language of verse 10, what creatures inhabit the same territory? Can animals live in a place where fire is still burning?

Cormorants, bitterns, owls, ravens, wild goats, and other creatures inhabit the territory. Animals cannot dwell in a place where fire is actively burning. The text itself demonstrates that the "smoke ascending for ever" formula does not describe perpetual combustion -- it describes permanent desolation.

"But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it." -- Isaiah 34:11

3. Isaiah 34:14 says the screech owl "shall rest there" in the land whose fire was "not quenched night nor day." What does it tell you that an animal rests in a place described with "forever fire" language?

The animal rests where the fire burned. The fire completed its destructive work and went out. The "forever" fire language describes the permanent result of judgment -- irreversible desolation -- not a flame that never ceases. The owl's rest is proof that the fire is finished.

"The screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest." -- Isaiah 34:14

4. Is the fire of Edom's judgment still burning today? What does the "smoke ascending for ever" formula describe -- a fire that never stops, or a destruction whose results are permanent?

Edom is not still burning. The formula describes a destruction whose results are permanent. The strongest "forever" language in the OT is applied to a judgment that has demonstrably ended as an active process. The desolation remains; the fire does not.

docs.title: Section B: The First Fire and Brimstone -- Sodom
docs.text:
5. Read Genesis 19:24-25. What did God rain upon Sodom and Gomorrah? What was the result -- does the text say the cities were tormented or overthrown?

God rained brimstone and fire. The text says He "overthrew those cities" -- destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary. This is the first fire-and-brimstone judgment in Scripture, and it establishes the paradigm: fire and brimstone destroy.

"Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; and he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities." -- Genesis 19:24-25

6. Read Genesis 19:28. Abraham looked toward Sodom and saw "the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace." Was this smoke from an ongoing fire, or from a completed destruction?

Abraham observed ascending smoke from a completed destruction. The cities had already been overthrown. The smoke was evidence of what had happened -- the aftermath of judgment, not an ongoing process.

"And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace." -- Genesis 19:28

7. Read Jude 1:7. Sodom and Gomorrah suffered "the vengeance of eternal fire" and are "set forth for an example." Are those cities still burning? What kind of "example" is Sodom -- an example of ongoing torment, or an example of completed destruction?

Sodom is not still burning. Jude calls the fire "eternal" even though it went out long ago. The cities are an example of completed destruction -- the fire was "eternal" in its effect (permanent destruction), not in its duration (the fire stopped). This is the same pattern as Isaiah 34.

"Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire." -- Jude 1:7

8. Read 2 Peter 2:6. Peter says God turned Sodom and Gomorrah "into ashes" as "an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly." What is the end product -- ashes or ongoing fire?

Ashes. Peter describes the result as ashes -- complete consumption. This is what the fire-and-brimstone paradigm produces: total destruction. The cities are held up as an example of what happens to the ungodly, and the example is ashes, not ongoing torment.

"And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly." -- 2 Peter 2:6

docs.title: Section C: Malachi's Eschatological Fire
docs.text:
9. Read Malachi 4:1. How does this verse describe the wicked on the day that comes? What does "burn them up" mean? What is left -- root or branch?

The day "shall burn them up" and "shall leave them neither root nor branch." The wicked are consumed like stubble in an oven. Nothing remains -- no root (hidden, underground) and no branch (visible, above ground). Total consumption.

"For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch." -- Malachi 4:1

10. Read Malachi 4:3. What will the wicked become? Where will they be?

The wicked "shall be ashes under the soles of your feet." They have been reduced to ashes -- the end product of combustion. The righteous walk over them. This is the opposite of ongoing torment: the wicked no longer exist except as residue.

"And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do this, saith the LORD of hosts." -- Malachi 4:3

11. Malachi 4:1-3 is the OT's clearest eschatological fire-judgment passage. Does it describe the wicked as being tormented forever, or as being completely consumed?

Completely consumed. The passage describes the wicked as stubble burned up, leaving neither root nor branch, reduced to ashes. Every image points to total destruction with nothing remaining. There is no language of ongoing torment anywhere in this eschatological fire text.

docs.title: Section D: Revelation 14:9-11
docs.text:
12. Read Revelation 14:10-11. What does this passage say about those who worship the beast? What imagery does it use?

Beast-worshippers will be "tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb." The smoke of their torment "ascendeth up for ever and ever" and they have "no rest day nor night." The passage uses fire-and-brimstone imagery, smoke-ascending language, and "no rest" language -- all of which have OT source texts.

"The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: and the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name." -- Revelation 14:10-11

13. The phrase "the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever" uses the same formula as Isaiah 34:10 ("the smoke thereof shall go up for ever"). Given what you learned in Section A about how this formula works in Isaiah 34, what might it mean in Revelation 14?

In Isaiah 34, the identical formula describes Edom's judgment -- a completed destruction followed by permanent desolation (animals dwell in the ruins). The fire went out; the desolation is permanent. If the formula means "permanent result of completed destruction" in its OT source, it may carry the same meaning in Revelation 14. The imagery comes from a passage about ended judgment, not ongoing combustion.

14. Rev 14:11 says the beast-worshippers have "no rest day nor night." Now read Revelation 4:8, where the four living creatures "rest not day and night" as they praise God. The same Greek word anapausis is used in both verses. Does "no rest day and night" in Rev 4:8 mean the living creatures praise God for all eternity without pause, or does it describe the continuous, uninterrupted nature of what they are doing?

In Rev 4:8, "rest not day and night" describes the continuous, uninterrupted nature of the living creatures' praise during its execution. The same word (anapausis) in the same book by the same author describes the character of an activity -- its uninterrupted quality -- not necessarily its eternal duration. This same-book context informs how "no rest day nor night" functions in Rev 14:11.

"And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." -- Revelation 4:8

docs.title: Section E: Revelation 19:3 and Same-Book Context
docs.text:
15. Read Revelation 19:3. Whose smoke "rose up for ever and ever"? Now read Revelation 18:8, 10, 21. What happened to Babylon -- is she still burning, or was she "utterly burned," judged "in one hour," and "found no more at all"?

Babylon's smoke "rose up for ever and ever." But Babylon was already described as utterly destroyed: "she shall be utterly burned with fire" (18:8), her judgment came "in one hour" (18:10), and she was "thrown down, and shall be found no more at all" (18:21). The same "smoke for ever and ever" formula that appears in Rev 14:11 is applied to a completed destruction.

"And her smoke rose up for ever and ever." -- Revelation 19:3

"Therefore shall her plagues come in one day, death, and mourning, and famine; and she shall be utterly burned with fire." -- Revelation 18:8

"And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all." -- Revelation 18:21

16. The same "smoke for ever and ever" formula is used for Babylon in Rev 19:3 and for beast-worshippers in Rev 14:11. If the formula means "ongoing conscious torment" in Rev 14:11, what does it mean in Rev 19:3 for a city that has been utterly destroyed?

If "smoke for ever and ever" means ongoing conscious torment, then Babylon -- a symbolic city already described as utterly burned and "found no more at all" -- would also be experiencing ongoing conscious torment. But Babylon is destroyed. The same formula, same author, same book. Either the formula means "permanent result of completed destruction" in both places, or it means different things in different verses by the same author -- which requires explanation.

17. Read Revelation 20:9. When human enemies attack the camp of the saints, what happens to them? Does the text say they are tormented or devoured?

Fire came down from God out of heaven and "devoured" them. The word is katephagen -- destruction vocabulary. When Revelation describes human enemies facing divine fire, the word is "devoured," not "tormented."

"And fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them." -- Revelation 20:9

18. Read Revelation 20:14-15 and 21:8. When humans enter the lake of fire, what term does the text use -- "torment" or "second death"?

"Second death." Rev 21:8 explicitly defines the lake of fire and brimstone as "the second death." When humans enter the lake of fire, the identifying term is death -- not torment. The text uses death vocabulary for humans and reserves "torment" language for the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10), the latter two being symbolic entities.

"But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." -- Revelation 21:8

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? -- Answers
docs.text:
A. "Isaiah 34:10 uses the 'smoke ascending for ever' and 'not quenched night nor day' formula for Edom's judgment, and Isaiah 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the desolated ruins afterward." - Explicit. Both statements are directly readable from the text of Isaiah 34. Verse 10 contains the smoke formula. Verses 11-17 describe the animals. No interpretation is required.

B. "The 'smoke ascending for ever' formula in Revelation 14:11 describes ongoing conscious eternal torment." - Inference. Rev 14:11 states the smoke ascends and uses "for ever and ever." The claim that this means ongoing conscious eternal torment is an interpretation of the imagery. The same formula in Isaiah 34:10 describes a judgment that ended (animals inhabit the ruins). The same formula in Rev 19:3 describes Babylon's completed destruction. Deciding that the formula means something different in Rev 14:11 requires choosing between readings.

C. "When humans enter the lake of fire (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8), the identifying term is 'second death,' not 'torment.'" - Explicit. Rev 21:8 says "the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." Rev 20:14 says "This is the second death." The text uses the term "second death" for humans in the lake of fire. This is directly quotable.

D. "The fire-and-brimstone imagery in Rev 14:10-11 describes the permanence and completeness of destruction, not ongoing torment." - Inference. This is a well-supported inference based on the OT source imagery (Isa 34:10; Gen 19:24-28; Mal 4:1-3), same-book context (basanismos for Babylon's completed destruction; same formula for destroyed Babylon), and the genre of Revelation (apocalyptic vision). But it is still an inference -- the passage does not explicitly state "this means completed destruction." The interpretation systematizes the evidence.

E. "The fate described for the devil, beast, and false prophet in Rev 20:10 ('tormented day and night for ever and ever') applies equally to all unsaved humans." - Inference. Rev 20:10 names three subjects: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. The beast and false prophet are symbolic entities. The text does not state that all humans share this fate. The immediately preceding verse (20:9) uses "devoured" for humans. Verses 14-15 use "second death" for humans. Extending Rev 20:10 to all humans adds something the text does not say.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... Isa 34:10 uses "smoke ascending for ever" for Edom; Isa 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins "Smoke ascending forever" means perpetual, ongoing combustion Gen 19:24-25 says fire and brimstone "overthrew" Sodom; 2 Pet 2:6 says it produced "ashes" Fire and brimstone describe ongoing torment Mal 4:1-3 says the wicked are burned up like stubble, reduced to "ashes under the soles of your feet" The wicked survive fire-judgment and are tormented endlessly Rev 19:3 uses the same "smoke for ever and ever" formula for utterly destroyed Babylon The formula must mean ongoing conscious torment in Rev 14:11 Rev 4:8 uses the same "rest not day and night" for living creatures' praise "No rest day nor night" proves eternal conscious suffering Rev 20:9 says human enemies were "devoured"; Rev 21:8 defines the lake of fire as "the second death" All humans in the lake of fire experience the same fate as the devil in Rev 20:10

docs.title: Study 11: Smoke Ascending Forever
docs.text:
Revelation 14:9-11 and 19:3 -- What Does the Imagery Mean?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is critical in this study. Revelation 14:10-11 is one of the most frequently cited passages in the eternal torment debate. Before deciding what it means, we need to examine where its imagery comes from.

docs.title: Section A: The OT Source -- Isaiah 34 on Edom
docs.text:
1. Read Isaiah 34:9-10. What happens to Edom's land? What does the text say about the fire and the smoke?

  2. Now read Isaiah 34:11-14. After the "smoke ascending for ever" and "not quenched night nor day" language of verse 10, what creatures inhabit the same territory? Can animals live in a place where fire is still burning?

  3. Isaiah 34:14 says the screech owl "shall rest there" in the land whose fire was "not quenched night nor day." What does it tell you that an animal rests in a place described with "forever fire" language?

  4. Is the fire of Edom's judgment still burning today? What does the "smoke ascending for ever" formula describe -- a fire that never stops, or a destruction whose results are permanent?

docs.title: Section B: The First Fire and Brimstone -- Sodom
docs.text:
1. Read Genesis 19:24-25. What did God rain upon Sodom and Gomorrah? What was the result -- does the text say the cities were tormented or overthrown?

  2. Read Genesis 19:28. Abraham looked toward Sodom and saw "the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace." Was this smoke from an ongoing fire, or from a completed destruction?

  3. Read Jude 1:7. Sodom and Gomorrah suffered "the vengeance of eternal fire" and are "set forth for an example." Are those cities still burning? What kind of "example" is Sodom -- an example of ongoing torment, or an example of completed destruction?

  4. Read 2 Peter 2:6. Peter says God turned Sodom and Gomorrah "into ashes" as "an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly." What is the end product -- ashes or ongoing fire?

docs.title: Section C: Malachi's Eschatological Fire
docs.text:
1. Read Malachi 4:1. How does this verse describe the wicked on the day that comes? What does "burn them up" mean? What is left -- root or branch?

  2. Read Malachi 4:3. What will the wicked become? Where will they be?

  3. Malachi 4:1-3 is the OT's clearest eschatological fire-judgment passage. Does it describe the wicked as being tormented forever, or as being completely consumed?

docs.title: Section D: Revelation 14:9-11
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 14:10-11. What does this passage say about those who worship the beast? What imagery does it use?

  2. The phrase "the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever" uses the same formula as Isaiah 34:10 ("the smoke thereof shall go up for ever"). Given what you learned in Section A about how this formula works in Isaiah 34, what might it mean in Revelation 14?

  3. Rev 14:11 says the beast-worshippers have "no rest day nor night." Now read Revelation 4:8, where the four living creatures "rest not day and night" as they praise God. The same Greek word anapausis is used in both verses. Does "no rest day and night" in Rev 4:8 mean the living creatures praise God for all eternity without pause, or does it describe the continuous, uninterrupted nature of what they are doing?

docs.title: Section E: Revelation 19:3 and Same-Book Context
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 19:3. Whose smoke "rose up for ever and ever"? Now read Revelation 18:8, 10, 21. What happened to Babylon -- is she still burning, or was she "utterly burned," judged "in one hour," and "found no more at all"?

  2. The same "smoke for ever and ever" formula is used for Babylon in Rev 19:3 and for beast-worshippers in Rev 14:11. If the formula means "ongoing conscious torment" in Rev 14:11, what does it mean in Rev 19:3 for a city that has been utterly destroyed?

  3. Read Revelation 20:9. When human enemies attack the camp of the saints, what happens to them? Does the text say they are tormented or devoured?

  4. Read Revelation 20:14-15 and 21:8. When humans enter the lake of fire, what term does the text use -- "torment" or "second death"?

docs.title: Explicit or Inference?
docs.text:
For each statement below, decide: Does the Bible explicitly say this (you can point to a verse), or is it an inference (a conclusion someone draws that no verse directly states)?

A. "Isaiah 34:10 uses the 'smoke ascending for ever' and 'not quenched night nor day' formula for Edom's judgment, and Isaiah 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the desolated ruins afterward." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

B. "The 'smoke ascending for ever' formula in Revelation 14:11 describes ongoing conscious eternal torment." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

C. "When humans enter the lake of fire (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8), the identifying term is 'second death,' not 'torment.'" - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

D. "The fire-and-brimstone imagery in Rev 14:10-11 describes the permanence and completeness of destruction, not ongoing torment." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

E. "The fate described for the devil, beast, and false prophet in Rev 20:10 ('tormented day and night for ever and ever') applies equally to all unsaved humans." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

docs.title: Study 12: Tormented Forever -- Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Revelation 20:10 -- Subject Identification, Basanizo Semantic Range, and Vocabulary Differentiation

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Subject Gate Analysis -- Who Are the Three Entities?
docs.text:
1. Document the nature of each subject from the text.

The devil: Rev 12:9 identifies him as "the great dragon... that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." Rev 20:2 confirms: "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan." The devil is a non-human supernatural spirit being.

"And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." -- Revelation 12:9

The beast: Rev 13:1-2: rises from the sea, seven heads, ten horns, composite body (leopard, bear, lion). Rev 17:8: "was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition." The beast is identified by a number (Rev 13:18). No literal human being rises from the sea with seven heads and ten horns, or "was, and is not." This is a symbolic apocalyptic entity.

"The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition." -- Revelation 17:8

The false prophet: Rev 19:20 identifies the false prophet as the entity that "wrought miracles before" the beast -- the second beast of Rev 13:11-17. The Greek pseudoprophetes appears 3 times in Revelation (16:13; 19:20; 20:10) as a singular specific apocalyptic figure. It appears 8 times elsewhere in the NT (Matt 7:15; 24:11,24; Mark 13:22; Luke 6:26; Acts 13:6; 2 Pet 2:1; 1 John 4:1) as a generic plural class of human beings. The Revelation usage is distinct: a specific symbolic entity, not a human individual.

2. Subject Gate application.

  • The devil: non-human supernatural spirit being. Automatic FAIL: "A non-human spirit being."
  • The beast: symbolic entity in an apocalyptic vision (seven heads, ten horns, rises from sea, "was, and is not"). Automatic FAIL: "A symbolic entity (a figure in an apocalyptic vision)."
  • The false prophet: symbolic entity (the second beast of Rev 13:11-17). Automatic FAIL: "A symbolic entity."

All three subjects FAIL the Subject Gate. Rev 20:10 cannot serve as positional evidence about the fate of literal human beings. The torment formula is applied to entities that are not literal human beings.

3. Genre classification.

Rev 1:1 uses semaino (to signify, to communicate through signs): "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel." Nave's Topical Bible classifies Revelation under VISION. The Genre Gate FAILS: Revelation is apocalyptic vision, not didactic teaching. Apocalyptic imagery is governed by, not governor of, didactic teaching from epistles and Gospels.

docs.title: Section B: Word Study -- Basanizo (G928) Full NT Usage
docs.text:
4. All 12 NT occurrences of basanizo.

Non-judgment uses (7 of 12):

Passage Subject Context KJV Translation Matt 8:6 Centurion's servant Physical illness (palsy) "Grievously tormented" Matt 14:24 Ship/boat Waves tossing "Tossed" Mark 6:48 Disciples Difficulty rowing "Toiling" Mark 5:7 Demon (Legion) Demonic fear at Jesus' presence "Torment" Luke 8:28 Demon (Legion) Demonic fear at Jesus' presence "Torment" 2 Pet 2:8 Lot Emotional distress at Sodom's wickedness "Vexed" Rev 12:2 Woman (symbolic) Labor pains "Pained"

Judgment uses (5 of 12):

Passage Subject Context KJV Translation Matt 8:29 Demons Demons anticipating their own future judgment "Torment" Rev 9:5 Locusts' victims Judgment with 5-month time limit "Tormented" Rev 11:10 Two witnesses' effect Prophets' testimony as "torment" to the earthly "Tormented" Rev 14:10 Beast-worshippers Apocalyptic judgment scene "Tormented" Rev 20:10 Devil, beast, false prophet Lake of fire "Tormented"

58% of basanizo uses (7 of 12) are non-judgment contexts. The word covers physical illness, waves tossing a boat, toiling at rowing, emotional distress, labor pains, and demonic fear. It is not a technical term for eschatological eternal punishment.

5. Location of the five judgment uses.

All five judgment uses are either in Revelation's apocalyptic framework (Rev 9:5; 11:10; 14:10; 20:10) or involve demons speaking of their own future (Matt 8:29). Zero are in epistles. Zero are in Gospel didactic teaching about human fate. Zero are in the OT. The judgment use of basanizo is confined to apocalyptic genre and demonic self-reference.

6. Revelation 9:5 -- the five-month limit.

"And to them it was given that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented five months." -- Revelation 9:5

Basanizo here carries an explicit time limit. This demonstrates that the word does not inherently encode duration. It describes the experience (pain, suffering, distress) but says nothing about how long. Duration is determined by context -- "five months" in Rev 9:5, "day and night for ever and ever" in Rev 20:10. The word itself is neutral regarding duration.

7. Related word group.

Basanismos (G929): 6 NT occurrences, ALL in Revelation (9:5; 14:11; 18:7,10,15). Three of six describe Babylon's basanismos. But Babylon's basanismos IS her completed destruction: - Rev 18:8: "utterly burned with fire" - Rev 18:10: "in one hour is thy judgment come" - Rev 18:21: "shall be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all"

Babylon's "torment" (basanismos) results in her total annihilation. She is "found no more at all." The torment word group in Revelation does not require ongoing existence -- it can describe the process of destruction.

Basanos (G931): 3 NT occurrences: Matt 4:24 (physical diseases), Luke 16:23 (parabolic context -- rich man), Luke 16:28 (parabolic context -- rich man). Basanos is NOT used in any eschatological judgment passage.

docs.title: Section C: Vocabulary Differentiation in Revelation 20:7-15
docs.text:
8. Vocabulary mapping.

Passage Subject Vocabulary Greek Word Rev 19:20 Beast and false prophet "Cast alive" zontes (living) Rev 19:21 Human remnant "Slain" apektanthesan (killed) Rev 20:9 Human armies "Devoured" katephagen (consumed) Rev 20:10 Devil, beast, false prophet "Tormented day and night for ever and ever" basanisthesontai Rev 20:14-15 Humans not in book of life "The second death" / "cast into the lake of fire" ho thanatos ho deuteros Rev 21:8 Eight categories of human wicked "The second death" ho thanatos ho deuteros

The text consistently distinguishes between the three non-human/symbolic entities and human beings. Symbolic entities receive torment vocabulary and are cast "alive." Human beings are "slain," "devoured," and consigned to "the second death." The vocabulary differentiation is not occasional -- it is systematic across every mention.

9. The "tormented for ever and ever" formula.

The specific formula basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon appears once in Scripture -- Revelation 20:10. It names three subjects: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. It is never applied to human beings anywhere in the Bible. Rev 20:15 casts humans into the lake without the formula. Rev 21:8 names eight categories of human wicked and calls the lake "the second death." The text had the opportunity to extend the formula to humans and instead used death vocabulary.

10. Revelation 20:6 -- "the second death has no power."

"Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power." -- Revelation 20:6

The word "power" (exousia) is death language, not torment language. We speak of death having "power" or "dominion" (cf. Rom 6:9: "death hath no more dominion over him"). The second death is presented as something that exercises authority over a person -- consistent with death terminology. This is the text's own characterization of the second death: it has exousia, the kind of language that belongs to the domain of death, not the domain of conscious experience.

docs.title: Section D: The "Ages of Ages" Formula
docs.text:
11. Distribution of eis tous aionas ton aionon.

The formula appears approximately 22 times in the NT: - Approximately 19 times doxologically: for God's glory, reign, and existence (Gal 1:5; Phil 4:20; 1 Tim 1:17; 2 Tim 4:18; Heb 1:8; 13:21; 1 Pet 4:11; 5:11; Rev 1:6,18; 4:9,10; 5:13; 7:12; 10:6; 11:15; 15:7; 22:5, etc.) - 3 times in judgment contexts: Rev 14:11 (smoke of beast-worshippers), Rev 19:3 (smoke of Babylon), Rev 20:10 (torment of devil, beast, false prophet)

All three judgment uses are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. None is in an epistle or Gospel. The formula's overwhelming use is doxological (for God). Its judgment uses are confined to one apocalyptic book.

12. Revelation 19:3 and the "for ever and ever" formula for Babylon.

"And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever." -- Revelation 19:3

"And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all." -- Revelation 18:21

The identical "for ever and ever" formula describes the smoke of Babylon -- an entity that is "found no more at all," "utterly burned with fire" (18:8), destroyed "in one hour" (18:10). The "for ever and ever" language coexists with total annihilation in the same book, applied to the same entity. Within Revelation's apocalyptic framework, "smoke ascending for ever and ever" can describe the aftermath of completed destruction -- permanent results, not ongoing process.

docs.title: Section E: The Extension Argument
docs.text:
13. Evaluation of the "same destination = same experience" argument.

The argument requires three unstated premises: 1. That all inhabitants of the lake share the same experience -- the text does not state this. 2. That the torment formula extends beyond its named subjects -- the text names the devil, beast, and false prophet, not humans. 3. That the vocabulary difference is insignificant -- but the text uses "devoured" (v.9), "tormented" (v.10), and "second death" (vv.14-15) in the same passage, systematically distinguishing subjects.

The text itself provides different terminology for different subjects at the same destination. "Same destination = same experience" must be added from outside the text. This is an I-C inference (compatible external): it does not contradict any explicit statement (the text does not deny humans could experience torment), but it extends beyond what the text states. The text had the opportunity to append the torment formula to Rev 20:15 or 21:8 and instead used "the second death."

14. The beast-as-representative argument.

The argument that the beast's torment transfers to its human referents is undermined by Revelation's own vocabulary distinctions: - The symbolic trio (devil, beast, false prophet) receives "torment" (basanizo) -- Rev 20:10. - Human beings receive different vocabulary: "slain" (apokteino -- Rev 19:21), "devoured" (katesthio -- Rev 20:9), "second death" (Rev 20:14-15).

The text distinguishes the subjects and defines the lake of fire as "the second death" -- its own self-interpretation. If the beast's experience were meant to transfer to humans, the text's consistent vocabulary differentiation between the two groups would be inexplicable.

15. Matthew 25:41 and 25:46 -- vocabulary difference.

Matt 25:41: the everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- its primary designation is for supernatural entities.

Matt 25:46: the human punishment vocabulary is kolasis (G2851, "punishment"), not basanizo (G928, "torment"). Kolasis occurs only twice in the NT: Matt 25:46 and 1 John 4:18 ("fear hath torment/punishment"). Even in the one passage where humans share a destination with the devil, the vocabulary shifts: the fire was prepared for the devil; the human term is kolasis, not basanizo. The text maintains the vocabulary distinction even here.

docs.title: Section F: What Vocabulary Does the NT Use for Human Fate Outside Revelation?
docs.text:
16. NT vocabulary for the final fate of human wicked outside Revelation.

Passage Author Genre Vocabulary Greek Matt 10:28 Jesus Didactic "Destroy" soul and body apollymi John 3:16 John Didactic "Perish" vs. everlasting life apollymi Rom 6:23 Paul Didactic "Death" vs. eternal life thanatos 2 Thess 1:9 Paul Didactic "Everlasting destruction" olethros aionios Phil 3:19 Paul Didactic "Destruction" apoleia 2 Pet 3:7 Peter Didactic "Perdition of ungodly men" apoleia Matt 7:13 Jesus Didactic "Destruction" (the broad way) apoleia Gal 6:8 Paul Didactic "Corruption" phthora Heb 10:27 Author of Hebrews Didactic "Devour" the adversaries katesthio

All are didactic genre. All use destruction/death vocabulary. None uses basanizo or basanismos. The NT's consistent vocabulary for human fate outside Revelation is destruction, death, perdition, corruption, and perishing.

17. Hebrews 2:14 -- destruction vocabulary for the devil.

"That through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil." -- Hebrews 2:14

Even the devil -- whose future judgment includes basanizo according to Rev 20:10 -- is described with destruction vocabulary (katargeo) in a didactic epistle. Katargeo has a wide semantic range (27 NT occurrences: "abolish," "render powerless," "nullify," "do away with"), and genuine lexical ambiguity exists for the Heb 2:14 application. But it is noteworthy that when an epistle writer describes the devil's fate, destruction vocabulary is used rather than torment vocabulary.

18. Matthew 8:29 -- demons anticipate basanizo.

"And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?" -- Matthew 8:29

The subjects anticipating basanizo are demons -- supernatural entities, not human beings. They recognize torment as their own appointed future judgment. This is one of only two basanizo uses outside Revelation, and it involves supernatural entities referring to their own fate. It reinforces the pattern: basanizo as judgment vocabulary is associated with non-human/supernatural entities, not with generic human wicked.

docs.title: Section G: Evidence Classification Exercise -- Answers
docs.text:
1. "Rev 20:10 names three subjects for 'tormented day and night for ever and ever': the devil, the beast, and the false prophet." - Explicit (E). The verse directly names all three subjects. Quotable.

2. "The 'tormented for ever and ever' formula appears once in Scripture (Rev 20:10), applied only to the devil, beast, and false prophet -- never to human beings." - Necessary Implication (N). The formula's single occurrence is an observable textual fact. Its application to these three subjects and not to humans is verifiable by distribution. Both sides accept the textual observation. They disagree about whether the formula extends beyond its stated subjects -- but the distribution itself is a necessary implication of the data.

3. "The torment described for these three entities in Rev 20:10 applies equally to all unsaved humans who enter the lake of fire." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-C (Compatible External). The text names three non-human/symbolic subjects. It does not state that humans experience the same. The claim adds "all unsaved humans experience what Rev 20:10 describes" -- not stated in text. It does not contradict any explicit statement (the text does not deny humans could experience torment), but extends beyond what the text contains. What is added: "same destination = same experience."

4. "Basanizo is not a technical term for eschatological eternal punishment because 7 of 12 uses are non-judgment contexts and one judgment use has an explicit 5-month time limit." - Necessary Implication (N). The distribution data is observable: 7 of 12 non-judgment, Rev 9:5 has a five-month limit. Both sides accept these translation facts. The conclusion that the word is not a technical eschatological term follows unavoidably from the distribution.

5. "Rev 20:10 proves eternal conscious torment for all inhabitants of the lake of fire because the torment formula is stated for entities in the lake, and humans are also cast into the lake." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). FOR: Rev 20:10 states the torment formula for entities in the lake; Rev 20:15 states humans are cast into the same lake. AGAINST: the text uses different vocabulary for different subjects (E), the formula is applied only to non-human/symbolic entities (N), the text defines the lake as "the second death" for humans (E), basanizo is not used for human fate outside Revelation (E). The FOR side rests on 2 Ambiguous items; the AGAINST side rests on 10+ Plain items. What is added: "same lake = same experience" when the text provides different terminology.

6. "The text of Rev 20:7-15 uses distinct vocabulary for distinct subjects: 'devoured' for humans (v.9), 'tormented' for devil/beast/false prophet (v.10), 'second death' for humans (vv.14-15)." - Explicit (E). Each vocabulary choice is directly observable in the text. Katephagen (Rev 20:9), basanisthesontai (Rev 20:10), ho thanatos ho deuteros (Rev 20:14). The vocabulary pattern is a textual observation, not an interpretation.

7. "No epistle, no Gospel, and no OT passage uses basanizo or basanismos for the final fate of generic human wicked." - Explicit (E). This is a verifiable distribution fact. One can survey every occurrence of basanizo (12x) and basanismos (6x) and confirm that none applies these words to generic human eschatological fate outside Revelation's apocalyptic framework (and Matt 8:29, where demons reference their own future).

docs.title: Section H: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said -- Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (the Bible explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. Rev 20:10 names three subjects for "tormented day and night for ever and ever": the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. The devil is a non-human supernatural spirit being (Rev 12:9; 20:2). The beast is a symbolic apocalyptic entity (rises from sea, seven heads, ten horns, "was, and is not" -- Rev 13:1; 17:8). The false prophet is a symbolic apocalyptic entity (the second beast of Rev 13:11-17). None is a literal human being.

  2. The Subject Gate FAILS for all three subjects. The devil is a non-human spirit being. The beast and false prophet are symbolic entities in an apocalyptic vision. The Genre Gate FAILS because Revelation is classified as VISION (Nave's) and communicates through signs (semaino, Rev 1:1).

  3. The "tormented for ever and ever" formula appears once in Scripture -- Rev 20:10 -- applied to three non-human/symbolic entities. It is not applied to human beings anywhere in the Bible.

  4. The text of Rev 20:7-15 uses distinct vocabulary for distinct subjects: "devoured" for human armies (v.9), "tormented" for the three non-human/symbolic entities (v.10), "the second death" for humans entering the lake (vv.14-15; 21:8). Rev 19:20-21 maintains the same distinction: symbolic entities cast "alive," humans "slain."

  5. Basanizo has a wide semantic range (illness, waves, rowing, distress, childbirth, demonic fear, judgment). Seven of twelve uses (58%) are non-judgment contexts. Rev 9:5 uses basanizo with a five-month limit. It is not a technical term for eschatological eternal punishment.

  6. All five basanizo judgment uses are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework or involve demons speaking of their own future (Matt 8:29). No epistle, no Gospel, and no OT passage uses basanizo or basanismos for the final fate of generic human wicked.

  7. Outside Revelation, the NT consistently uses destruction/death vocabulary for the final fate of human wicked: "destroy" (apollymi, Matt 10:28; John 3:16), "everlasting destruction" (olethros aionios, 2 Thess 1:9), "death" (thanatos, Rom 6:23), "destruction" (apoleia, Phil 3:19; 2 Pet 3:7; Matt 7:13), "corruption" (phthora, Gal 6:8), "devour" (katesthio, Heb 10:27).

  8. The everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matt 25:41). The human punishment vocabulary in Matt 25:46 is kolasis (punishment), not basanizo (torment).

  9. The "for ever and ever" formula in Rev 19:3 describes Babylon's smoke -- an entity that is "found no more at all" (Rev 18:21), "utterly burned with fire" (18:8), destroyed "in one hour" (18:10). Within Revelation's apocalyptic framework, the formula coexists with total annihilation.

  10. Rev 20:6 characterizes the second death as having "power" (exousia) -- death language, consistent with its identification as "the second death" rather than "the second torment."

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied -- requires adding something):

  1. It cannot be said that Rev 20:10 teaches eternal conscious torment for human beings. The three named subjects are the devil (non-human), the beast (symbolic), and the false prophet (symbolic). The Subject Gate FAILS for all three. The torment formula is applied to these entities, not to humans. When humans appear in the same passage, the vocabulary is "devoured" (v.9) and "second death" (vv.14-15; 21:8).

  2. It cannot be said that "same destination = same experience." The text itself provides different vocabulary for different subjects at the same destination (the lake of fire). The devil/beast/false prophet receive the torment formula. Humans receive death terminology. Extending the torment formula to humans requires adding a concept the text does not contain.

  3. It cannot be said that basanizo is a technical term for eternal conscious punishment. Seven of twelve uses are non-judgment (illness, waves, rowing, distress, childbirth, demonic fear). One judgment use has a five-month limit. The word covers physical suffering, labor exertion, emotional distress, and divine judgment. Its eschatological uses are confined to Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

  4. It cannot be said that the "tormented for ever and ever" formula is applied to humans anywhere in Scripture. The formula appears once (Rev 20:10) and names three non-human/symbolic entities. Rev 20:15 casts humans into the lake without the formula. Rev 21:8 names eight categories of human wicked and calls the lake "the second death." Extending the formula to humans is an inference, not a textual statement.

  5. It cannot be said that the Bible uses torment vocabulary for the final fate of human wicked outside Revelation. No epistle, no Gospel, and no OT passage applies basanizo or basanismos to generic human judgment. The consistent vocabulary across epistles and Gospels is destruction, death, perdition, corruption, and perishing.

  6. It cannot be said that the extension of Rev 20:10 to humans is a necessary implication. The text provides the opportunity to state the torment formula for humans (Rev 20:15; 21:8) and instead uses "second death." The text provides the opportunity to use basanizo for human fate across the NT and instead uses apollymi, olethros, thanatos, apoleia, and phthora. The consistent choice to use different vocabulary when describing human fate is an observable textual pattern.

docs.title: Study 12: Tormented Forever -- Advanced Study
docs.text:
Revelation 20:10 -- Subject Identification, Basanizo Semantic Range, and Vocabulary Differentiation

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Subject Gate Analysis -- Who Are the Three Entities?
docs.text:
1. Revelation 20:10 names three subjects for the "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. For each, document its nature from the text:
  2. The devil: Read Revelation 12:9 and 20:2. What is the devil identified as? Is this entity a human being?
  3. The beast: Read Revelation 13:1-2 and 17:8. What characteristics does the text assign to the beast (origin, appearance, description)? Could these characteristics apply to a literal human person?

  4. The false prophet: Read Revelation 19:20 and trace the identification back to Revelation 13:11-17. The Greek word pseudoprophetes appears 3 times in Revelation (16:13; 19:20; 20:10) as a singular specific figure, and 8 times elsewhere in the NT as a generic plural class of human beings. What is the significance of this distinction?

  5. Apply the Subject Gate to each entity in Rev 20:10. For each subject, determine: Is this (a) a literal human being, (b) a non-human supernatural spirit being, or (c) a symbolic entity in an apocalyptic vision? What does the gate result mean for using this verse as evidence about the fate of literal human beings?

  6. Read Revelation 1:1. The Greek word semaino (to signify, to communicate through signs) describes how the book's content is delivered. Read also the classification in Nave's Topical Bible, which lists Revelation under VISION. What does the genre classification mean for reading Rev 20:10 as literal didactic teaching about human eschatology?

docs.title: Section B: Word Study -- Basanizo (G928) Full NT Usage
docs.text:
1. Document all 12 NT occurrences of basanizo (G928), noting the subject, the context, and the KJV translation for each:

Non-judgment uses (7 of 12): - Matthew 8:6 -- ___ - Matthew 14:24 -- ___ - Mark 6:48 -- ___ - Mark 5:7 -- ___ - Luke 8:28 -- ___ - 2 Peter 2:8 -- ___ - Revelation 12:2 -- ___

Judgment uses (5 of 12): - Matthew 8:29 -- ___ - Revelation 9:5 -- ___ - Revelation 11:10 -- ___ - Revelation 14:10 -- ___ - Revelation 20:10 -- ___

What percentage of basanizo uses are non-judgment? What does this distribution tell you about whether the word is a technical term for eschatological punishment?

  1. Examine the five judgment uses more closely. Where are they found? Are any in epistles? Are any in Gospels (aside from Matt 8:29, where demons speak of their own future)? What genre contains all five?

  2. Read Revelation 9:5. The basanizo in this verse has an explicit five-month time limit. What does this demonstrate about the word's inherent meaning? Does basanizo carry its own duration, or does duration come from context?

  3. Document the related word group:

  4. Basanismos (G929, noun) -- How many NT occurrences? Where do they appear? Three of six describe Babylon's basanismos (Rev 18:7,10,15). Now read Rev 18:8 ("utterly burned with fire"), Rev 18:10 ("in one hour"), and Rev 18:21 ("thrown down, and shall be found no more at all"). What is the relationship between Babylon's basanismos and Babylon's destruction?
  5. Basanos (G931, noun) -- How many NT occurrences? Where (Matt 4:24; Luke 16:23,28)? Is basanos used in any eschatological judgment passage?

docs.title: Section C: Vocabulary Differentiation in Revelation 20:7-15
docs.text:
1. Map the vocabulary the text uses for each subject group in Revelation 19:20 through 21:8:
Passage Subject Vocabulary Greek Word Rev 19:20 Beast and false prophet ___ ___ Rev 19:21 Human remnant ___ ___ Rev 20:9 Human armies ___ ___ Rev 20:10 Devil, beast, false prophet ___ ___ Rev 20:14-15 Humans not in book of life ___ ___ Rev 21:8 Eight categories of human wicked ___ ___

Does the text use one vocabulary for all subjects, or does it consistently distinguish between the three non-human/symbolic entities and human beings?

  1. The "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears in Rev 20:10. How many times does this specific formula appear in Scripture? To whom is it applied? Is it ever applied to human beings?

  2. Read Revelation 20:6. The second death "has no power" (exousia) over those in the first resurrection. What kind of language is this -- torment language or death language? What does the use of "power" (exousia) suggest about the nature of the second death?

docs.title: Section D: The "Ages of Ages" Formula
docs.text:
1. The Greek phrase eis tous aionas ton aionon ("for ever and ever" / "unto the ages of the ages") appears approximately 22 times in the NT. Document its distribution:

    • How many times is it used doxologically (for God/Christ's glory, reign, etc.)?
    • How many times is it used in judgment contexts?
    • Where do the judgment uses appear (which book)?

  2. Read Revelation 19:3. The "smoke rose up for ever and ever" formula is applied to Babylon. Now read Revelation 18:21: Babylon is "thrown down, and shall be found no more at all." If the same "for ever and ever" formula describes the smoke of an entity that is "found no more at all," what does this tell you about how the formula functions in Revelation's apocalyptic framework?

docs.title: Section E: The Extension Argument
docs.text:
1. The most common argument for applying Rev 20:10 to humans is: "The devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented in the lake of fire. Humans are also cast into the lake of fire (Rev 20:15). Therefore humans experience the same torment." Evaluate this argument:

    • Does the text state that all inhabitants of the lake share the same experience?
    • What vocabulary does the text use when it describes human beings entering the lake?
    • If "same destination = same experience," why does the text use different vocabulary for different subjects at the same destination?

  2. A related argument holds that the beast represents a human institution, so its torment transfers to its human referents. Evaluate this claim against the text's vocabulary distinctions:

    • The symbolic trio (devil, beast, false prophet) receives which vocabulary in Rev 20:10?
    • Human beings receive which vocabulary in Rev 19:21, 20:9, and 20:14-15?
    • The text defines the lake of fire as ___ (Rev 20:14) -- whose own self-interpretation is this?

  3. Read Matthew 25:41 and Matthew 25:46. The everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels." The punishment vocabulary for humans in Matt 25:46 is kolasis (G2851, "punishment"), not basanizo (G928, "torment"). Kolasis appears only twice in the NT: Matt 25:46 and 1 John 4:18. What is the significance of the vocabulary difference between the fire's preparation (for the devil) and the human punishment term (kolasis)?

docs.title: Section F: What Vocabulary Does the NT Use for Human Fate Outside Revelation?
docs.text:
1. Document the NT vocabulary for the final fate of human wicked outside Revelation:

    • Matthew 10:28 -- ___ (apollymi)
    • John 3:16 -- ___ (apollymi)
    • Romans 6:23 -- ___ (thanatos)
    • 2 Thessalonians 1:9 -- ___ (olethros aionios)
    • Philippians 3:19 -- ___ (apoleia)
    • 2 Peter 3:7 -- ___ (apoleia)
    • Matthew 7:13 -- ___ (apoleia)
    • Galatians 6:8 -- ___ (phthora)
    • Hebrews 10:27 -- ___ (katesthio)

    What vocabulary family do these passages use -- destruction/death or torment?

  2. Read Hebrews 2:14. Christ came to "destroy" (katargeo) "him that had the power of death, that is, the devil." What is noteworthy about the fact that even the devil -- whose future judgment includes basanizo according to Rev 20:10 -- is described with destruction vocabulary in a didactic epistle?

  3. Read Matthew 8:29. Demons (supernatural entities, not humans) ask: "Art thou come hither to torment (basanizo) us before the time?" Who are the subjects anticipating basanizo as their judgment? Are they human beings?
