docs.title: Study 12: Tormented Forever -- Answer Key
docs.text:
Revelation 20:10 -- Who Are the Subjects?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is especially important in this study. Revelation 20:10 is one of the most frequently cited verses in support of eternal conscious torment. But who exactly does the verse describe? And what vocabulary does the passage use when it turns to human beings?

docs.title: Section A: Who Are the Three Subjects?
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 20:10. The verse names three subjects who are "tormented day and night for ever and ever." Who are they?

The devil, the beast, and the false prophet.

"And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." -- Revelation 20:10

2. Read Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2. The devil is identified as the dragon, that old serpent, and Satan. Is the devil a human being?

No. The devil is a non-human supernatural spirit being. Scripture identifies him as the dragon, that old serpent, the Devil, and Satan.

"And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." -- Revelation 12:9

3. Read Revelation 13:1-2. The beast rises from the sea, has seven heads and ten horns, and receives its power from the dragon. Is this a description of a literal human being?

No. A creature with seven heads and ten horns that rises from the sea is a symbolic apocalyptic entity, not a literal human being.

"And I stood upon the sand of the sea, and saw a beast rise up out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns." -- Revelation 13:1

4. Read Revelation 17:8. The beast "was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition." Could this description apply to a literal human person?

No. An entity that "was, and is not" and ascends from the bottomless pit is not a description that could apply to a literal human being. This is apocalyptic symbolism.

"The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition." -- Revelation 17:8

5. Read Revelation 19:20. The false prophet is identified as the entity that "wrought miracles before" the beast -- the second beast of Revelation 13:11-17. Is the false prophet of Revelation a literal human being, or a symbolic apocalyptic figure?

The false prophet is a symbolic apocalyptic figure. The word pseudoprophetes in Revelation (used 3 times: Rev 16:13; 19:20; 20:10) refers to a singular specific apocalyptic entity -- the second beast of Revelation 13:11-17. This is distinct from the generic plural "false prophets" (a class of human beings) used 8 times elsewhere in the NT.

"And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him." -- Revelation 19:20

docs.title: Section B: What Happens to Humans in the Same Passage?
docs.text:
6. Read Revelation 20:9. When fire comes down on the human armies surrounding the holy city, what word does the text use? Are they "tormented" or "devoured"?

They are "devoured" (katephagen) -- destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

"And fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them." -- Revelation 20:9

7. Read Revelation 20:14-15. When humans who are not found in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire, what term does the text use to identify their fate? Does the text add "tormented day and night for ever and ever" to their description?

The text calls it "the second death." It does not add the torment formula. Rev 20:15 states humans are cast into the lake of fire -- and stops. No basanizo. No "day and night for ever and ever."

"And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire." -- Revelation 20:14-15

8. Read Revelation 21:8. Eight categories of human wicked are listed -- the fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars. What does the text call their fate in the lake of fire?

"The second death." Death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

"But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." -- Revelation 21:8

9. Read Revelation 19:20-21. In verse 20, the beast and false prophet are cast "alive" into the lake of fire. In verse 21, what happens to the human remnant? What is the difference in vocabulary?

The symbolic entities (beast and false prophet) are cast "alive" (zontes) into the lake. The human remnant were "slain" (apektanthesan) -- they died. The text uses different vocabulary: symbolic entities continue; humans die.

"And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet... These both were cast alive into a lake of fire." -- Revelation 19:20

"And the remnant were slain with the sword." -- Revelation 19:21

docs.title: Section C: The Vocabulary Pattern
docs.text:
10. Look at the vocabulary the passage uses for each group:

Group Vocabulary Reference Devil, beast, false prophet "Tormented day and night for ever and ever" Rev 20:10 Human armies "Devoured" (katephagen) Rev 20:9 Humans cast into the lake "The second death" Rev 20:14-15; 21:8

The text uses different words for different subjects. The torment formula is reserved for the three non-human/symbolic entities. When the text turns to humans, it switches to destruction and death vocabulary.

11. The "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula appears in Revelation 20:10. Search the rest of the Bible. Is this formula ever applied to human beings anywhere in Scripture?

No. The formula appears once in Scripture -- Revelation 20:10 -- and names three subjects: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. It is never applied to human beings anywhere in the Bible.

12. Read Matthew 25:41. Jesus says the everlasting fire was "prepared for" whom? Was it originally prepared for human beings?

It was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- supernatural entities, not human beings.

"Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels." -- Matthew 25:41

docs.title: Section D: What Does "Basanizo" Mean?
docs.text:
13. The Greek word behind "tormented" in Revelation 20:10 is basanizo (G928). Based on the five non-judgment uses listed, does basanizo always mean "eternal torment," or does it have a wider range of meaning?

Basanizo has a wide semantic range. It covers physical illness (Matt 8:6), waves tossing a boat (Matt 14:24), toiling at rowing (Mark 6:48), emotional distress (2 Pet 2:8), and labor pains (Rev 12:2). Seven of its twelve NT occurrences are non-judgment contexts. It is not a technical term for eternal torment.

14. Read Revelation 9:5. Here basanizo is used with an explicit time limit: five months. What does this tell you about whether the word inherently means "eternal"?

The five-month time limit demonstrates that basanizo does not inherently mean "eternal." The word describes pain, suffering, or torment -- but says nothing about duration. Duration is determined by context, not by the word itself.

"And to them it was given that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented five months." -- Revelation 9:5

docs.title: Section E: Outside Revelation
docs.text:
15. Outside the book of Revelation, what vocabulary does the New Testament use for the final fate of human wicked?

Consistently destruction and death vocabulary:

Passage Author Vocabulary Matthew 10:28 Jesus "Destroy" (apollymi) soul and body John 3:16 John "Perish" (apollymi) vs. everlasting life Romans 6:23 Paul "Death" (thanatos) vs. eternal life 2 Thessalonians 1:9 Paul "Everlasting destruction" (olethros) Philippians 3:19 Paul "Destruction" (apoleia)

The vocabulary is destruction/death, not torment.

16. Does any epistle, any Gospel, or any Old Testament passage use basanizo or basanismos for the final fate of generic human wicked?

No. No epistle, no Gospel, and no OT passage uses basanizo or basanismos for the final fate of generic human wicked. All five judgment uses of basanizo are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework or involve demons speaking of their own future (Matt 8:29). The consistent vocabulary for human fate outside Revelation is destruction and death.

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? -- Answers
docs.text:
A. "Revelation 20:10 names three subjects for 'tormented day and night for ever and ever': the devil, the beast, and the false prophet." - Explicit. Revelation 20:10 directly names all three subjects. You can point to the verse and quote it.

B. "The 'tormented for ever and ever' formula applies to all unsaved human beings who enter the lake of fire." - Inference. No verse states this. The formula appears once (Rev 20:10), applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet. When humans enter the lake (Rev 20:15; 21:8), the text does not use the torment formula -- it uses "the second death." Extending the formula to humans requires adding a concept the text does not contain: "same destination = same experience."

C. "When humans enter the lake of fire (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8), the text's own term for their fate is 'the second death.'" - Explicit. Revelation 20:14 directly states: "This is the second death." Revelation 21:8 directly states: "which is the second death." Both are quotable.

D. "Because the devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented in the lake of fire, and humans are also cast into the lake of fire, humans must experience the same torment." - Inference. No verse states this conclusion. The text itself provides different vocabulary for different subjects at the same destination. The claim "same lake = same experience" must be added from outside the text.

E. "The text uses different vocabulary for different subjects: 'tormented' for the devil/beast/false prophet, 'devoured' for human armies, and 'second death' for humans in the lake." - Explicit. Each vocabulary choice is directly observable in the text: basanizo (Rev 20:10), katephagen (Rev 20:9), "second death" (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8). The pattern is a textual observation, not an interpretation.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... Rev 20:10 names three subjects: the devil, the beast, the false prophet -- none is a literal human being Rev 20:10 teaches eternal conscious torment for all unsaved humans The "tormented for ever and ever" formula appears once and is applied to these three non-human/symbolic entities The torment formula applies to everyone in the lake of fire Humans in the same passage are "devoured" (v.9) and experience "the second death" (vv.14-15; 21:8) All inhabitants of the lake share the same experience No epistle, Gospel, or OT passage uses basanizo for the final fate of human wicked Basanizo/torment is the Bible's teaching about human fate The everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matt 25:41) The everlasting fire was prepared equally for humans Basanizo has a wide semantic range (illness, waves, rowing, distress, childbirth) and one use has a 5-month limit Basanizo is a technical term for eternal torment

docs.title: Study 12: Tormented Forever
docs.text:
Revelation 20:10 -- Who Are the Subjects?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is especially important in this study. Revelation 20:10 is one of the most frequently cited verses in support of eternal conscious torment. But who exactly does the verse describe? And what vocabulary does the passage use when it turns to human beings?

docs.title: Section A: Who Are the Three Subjects?
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 20:10. The verse names three subjects who are "tormented day and night for ever and ever." Who are they?

  2. Read Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2. The devil is identified as the dragon, that old serpent, and Satan. Is the devil a human being?

  3. Read Revelation 13:1-2. The beast rises from the sea, has seven heads and ten horns, and receives its power from the dragon. Is this a description of a literal human being?

  4. Read Revelation 17:8. The beast "was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition." Could this description apply to a literal human person?

  5. Read Revelation 19:20. The false prophet is identified as the entity that "wrought miracles before" the beast -- the second beast of Revelation 13:11-17. Is the false prophet of Revelation a literal human being, or a symbolic apocalyptic figure?

docs.title: Section B: What Happens to Humans in the Same Passage?
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 20:9. When fire comes down on the human armies surrounding the holy city, what word does the text use? Are they "tormented" or "devoured"?

  2. Read Revelation 20:14-15. When humans who are not found in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire, what term does the text use to identify their fate? Does the text add "tormented day and night for ever and ever" to their description?

  3. Read Revelation 21:8. Eight categories of human wicked are listed -- the fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars. What does the text call their fate in the lake of fire?

  4. Read Revelation 19:20-21. In verse 20, the beast and false prophet are cast "alive" into the lake of fire. In verse 21, what happens to the human remnant? What is the difference in vocabulary?

docs.title: Section C: The Vocabulary Pattern
docs.text:
1. Look at the vocabulary the passage uses for each group:

    • Devil, beast, false prophet (Rev 20:10): ___
    • Human armies (Rev 20:9): ___
    • Humans cast into the lake (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8): ___

    Does the text use the same word for all three groups, or different words for different subjects?

  2. The "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula appears in Revelation 20:10. Search the rest of the Bible. Is this formula ever applied to human beings anywhere in Scripture?

  3. Read Matthew 25:41. Jesus says the everlasting fire was "prepared for" whom? Was it originally prepared for human beings?

docs.title: Section D: What Does "Basanizo" Mean?
docs.text:
1. The Greek word behind "tormented" in Revelation 20:10 is basanizo (G928). It appears 12 times in the New Testament. Read the following non-judgment uses:

    • Matthew 8:6 -- a servant "grievously tormented" (sick with palsy)
    • Matthew 14:24 -- a ship "tossed" by waves
    • Mark 6:48 -- disciples "toiling" at rowing
    • 2 Peter 2:8 -- Lot "vexed" his righteous soul
    • Revelation 12:2 -- a woman "pained" in childbirth

    Based on these uses, does basanizo always mean "eternal torment," or does it have a wider range of meaning?

  2. Read Revelation 9:5. Here basanizo is used with an explicit time limit: five months. What does this tell you about whether the word inherently means "eternal"?

docs.title: Section E: Outside Revelation
docs.text:
1. Outside the book of Revelation, what vocabulary does the New Testament use for the final fate of human wicked? Look at these passages:

    • Matthew 10:28 -- "destroy" (apollymi)
    • John 3:16 -- "perish" (apollymi)
    • Romans 6:23 -- "death" (thanatos)
    • 2 Thessalonians 1:9 -- "everlasting destruction" (olethros)
    • Philippians 3:19 -- "destruction" (apoleia)

    Is the vocabulary destruction/death or torment?

  2. Does any epistle, any Gospel, or any Old Testament passage use basanizo or basanismos for the final fate of generic human wicked?

docs.title: Explicit or Inference?
docs.text:
For each statement below, decide: Does the Bible explicitly say this (you can point to a verse), or is it an inference (a conclusion someone draws that no verse directly states)?

A. "Revelation 20:10 names three subjects for 'tormented day and night for ever and ever': the devil, the beast, and the false prophet." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

B. "The 'tormented for ever and ever' formula applies to all unsaved human beings who enter the lake of fire." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

C. "When humans enter the lake of fire (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8), the text's own term for their fate is 'the second death.'" - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

D. "Because the devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented in the lake of fire, and humans are also cast into the lake of fire, humans must experience the same torment." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

E. "The text uses different vocabulary for different subjects: 'tormented' for the devil/beast/false prophet, 'devoured' for human armies, and 'second death' for humans in the lake." - [ ] Explicit -- the Bible says this - [ ] Inference -- someone concluded this

docs.title: Study 13: The Lake of Fire and the Second Death -- Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Revelation 20:14; 21:8; 2:11; 20:6

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Word Study -- Thanatos Deuteros (Second Death)
docs.text:
1. The phrase "second death" (deuteros thanatos) occurs four times in Scripture -- all in Revelation (2:11; 20:6; 20:14; 21:8). The Aramaic Targum tradition uses mota tinyana ("second death") in multiple OT passages. In the Targums, mota tinyana consistently means dying a second time or exclusion from the world to come -- death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary. What does this pre-Christian Jewish usage reveal about the expected meaning of "second death"?

The Targum tradition demonstrates that pre-Christian Judaism understood "second death" as death vocabulary -- dying again, being excluded from future life. The Targums use mota tinyana in passages such as Deuteronomy 33:6, Isaiah 22:14, 65:6,15, and Jeremiah 51:39,57. In every case, the phrase describes dying a second time or being cut off from the world to come. No Targum passage defines the "second death" as eternal conscious torment or separation from God. This pre-existing semantic field -- death, not torment -- is the context in which John's audience would have understood the phrase.

2. The word thanatos (G2288, "death") appears three times in Revelation 20:14 alone. The text chose thanatos to identify what the lake of fire does. The Greek language had basanizo (G928, "to torment") and basanismos (G929, "torment") available -- and in fact uses them in Rev 20:10 for non-human entities. Why is the vocabulary the author chose for the identification statement significant?

The author had both vocabulary sets available and demonstrably knew both -- basanizo is used in Rev 20:10 just four verses earlier. When the text identifies what the lake of fire IS, the author chose thanatos (death) rather than basanismos (torment). This is a deliberate vocabulary choice. The text's own name for the lake's function is "death" -- a second death. If the author intended to convey that the lake produces torment, the vocabulary was at hand. The author chose a different word.

3. The adjective deuteros (G1208, "second") is an ordinal number implying a first. Read Revelation 2:10-11. What does the ordinal distinction tell you about the nature of the second death in relation to the first?

The ordinal creates a direct parallel: there is a first death (physical death, which all humans experience) and a second death (which follows for those not in the book of life). Rev 2:10-11 makes the pairing explicit: "faithful unto death" (physical death -- the first death) is paired with the promise of exemption from "the second death." The second death is a second instance of death -- a dying again -- not a fundamentally different category (such as torment or separation). The word "death" carries the same core meaning in both uses; only the ordinal adjective distinguishes them.

"Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." -- Revelation 2:10

"He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." -- Revelation 2:11

4. Read Romans 6:23: "The wages of sin is death (thanatos)." In the SIS framework, how does this didactic passage govern the interpretation of "second death" in Revelation's apocalyptic genre?

Romans 6:23 is a didactic epistle -- the clearest genre of Scripture for direct theological teaching. It defines the penalty for sin as thanatos (death). The "second death" (deuteros thanatos) uses the same word. In the SIS (Scripture Interprets Scripture) framework, clearer genres govern more obscure genres: didactic governs apocalyptic. Paul's plain statement that the wages of sin is death governs the reading of Revelation's apocalyptic imagery. The shared vocabulary (thanatos) creates a verified SIS connection (#4a): the penalty for sin in didactic teaching (death) is the same word used for what happens in the lake of fire (the second death).

"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." -- Romans 6:23

docs.title: Section B: The Lake of Fire as the Text's Own Interpretation
docs.text:
5. Read Revelation 20:14: "This is the second death." This follows the same "X is Y" interpretive formula used throughout Scripture. What is the symbolic image here, and what is the plain-language explanation?

The symbolic image is the lake of fire. The plain-language explanation is "the second death." The text follows the same interpretive pattern found throughout Scripture's visions: the symbolic object is named, then explained in plainer terms. In Genesis 41:26-27, the seven kine ARE seven years. In Daniel 2:38, "Thou art this head of gold." In Revelation 17:9, the seven heads ARE seven mountains. In Revelation 5:8, the odours ARE the prayers of saints. In Rev 20:14, the lake of fire IS the second death. The text interprets its own symbol: the fiery image is a way of depicting what is, at its core, a second death.

6. The phrase "lake of fire" (limne tou puros) is unique to Revelation. The text provides its own definition ("the second death"). What evidence supports reading the lake of fire as a literal place rather than as symbolic imagery the text itself interprets?

The text itself provides the interpretive framework: "This is the second death." The lake of fire is Revelation's own apocalyptic imagery, and the text explains what the imagery represents -- death. The phrase appears exclusively in a book filled with symbolic imagery (beasts, horns, seals, trumpets, bowls). The word limne (lake) in its other five NT uses refers to a literal body of water in Luke. In Revelation, it becomes "lake of fire" -- a construction that appears nowhere else in Scripture. The text does not treat this as a geographic location; it treats it as an image that is explained by the phrase "the second death."

7. Five categories of subjects enter the lake. Document the vocabulary used for each category.

Subject Category Reference Vocabulary Used Beast and false prophet (symbolic entities) Rev 19:20 Cast "alive" (zontes) into the lake The devil (non-human supernatural being) Rev 20:10 "Tormented (basanisthesontai) day and night for ever and ever" Death and hades (personified conditions) Rev 20:14 "Cast into" the lake; result: "no more death" (Rev 21:4) Humans not in the book of life Rev 20:15 "Cast into the lake of fire" -- no torment formula Eight categories of human wicked Rev 21:8 "Shall have their part in the lake... which is the second death" Human armies (pre-lake) Rev 20:9 "Devoured" (katephagen) by fire from heaven Human remnant (pre-lake) Rev 19:21 "Slain" (apektanthesan) with the sword

The text uses torment vocabulary (basanizo) only for non-human/symbolic entities (the devil, beast, false prophet). For human subjects, the text uses death vocabulary (thanatos), destruction vocabulary (katephagen -- devoured), and killing vocabulary (apektanthesan -- slain). The vocabulary distinction is consistent and deliberate.

docs.title: Section C: Cross-Referencing with Prior Studies
docs.text:
8. In Study 12, we examined Revelation 20:10. In the present study, we see different vocabulary for human subjects. How does this vocabulary distinction inform the question of what the lake does to humans?

Study 12 established that the torment formula in Rev 20:10 is applied to three specific subjects: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. Gate 1 (subject) and Gate 3 (genre) of the Tree 3 classification framework both flagged this passage: the subjects are non-human/symbolic, and the genre is apocalyptic. The present study confirms that when the text addresses human subjects in the lake (Rev 20:15; 21:8), it switches vocabulary -- from basanizo (torment) to thanatos (death). The text does not extend the torment formula to humans. It provides a different identification: "the second death." This vocabulary distinction means the torment of Rev 20:10 cannot be assumed to apply to all subjects in the lake without importing it across a vocabulary boundary the text itself maintains.

9. In Study 11, we examined Revelation 14:9-11 ("the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever"). Compare this with Revelation 20:14-15 and 21:8. Are these the same vocabulary?

They are not the same vocabulary. Revelation 14:10-11 uses basanizo/basanismos (torment vocabulary) for "beast-worshippers" within a highly symbolic vision (the third angel's message). Revelation 20:14-15 and 21:8 use thanatos (death vocabulary) for humans in the lake of fire. These are different Greek word families with different semantic ranges. Basanizo means "to torment, to test with a touchstone." Thanatos means "death." No lexicon defines one as the other. The presence of torment vocabulary in Rev 14:10-11 does not change the vocabulary that the text uses in Rev 20:14-15 -- those passages use death vocabulary, and each passage must be read with its own terms.

10. Read Revelation 19:20-21 and 20:9. Document the vocabulary pattern for symbolic entities versus human beings.

The text maintains a consistent vocabulary distinction:

  • Symbolic entities (beast, false prophet): Cast "alive" (zontes) into the lake (Rev 19:20). They survive entry.
  • Human remnant (same passage): "Slain" (apektanthesan) with the sword (Rev 19:21). They die.
  • Human armies (Rev 20:9): "Devoured" (katephagen) by fire from heaven. They are consumed.
  • Human subjects generally (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8): "Cast into the lake of fire" -- identified as "the second death."

The pattern is: symbolic entities are cast alive, survive, and are tormented. Human beings are slain, devoured, and die the second death. The text does not use the same verbs for both categories.

11. Read Matthew 25:41. How does this primary designation -- prepared for non-human entities -- align with Revelation's pattern?

Matthew 25:41 states the everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- non-human entities. This aligns with Revelation's pattern: the torment formula is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10) -- non-human/symbolic entities. The fire's primary design is for supernatural beings. When human beings encounter the lake of fire, the text identifies the result differently: "the second death." Both Matthew and Revelation point to the same distinction: the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels; humans who enter it experience a different outcome described with different vocabulary.

"Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels." -- Matthew 25:41

docs.title: Section D: The Destruction of Death Itself
docs.text:
12. Death and hades are personified throughout Revelation. Trace the personification and explain what it means that death itself can be destroyed.

The personification of death forms a narrative arc across Revelation:

  • Rev 6:8: Death rides the pale horse -- an active agent, given authority to kill.
  • Rev 1:18: Christ holds "the keys of hell and of death" -- authority over death is in Christ's hands.
  • Rev 20:13: Death and hades "delivered up the dead which were in them" -- they are compelled to release their captives.
  • Rev 20:14: Death and hades are "cast into the lake of fire" -- they are themselves destroyed.

The arc moves from death as a powerful agent to death as a conquered enemy. The text treats death as a force that can be -- and ultimately is -- permanently eliminated. If death itself is cast into the lake and the result is "no more death" (Rev 21:4), then the lake of fire functions as the mechanism by which death is permanently destroyed.

13. Cross-reference the destruction-of-death vocabulary chain across five passages.

Passage Statement Vocabulary 1 Corinthians 15:26 "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" katargeo (G2673) -- to render inoperative, abolish Isaiah 25:8 "He will swallow up death in victory" bala (H1104) -- to swallow, engulf 1 Corinthians 15:54 "Death is swallowed up in victory" katapino (G2666) -- to swallow down Hosea 13:14 "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction" qeteb (H6986) -- destruction, plague 2 Timothy 1:10 Christ "hath abolished death" katargeo (G2673) -- same as 1 Cor 15:26

The vocabulary is consistently destruction/abolition. Death is destroyed (katargeo), swallowed up (bala/katapino), and plagued with destruction (qeteb). Across Isaiah, Hosea, Paul, and Revelation, the fate of death itself is described with destruction vocabulary. Rev 20:14 (death cast into the lake) and Rev 21:4 ("no more death") stand as the final realization of what these passages anticipate.

14. Revelation 21:4 states "no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain." How does this function if conscious suffering continues eternally?

The statement is unqualified and universal: "no more death... no more pain." If the lake of fire produces eternal conscious suffering, then pain continues forever -- and Rev 21:4 is not true in an absolute sense. The ECT position must qualify the statement: "no more death or pain for the redeemed -- but eternal death and pain for the wicked continue." Yet the text does not add this qualification. The declaration follows immediately after death is cast into the lake (Rev 20:14) and describes the resulting state of reality ("the former things are passed away"). The conditionalist reading takes the text at face value: death itself has been destroyed; the wicked have perished in the second death; "the former things" -- including the wicked who died the second death -- "are passed away." The result is genuinely "no more pain" in the entire created order.

"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." -- Revelation 21:4

docs.title: Section E: Counter-Arguments and Evaluation
docs.text:
15. "Humans are cast into the same lake where the devil is tormented (Rev 20:10,15), so they must experience the same torment." Evaluate.

The shared-destination argument assumes identical outcomes for all subjects. The text undermines this assumption: the text uses basanizo (torment) for the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10) but thanatos (death) for humans (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8). In Rev 19:20-21, symbolic entities are cast "alive" into the lake while humans are "slain." In Rev 20:9, fire from heaven "devours" human armies. The text maintains a consistent vocabulary distinction between what happens to non-human/symbolic entities and what happens to humans. Being cast into the same lake does not require the same outcome -- the text itself provides different vocabulary for different subjects. Consider: death and hades are also cast into the same lake (Rev 20:14), and their outcome is destruction ("no more death" -- Rev 21:4), not torment.

16. "The 'second death' is a metaphor -- it does not mean actual death but spiritual death, which is separation from God." Evaluate.

No verse in the Bible defines the second death as separation from God. The concept of "death as separation" is a theological framework, not a textual statement. The text uses thanatos without qualifying it as metaphorical or redefining it as separation. The same word thanatos is used in Rom 6:23 ("the wages of sin is death"), Ezek 18:4 ("the soul that sinneth, it shall die"), and throughout the NT for the penalty of sin -- in all cases meaning death, not separation. To read "second death" as "separation from God" requires adding a concept the text does not contain. Furthermore, Rev 2:10-11 pairs the second death with literal physical death ("faithful unto death") -- suggesting the second death is in the same category (death), not a different category (separation).

17. "Death and hades are abstract concepts cast into the lake, so the lake cannot mean literal death." Evaluate.

The text itself explains the outcome: the casting of death and hades into the lake results in "no more death" (Rev 21:4). Death is destroyed. This parallels 1 Cor 15:26 ("the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death") and Isa 25:8 ("He will swallow up death in victory"). Rather than proving that the lake does not deal in death, the casting of death into the lake demonstrates that the lake destroys what enters it. Death enters the lake and ceases to exist. This supports -- rather than undermines -- the reading that the lake's function is the permanent elimination of its subjects.

18. Nave's Topical Bible classifies "DEATH - SECOND" alongside death/destruction vocabulary passages. What does this indicate?

Nave's -- a widely used, traditional reference work -- classifies the second death alongside Ezek 18:4 ("the soul that sinneth, it shall die"), Matt 10:28 ("destroy soul and body in gehenna"), Rom 6:23 ("the wages of sin is death"), 2 Thess 1:9 ("everlasting destruction"), and 2 Pet 2:12 ("made to be taken and destroyed"). These are death/destruction vocabulary passages. Nave's also classifies fire in judgment under "Of the destruction of the wicked" and classifies everlasting fire as FIGURATIVE. This indicates that the traditional understanding of the second death connected it to the broader biblical theme of death and destruction as the fate of the wicked -- not to a separate category of eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise -- Answers
docs.text:
1. "Rev 20:14 states: 'This is the second death' -- a direct predicate nominative identifying the lake of fire as the second death." - Explicit (E). The verse directly states this. The predicate nominative is observable grammar.

2. "The text uses thanatos (death) vocabulary, not basanizo (torment) vocabulary, to identify what the lake does." - Necessary Implication (N). Both sides accept that the text says "This is the second death" (thanatos) and that basanizo is not used in the identification statement. The observation is about which vocabulary the text chose -- an observable, unavoidable fact that follows from the E-items.

3. "The second death means permanent cessation of existence -- the wicked die a second time and cease to exist." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-A (Evidence-Extending). This systematizes the death vocabulary (E: Rev 20:14 uses thanatos), the identification statement (E: "This is the second death"), the wages-of-sin-is-death principle (E: Rom 6:23), and the destruction-of-death theme (E/N: 1 Cor 15:26; Rev 21:4). Every component is text-derived. It is an inference because it extends the documented pattern to a categorical claim about the nature of the second death. Added: the conclusion that thanatos in "second death" means cessation -- a systematization, not a new concept.

4. "The second death involves eternal conscious torment -- 'death' here is a metaphor for separation from God." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). FOR: The torment formula in Rev 20:10 (same lake); humans cast into the same lake (Rev 20:15). AGAINST: The text identifies the lake as "the second death" using thanatos (not basanizo); no torment formula for humans; the text chose death vocabulary; wages of sin is death (didactic); humans slain/devoured; death itself destroyed; "no more death." Added: (a) "death means separation from God" -- no verse defines the second death this way; (b) importing the torment formula from non-human entities to humans across a vocabulary boundary.

5. "The torment formula is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10), not to human subjects." - Explicit (E). Rev 20:10 directly states who is tormented. The absence of the torment formula in Rev 20:15 and 21:8 is an observable textual fact.

6. "All subjects of the lake of fire experience the same fate -- since the devil is tormented, humans must also be tormented." - Inference (I) -- specifically I-B (Competing Evidence). This requires adding the assumption that shared destination = identical outcome. The text uses different vocabulary for different subjects (torment for non-human entities, death for humans, destruction for death itself). Added: the interpretive rule "same place = same outcome" when the text uses different vocabulary.

7. "Death itself is destroyed -- cast into the lake results in 'no more death' (Rev 21:4), paralleling 1 Cor 15:26." - Necessary Implication (N). Both sides accept that Rev 21:4 says "no more death" and that this follows the events of Rev 20:14. Both accept 1 Cor 15:26 says death is destroyed. The connection is immediate context (Rev 21:4 follows Rev 20:14) and shared vocabulary (thanatos/katargeo). Zero concepts added.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said -- Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. The "lake of fire" is unique to Revelation (five occurrences) and the "second death" appears four times, all in Revelation. The Aramaic Targum tradition uses "second death" (mota tinyana) consistently as death vocabulary -- dying a second time or exclusion from the world to come.

  2. Rev 20:14 identifies the lake of fire as "the second death" -- a direct predicate nominative following the "X is Y" interpretive formula used throughout Scripture's visions. The text uses thanatos (death) vocabulary, not basanizo (torment) vocabulary, to identify the lake's function.

  3. Five categories of subjects enter the lake, and the text uses different vocabulary for different subjects: torment for the devil, beast, and false prophet (non-human/symbolic); death for human subjects; destruction for death and hades.

  4. The torment formula ("tormented day and night for ever and ever") is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10). When humans enter the lake, the text's term is "the second death" (Rev 20:14-15; 21:8). No torment formula is stated for human subjects.

  5. Rev 2:11 promises overcomers will "not be hurt of the second death" (harm/injury language). Rev 20:6 states the second death has no "power" (exousia -- authority) over first-resurrection participants. Both passages use harm/authority language consistent with death terminology.

  6. The casting of death and hades into the lake results in "no more death" (Rev 21:4), paralleling 1 Cor 15:26 ("the last enemy destroyed is death"), Isa 25:8 ("swallow up death"), Hos 13:14 ("O death, I will be thy destruction"), and 2 Tim 1:10 ("abolished death"). The destruction-of-death vocabulary is consistent across Isaiah, Hosea, Paul, and John.

  7. Rom 6:23 states "the wages of sin is death" (thanatos) -- the same word used in "second death." The penalty for sin is death in didactic teaching; the lake of fire is "the second death" in apocalyptic vision.

  8. Matt 25:41 states the everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- its primary designation is for non-human entities.

  9. The "second death" is distinguished from the first death (physical death) by the ordinal adjective deuteros. Rev 2:10-11 pairs the two deaths in immediate context.

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied -- requires adding something):

  1. It cannot be said that the "second death" means eternal conscious torment. The text defines the second death using thanatos (death), not basanizo (torment). No torment formula is applied to humans at the lake. The claim requires adding "death means torment" -- a concept the text does not contain.

  2. It cannot be said that the "second death" means separation from God. No verse defines the second death as separation from God. The text uses thanatos without qualifying it as separation. The "death as separation" concept is a theological framework applied to the text, not derived from it.

  3. It cannot be said that all subjects of the lake of fire experience the same fate. The text uses "tormented" for the devil, beast, and false prophet; "devoured" for human armies; "slain" for the human remnant; and "second death" for humans in the lake. The vocabulary differs by subject category.

  4. It cannot be said that the lake of fire is the same as gehenna, sheol, or hades. Hades is explicitly cast INTO the lake of fire (Rev 20:14) -- they are not the same. Gehenna and the lake of fire are never equated in the text. These are distinct terms.

  5. It cannot be said that the "lake of fire" concept appears outside Revelation. The phrase occurs five times, all in Revelation. No OT passage, no Gospel, and no Epistle uses "lake of fire."

docs.title: Study 13: The Lake of Fire and the Second Death -- Advanced Study
docs.text:
Revelation 20:14; 21:8; 2:11; 20:6

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Word Study -- Thanatos Deuteros (Second Death)
docs.text:
1. The phrase "second death" (deuteros thanatos) occurs four times in Scripture -- all in Revelation (2:11; 20:6; 20:14; 21:8). It appears nowhere else in the Bible. However, the Aramaic Targum tradition uses mota tinyana ("second death") in multiple OT passages (Deut 33:6; Isa 22:14; 65:6,15; Jer 51:39,57). In the Targums, mota tinyana consistently means dying a second time or exclusion from the world to come -- death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary. What does this pre-Christian Jewish usage reveal about the expected meaning of "second death"?

  2. The word thanatos (G2288, "death") appears three times in Revelation 20:14 alone: "death (thanatos) and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death (thanatos)." The text chose thanatos to identify what the lake of fire does. The Greek language had basanizo (G928, "to torment") and basanismos (G929, "torment") available -- and in fact uses them in Rev 20:10 for non-human entities. Why is the vocabulary the author chose for the identification statement significant?

  3. The adjective deuteros (G1208, "second") is an ordinal number implying a first. Read Revelation 2:10-11: "faithful unto death" (physical death -- the first death) is immediately paired with "not be hurt of the second death." What does the ordinal distinction tell you about the nature of the second death in relation to the first?

  4. Read Romans 6:23: "The wages of sin is death (thanatos)." This is the same word used in "second death." Paul's statement is in a didactic epistle -- direct theological teaching. In the SIS (Scripture Interprets Scripture) framework, how does this didactic passage govern the interpretation of "second death" in Revelation's apocalyptic genre?

docs.title: Section B: The Lake of Fire as the Text's Own Interpretation
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 20:14: "This is the second death." This follows the same "X is Y" interpretive formula used throughout Scripture for explaining symbolic imagery: "the seven good kine are seven years" (Gen 41:26), "Thou art this head of gold" (Dan 2:38), "the seven heads are seven mountains" (Rev 17:9), "the odours are the prayers of saints" (Rev 5:8). In each case, the symbolic image is explained in plain language. What is the symbolic image here, and what is the plain-language explanation?

  2. The phrase "lake of fire" (limne tou puros) appears five times in Scripture -- all in Revelation (19:20; 20:10; 20:14; 20:15; 21:8). The Greek word limne (G3041) occurs 10 times in the NT: 5 literal uses in Luke for the Lake of Gennesaret, and 5 "lake of fire" uses in Revelation. Given that the phrase is unique to Revelation's apocalyptic vision and the text provides its own definition ("the second death"), what evidence supports reading the lake of fire as a literal place rather than as symbolic imagery the text itself interprets?

  3. Five categories of subjects enter the lake: (a) the beast and false prophet (symbolic entities, cast "alive," Rev 19:20), (b) the devil (non-human, "tormented day and night for ever and ever," Rev 20:10), (c) death and hades (personified conditions, Rev 20:14), (d) humans not in the book of life (Rev 20:15, no torment formula), (e) eight categories of human wicked (Rev 21:8, identified as "the second death"). The text uses different vocabulary for different subjects. Document the vocabulary used for each category.

docs.title: Section C: Cross-Referencing with Prior Studies
docs.text:
1. In Study 12, we examined Revelation 20:10 ("tormented day and night for ever and ever"). The subjects of this torment formula are the devil, beast, and false prophet. In the present study, we see that when human subjects enter the lake (Rev 20:15; 21:8), the text uses "the second death" rather than the torment formula. How does this vocabulary distinction between subjects inform the question of what the lake does to humans?

  2. In Study 11, we examined Revelation 14:9-11 ("the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever"). That passage uses basanizo (torment vocabulary) for "beast-worshippers" within a highly symbolic vision. Compare this with Revelation 20:14-15 and 21:8, where the text uses thanatos (death vocabulary) for humans. Are these the same vocabulary? Does the presence of torment vocabulary in Rev 14:10-11 change the vocabulary the text uses in Rev 20:14-15?

  3. Read Revelation 19:20-21. The beast and false prophet are cast "alive" into the lake. The human remnant is "slain" (apektanthesan) with the sword. Read Revelation 20:9: fire from heaven "devoured" (katephagen) human armies. Document the vocabulary pattern: what verbs does the text use for symbolic entities versus human beings?

  4. Read Matthew 25:41. The everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels." How does this primary designation -- prepared for non-human entities -- align with Revelation's pattern of applying the torment formula to non-human/symbolic entities?

docs.title: Section D: The Destruction of Death Itself
docs.text:
1. Death and hades are personified throughout Revelation: Death rides a pale horse (6:8), Christ holds keys of death and hades (1:18), death and hades deliver up the dead (20:13), death and hades are cast into the lake (20:14). Read these four passages and trace the personification. What does it mean that death itself is treated as an entity that can be destroyed?

  2. The casting of death into the lake results in Revelation 21:4: "no more death." Cross-reference this with the following vocabulary chain:

  3. 1 Corinthians 15:26: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed (katargeo) is death."
  4. Isaiah 25:8: "He will swallow up death in victory."
  5. 1 Corinthians 15:54: "Death is swallowed up in victory" (quoting Isa 25:8).
  6. Hosea 13:14: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction."

  7. 2 Timothy 1:10: Christ "hath abolished (katargeo) death." What is the consistent vocabulary used for the fate of death across these five passages?

  8. The ECT (Eternal Conscious Torment) position requires ongoing pain and suffering. Read Revelation 21:4 again: "there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain." This is an unqualified, universal declaration. How does this statement function if conscious suffering continues eternally in the lake of fire?

docs.title: Section E: Counter-Arguments and Evaluation
docs.text:
1. An ECT defender argues: "Humans are cast into the same lake where the devil is tormented (Rev 20:10,15), so they must experience the same torment." Evaluate this claim. Does the text apply the same vocabulary to both? Does being cast into the same place necessarily mean experiencing the same outcome when the text uses different vocabulary for each subject?

  2. An ECT defender argues: "The 'second death' is a metaphor -- it does not mean actual death but spiritual death, which is separation from God." Evaluate this claim. Does any verse define the second death as separation from God? Does the text qualify thanatos in the phrase "second death" as meaning something other than death?

  3. An ECT defender argues: "Death and hades are cast into the lake, and they are abstract concepts, so the lake cannot mean literal death for anyone -- it must represent something else." Evaluate this claim. The text states that the casting of death into the lake results in "no more death" (Rev 21:4). Does the text itself explain what happens when death is cast in? Does this explanation support or undermine the claim?

  4. Nave's Topical Bible classifies "DEATH - SECOND" and lists passages using death/destruction vocabulary (Ezek 18:4; Matt 10:28; Rom 6:23; 2 Thess 1:9; 2 Pet 2:12) alongside the four "second death" references. Nave's also classifies fire in judgment under "Of the destruction of the wicked" and classifies everlasting fire as FIGURATIVE. What does this traditional reference work's classification indicate about how the second death has historically been understood?

docs.title: Study 13: The Lake of Fire and the Second Death -- Answer Key
docs.text:
Revelation 20:14; 21:8; 2:11; 20:6

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is especially important in this study. The phrase "lake of fire" evokes vivid images -- but what does the text itself say about it? And what does the text's own explanation -- "the second death" -- actually mean?

docs.title: Section A: The Lake of Fire -- What the Text Says
docs.text:
1. Read Revelation 20:14. The verse states: "And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death." What does the text say the lake of fire IS?

The text says the lake of fire IS the second death. This is a direct predicate nominative -- an identification statement. The text does not say "the lake of fire involves torment" or "the lake of fire represents separation from God." It says "This is the second death."

"And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death." -- Revelation 20:14

2. Read Revelation 21:8. Eight categories of wicked people "shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." When the text describes what happens to human beings in the lake, what term does it use -- "torment" or "the second death"?

The text uses "the second death." When addressing human subjects, the text identifies the lake's function as death -- specifically, a second death. It does not use the word "torment" (basanizo) for humans in the lake.

"But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." -- Revelation 21:8

3. The phrase "lake of fire" (limne tou puros) appears five times in the Bible -- all in Revelation (19:20; 20:10; 20:14; 20:15; 21:8). It appears nowhere else in Scripture. What does this tell you about treating the "lake of fire" as a concept found throughout the Bible?

The "lake of fire" is unique to Revelation. It does not appear in any Old Testament passage, any Gospel, or any Epistle. The concept cannot be imported from other parts of Scripture, because no other part of Scripture uses the phrase. The Greek word limne (G3041, "lake") occurs 10 times in the NT: 5 literal uses in Luke (the Lake of Gennesaret) and 5 "lake of fire" uses in Revelation.

docs.title: Section B: Who Enters the Lake?
docs.text:
4. Read Revelation 19:20. Who is cast into the lake of fire first? Are these human beings or symbolic entities?

The beast and the false prophet are cast into the lake first. They are cast in "alive." These are symbolic entities within John's apocalyptic vision -- not literal human beings.

"And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him... These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone." -- Revelation 19:20

5. Read Revelation 19:21. What happens to the human "remnant" in this passage? Does the text use the same vocabulary for the humans as for the beast and false prophet?

The human remnant is "slain" (apektanthesan) -- killed with the sword. The text uses different vocabulary for humans (slain) than for the symbolic entities (cast alive into the lake). This is a deliberate distinction.

"And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse." -- Revelation 19:21

6. Read Revelation 20:10. Who is tormented "day and night for ever and ever" in the lake? Is this statement applied to human beings or to the devil, beast, and false prophet?

The torment formula ("tormented day and night for ever and ever") is applied to the devil, the beast, and the false prophet -- non-human and symbolic entities. The text does not apply this formula to human beings.

"And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." -- Revelation 20:10

7. Read Revelation 20:15. "Whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire." Does this verse add any statement about torment for these human subjects?

No. The verse states that humans are cast into the lake of fire but does not add any torment formula. No basanizo (torment) language appears. The preceding verse (Rev 20:14) identifies the lake as "the second death."

"And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire." -- Revelation 20:15

8. Read Revelation 20:9. What does the fire from heaven do to the human armies? The word is "devoured" (katephagen). What does "devoured" mean?

"Devoured" means consumed, eaten up, destroyed. Fire from heaven devoured the human armies. This is destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

"And fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them." -- Revelation 20:9

docs.title: Section C: What Does "Second Death" Mean?
docs.text:
9. The word "death" (thanatos) appears three times in Revelation 20:14 alone: "death (thanatos) and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death (thanatos)." When the text identifies what the lake of fire does, does it use death vocabulary or torment vocabulary?

The text uses death vocabulary. Thanatos (death) appears three times in this single verse. The text chose "death" -- not "torment" (basanizo) -- to identify what the lake of fire does. The author's own name for the lake's function is "death."

10. Read Romans 6:23. "The wages of sin is death" (thanatos). This is the same Greek word used in "second death." According to Paul, what is the penalty for sin?

The penalty for sin is death -- thanatos. This is the same word used in "second death" (deuteros thanatos). Paul defines the wages of sin as death, and the lake of fire is identified as "the second death."

"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." -- Romans 6:23

11. The adjective "second" (deuteros) implies a first. Read Revelation 2:10-11. Verse 10 says "be thou faithful unto death" -- that is, physical death (the first death). Verse 11 promises overcomers will "not be hurt of the second death." How does the text distinguish between the first death and the second death?

The text pairs them in immediate context. "Faithful unto death" refers to physical death -- the first death that all humans experience. The "second death" is a distinct, subsequent death. The ordinal adjective "second" (deuteros) creates this distinction: there is a first death (physical) and a second death (at the lake of fire).

"Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." -- Revelation 2:10

"He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." -- Revelation 2:11

12. If the "second death" meant eternal conscious torment rather than death, why would the text call it "death" at all? What does the word "death" normally mean?

The word "death" (thanatos) normally means the cessation of life. If the text meant to describe ongoing conscious torment, calling it "death" would be misleading -- torment is the opposite of death. The text had torment vocabulary available (basanizo, basanismos) and chose not to use it for the identification statement. It chose "death" -- twice calling the lake "the second death."

docs.title: Section D: Death and Hades Cast into the Lake
docs.text:
13. Read Revelation 20:13-14. Death and hades "delivered up the dead" and then were "cast into the lake of fire." What happens to death itself?

Death and hades are cast into the lake of fire. Death itself -- personified as a force throughout Revelation (riding a pale horse in 6:8, Christ holding its keys in 1:18, delivering up the dead in 20:13) -- is thrown into the lake. The result is stated in Rev 21:4: "no more death."

"And death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works. And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death." -- Revelation 20:13-14

14. Read Revelation 21:4. "There shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." This appears immediately after the lake of fire passages. What is the result of death being cast into the lake?

The result is "no more death." The casting of death into the lake achieves the elimination of death itself. The unqualified statement "no more death... neither shall there be any more pain" describes a future state in which death and pain have been permanently removed.

"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." -- Revelation 21:4

15. Read 1 Corinthians 15:26. "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Read Isaiah 25:8. "He will swallow up death in victory." What do these passages say happens to death?

Death is destroyed. Death is swallowed up. Both passages use destruction/abolition vocabulary for death itself. This matches Rev 20:14, where death is cast into the lake (resulting in Rev 21:4, "no more death").

"The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." -- 1 Corinthians 15:26

"He will swallow up death in victory." -- Isaiah 25:8

16. Read 2 Timothy 1:10. Christ "hath abolished death." The Greek word is katargeo (G2673) -- the same word used in 1 Corinthians 15:26. What does this vocabulary tell you about the fate of death?

The vocabulary is consistent: katargeo means to render inoperative, to abolish, to do away with. Death is abolished, destroyed, swallowed up. The vocabulary chain across Isaiah, Hosea ("O death, I will be thy destruction" -- Hos 13:14), Paul, and John consistently uses destruction/abolition language for death itself.

"But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death." -- 2 Timothy 1:10

docs.title: Section E: Overcomers and the Second Death
docs.text:
17. Read Revelation 2:11. "He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." The verb adikeo (G91) means "to wrong, injure, or harm." What kind of language is this -- torment language or harm/injury language?

This is harm/injury language, not torment language. The text says overcomers will not be "hurt" or "harmed" by the second death. The second death is described as something that injures or harms -- consistent with death vocabulary, not with a framework of eternal conscious experience.

"He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." -- Revelation 2:11

18. Read Revelation 20:6. "Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power." The word "power" is exousia (G1849), meaning authority or jurisdiction. What does it mean that the second death has no authority over first-resurrection participants?

It means the second death cannot exercise jurisdiction or authority over those in the first resurrection. The language treats the second death as a force or power that has dominion over certain subjects but not others. This is authority/death language, consistent with treating the second death as actual death rather than ongoing torment.

"Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years." -- Revelation 20:6

19. Read Matthew 25:41. The everlasting fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels." According to this verse, who was the fire originally prepared for -- human beings or non-human entities?

The fire was prepared for the devil and his angels -- non-human entities. Its primary designation is for supernatural beings, not for human beings. This is consistent with Revelation's pattern: the torment formula is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10), while humans receive the designation "the second death."

"Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels." -- Matthew 25:41

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? -- Answers
docs.text:
A. "The lake of fire IS the second death" (Rev 20:14). - Explicit. Revelation 20:14 directly states: "This is the second death." It is a predicate nominative -- a direct identification statement in the text.

B. "The second death means eternal conscious torment." - Inference. No verse defines the second death as eternal conscious torment. The text defines the second death using thanatos (death), not basanizo (torment). This claim requires adding a concept -- "death means torment" -- that the text does not contain.

C. "The torment formula ('tormented day and night for ever and ever') is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet -- not to human beings" (Rev 20:10). - Explicit. Revelation 20:10 directly states who is tormented: "the devil... where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." No verse applies this formula to humans in the lake.

D. "There shall be no more death" (Rev 21:4). - Explicit. Revelation 21:4 directly states this.

E. "The second death means separation from God." - Inference. No verse defines the second death as separation from God. The text uses thanatos (death) without qualifying it as "separation." The concept of "death as separation" is a theological framework applied to the text, not derived from it.

F. "The wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23), and "death" is the same Greek word used in "second death." - Explicit. Romans 6:23 states "the wages of sin is death" (thanatos). The "second death" (deuteros thanatos) uses the same word. This is an observable vocabulary fact.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... The lake of fire IS the second death (Rev 20:14) The lake of fire is a place of eternal conscious torment The text uses thanatos (death), not basanizo (torment), to identify the lake The second death means something other than death The torment formula is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10) The torment formula applies to all subjects in the lake No torment formula is stated for humans in the lake (Rev 20:15) Humans experience the same torment as the devil Human armies are "devoured" by fire (Rev 20:9); the human remnant is "slain" (Rev 19:21) All subjects in the lake experience identical fates "There shall be no more death" after the lake events (Rev 21:4) Conscious suffering continues forever after the judgment The wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23) The wages of sin is eternal torment
