docs.title: Study 17: God's Character, Justice, and the Fate of the Wicked — Answer Key
docs.text:
Is Infinite Torment Consistent with Biblical Justice?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion — possibly a good one, possibly not — but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is especially important in this study. Many people assume they know what God's character requires regarding the fate of the wicked. But what does God Himself say about His own character — and what does that character tell us about the nature of His judgments?

docs.title: Section A: God's Self-Revealed Character
docs.text:
1. Read Exodus 34:6-7. God proclaims His own name and character: "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty." How many attributes describe mercy in this formula, and how many describe judgment?

Six attributes describe mercy (merciful, gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness, abundant in truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity/transgression/sin), while only two describe judgment (will not clear the guilty, visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation). God's own self-description proportions mercy-language to judgment-language roughly 6:2.

"The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children... unto the third and to the fourth generation." — Exodus 34:6-7

2. Read Exodus 34:7 again. God's mercy extends to "thousands" while His judgment of iniquity extends "unto the third and to the fourth generation." What is the ratio of mercy to judgment in God's own self-description?

Mercy extends to "thousands" of generations; judgment extends to "the third and fourth generation." The ratio is thousands to three or four — an overwhelming preponderance of mercy over judgment. This is not a theological inference; it is what the text itself states in God's own words.

3. This self-description formula is repeated throughout the Old Testament: Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Psalm 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2. What does the fact that Scripture repeats this formula at least five additional times tell you about its importance?

Scripture's repetition of a formula across multiple authors, genres, and centuries signals that this is not a passing comment but a foundational declaration of God's character. At least six passages echo Exodus 34:6-7, making it the most repeated character description of God in the Old Testament. This is how God wants to be known.

4. Read Lamentations 3:33. "He doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men." The Hebrew word translated "willingly" is milibo — literally "from his heart." According to this text, does God's heart desire to afflict people?

No. Affliction does not come "from his heart." The text states that when God afflicts, it is not because He desires it. This is consistent with the Ezekiel passages where God explicitly states He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

"For he doth not afflict willingly [milibo, 'from his heart'] nor grieve the children of men." — Lamentations 3:33

docs.title: Section B: God's Anger — Temporary or Permanent?
docs.text:
5. Read Psalm 103:9. "He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever." According to this text, is God's anger permanent or temporary?

Temporary. The text explicitly says God will NOT keep His anger "for ever." Both clauses reinforce the same point: God's chiding has an endpoint, and His anger is not permanent. This is a direct, didactic statement about God's character.

"He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever." — Psalm 103:9

6. Read Micah 7:18. "He retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." What reason does the text give for why God does not retain anger forever?

Because He "delighteth in mercy." This is not merely a statement about what God does — it is a statement about what God enjoys, what He takes pleasure in. God delights in mercy, not in anger. His anger has a terminus; His mercy does not.

"Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." — Micah 7:18

7. Read Psalm 30:5. "His anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." How does this verse compare the duration of anger to the duration of favor?

Anger is "a moment"; favor is "life." The contrast is stark: God's anger is brief and temporary, while His favor is enduring. The imagery of weeping for "a night" versus joy "in the morning" reinforces that anger is the exception, not the rule, in God's dealings.

"For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." — Psalm 30:5

8. If God "retaineth not his anger for ever" (Mic 7:18) and "will not always chide" (Ps 103:9), what would it mean for God to sustain conscious torment for eternity? Would that be consistent with these statements?

Eternal conscious torment would require God to sustain anger and punishment without end — precisely what these texts say He does NOT do. If God "retaineth not his anger for ever," then a punishment sustained by divine power for infinite duration contradicts what the text explicitly states about God's character.

docs.title: Section C: God's Attitude Toward the Death of the Wicked
docs.text:
9. Read Ezekiel 18:23. "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" What answer does this rhetorical question expect?

The expected answer is "No." God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The rhetorical question, coming from God Himself, reveals His preference: He desires that the wicked turn and live, not that they die.

"Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" — Ezekiel 18:23

10. Read Ezekiel 33:11. "As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live." God swears by His own life. What does He say He desires for the wicked?

God desires their repentance and life, not their death. This is stated three times in Ezekiel (18:23, 18:32, 33:11), and in chapter 33 God swears it with an oath — "As I live" — the strongest form of divine assurance. The repetition and the oath underscore how important this declaration is.

"As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?" — Ezekiel 33:11

11. Read 2 Peter 3:9. "Not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." Read also 1 Timothy 2:4. "Who will have all men to be saved." According to these texts, what is God's stated desire for all people?

God's desire is that ALL people be saved and that NONE perish. These are universal statements — "any," "all men" — not limited to a select group. God's will is for salvation, not destruction.

"The Lord is not slack concerning his promise... but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." — 2 Peter 3:9

"Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth." — 1 Timothy 2:4

12. If God has "no pleasure in the death of the wicked" and is "not willing that any should perish," what would eternal conscious torment — sustained by God's power, without end — say about God's character?

Eternal conscious torment would require God to perpetually sustain the suffering of beings whose death He takes no pleasure in, whose perishing He does not will. He would be actively maintaining — forever — the very condition He declares He does not desire. Destruction (cessation) aligns with these statements: the wicked perish (God does not desire this but permits it), and the affliction reaches its conclusion.

docs.title: Section D: Proportional Justice
docs.text:
13. Read Romans 2:5-6. God "will render to every man according to his deeds." Read also Job 34:11. "The work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways." What standard does God use to determine punishment — the nature of the offended party, or the deeds of the offender?

According to both texts, the standard is the offender's deeds — "according to his deeds," "according to his ways." The measure of punishment is the actions of the person, not the nature of the one offended. This principle appears in at least 11 passages across 9 authors in both testaments (Rom 2:6; Job 34:11; Ps 62:12; Jer 17:10; Matt 16:27; Rev 20:12-13; Col 3:25; and others).

"The righteous judgment of God; Who will render to every man according to his deeds." — Romans 2:5-6

"The work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways. Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment." — Job 34:11-12

14. Read Luke 12:47-48. The servant who knew his lord's will receives "many stripes"; the servant who did not know receives "few stripes." What does this parable teach about whether punishment is uniform or proportional?

Punishment is proportional, not uniform. Jesus explicitly teaches degrees of judgment based on knowledge and responsibility. "Many stripes" versus "few stripes" means different offenders receive different levels of punishment. If all punishment were infinite and identical (eternal conscious torment for all the lost), the distinction between "many" and "few" would be meaningless.

"And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes." — Luke 12:47-48

15. Read Matthew 10:15. "It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city." If judgment is "more tolerable" for some than others, what does that require about the nature of punishment?

It requires that punishment varies in degree. If punishment is "more tolerable" for Sodom than for the cities that rejected the apostles, then judgment is graduated — some experience more, others less. This is incompatible with a single uniform fate of infinite conscious torment for all the unsaved.

"Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city." — Matthew 10:15

16. Read Hebrews 2:2. "Every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward." The Greek word misthapodosia means "a paying back." If punishment is a "just recompense" — a proportional paying back — can finite sins produce an infinite penalty?

A "just recompense" — a proportional paying back — requires correspondence between the offense and the penalty. Human deeds are finite (committed by finite beings in finite time). A just recompense for finite deeds is a finite punishment. An infinite penalty for finite offenses is not a "paying back" proportional to what was done; it exceeds the offense by an infinite degree.

"Every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward." — Hebrews 2:2

docs.title: Section E: The Pattern of Historical Judgments
docs.text:
17. In all of these divine judgments, what is the result — death/destruction or ongoing torment?

Every recorded divine judgment in Scripture results in death and destruction, never ongoing torment:

  • The flood (Gen 7:21-23): "All flesh died... every man... all... were destroyed." The result is death.
  • Sodom (Gen 19:24-25): "The LORD overthrew those cities." The result is destruction.
  • Korah (Num 16:31-35): "They perished... the fire consumed them." The result is death and consumption.
  • Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1-2): "There went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them, and they died." The result is death.

In every case, the divine judgment ends in death or destruction. None results in ongoing conscious torment. This is the consistent pattern across the entire Old Testament.

18. Read Psalm 145:17,20. "The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works... The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy." The Hebrew word for "destroy" is shamad — meaning to annihilate, exterminate. According to this text, what does God do with the wicked?

God destroys (shamad) them. The text does not say God preserves the wicked in torment; it says He preserves those who love Him and destroys the wicked. The contrast is between preservation (for the righteous) and destruction (for the wicked) — not between two kinds of preservation (blissful vs. tormenting).

"The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works... The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy." — Psalm 145:17,20

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? — Answers
docs.text:
A. "God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 18:23; 33:11). - Explicit. God says this directly, three times (Ezek 18:23, 18:32, 33:11). In chapter 33 He swears it with an oath. This is a direct divine statement.

B. "Sin against an infinite God deserves infinite punishment." - Inference. No verse in the Bible states this. It is a philosophical argument originating with Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1098 AD), rooted in feudal concepts of honor (the gravity of an offense measured by the rank of the offended party). Every biblical passage that addresses the measure of punishment uses "according to deeds" (the offender's actions), not "according to the nature of the one offended."

C. "God will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:6). - Explicit. This is a direct quotation from Romans 2:6, and the same principle is stated in at least 10 other passages across both testaments (Job 34:11; Ps 62:12; Jer 17:10; Matt 16:27; Col 3:25; Rev 20:12-13; and others).

D. "God retaineth not his anger for ever" (Mic 7:18). - Explicit. This is a direct quotation from Micah 7:18, and the same principle is stated in Psalm 103:9 ("neither will he keep his anger for ever"), Psalm 30:5 ("his anger endureth but a moment"), and Isaiah 57:16 ("I will not contend for ever").

E. "Eternal conscious torment is the just penalty for sin." - Inference. No verse in the Bible states this. The stated penalty for sin is "death" (Rom 6:23; Ezek 18:4,20; Gen 2:17). The claim that the just penalty is eternal conscious torment requires substituting "torment" for "death" — a substitution no text makes.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... God's mercy extends to "thousands"; judgment to "the third and fourth generation" (Exo 34:7) God's justice demands infinite punishment for any sin God "retaineth not his anger for ever" (Mic 7:18; Ps 103:9) God's anger against the wicked is sustained eternally God has "no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 18:23; 33:11) God's holiness requires the perpetual torment of the lost Punishment is "according to deeds" — many stripes vs. few stripes (Rom 2:6; Luke 12:47-48) All the unsaved receive the same infinite punishment "The wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23) The wages of sin is eternal conscious torment Every divine judgment results in death/destruction (Gen 7:21; 19:24; Num 16:35) Divine judgment results in ongoing torment "All the wicked will he destroy" (Ps 145:20) God preserves the wicked alive in perpetual suffering

docs.title: Study 17: God's Character, Justice, and the Fate of the Wicked
docs.text:
Is Infinite Torment Consistent with Biblical Justice?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion — possibly a good one, possibly not — but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

This distinction is especially important in this study. Many people assume they know what God's character requires regarding the fate of the wicked. But what does God Himself say about His own character — and what does that character tell us about the nature of His judgments?

docs.title: Section A: God's Self-Revealed Character
docs.text:
1. Read Exodus 34:6-7. God proclaims His own name and character: "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty." How many attributes describe mercy in this formula, and how many describe judgment?

  2. Read Exodus 34:7 again. God's mercy extends to "thousands" while His judgment of iniquity extends "unto the third and to the fourth generation." What is the ratio of mercy to judgment in God's own self-description?

  3. This self-description formula is repeated throughout the Old Testament: Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Psalm 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2. What does the fact that Scripture repeats this formula at least five additional times tell you about its importance?

  4. Read Lamentations 3:33. "He doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men." The Hebrew word translated "willingly" is milibo — literally "from his heart." According to this text, does God's heart desire to afflict people?

docs.title: Section B: God's Anger — Temporary or Permanent?
docs.text:
1. Read Psalm 103:9. "He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever." According to this text, is God's anger permanent or temporary?

  2. Read Micah 7:18. "He retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." What reason does the text give for why God does not retain anger forever?

  3. Read Psalm 30:5. "His anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." How does this verse compare the duration of anger to the duration of favor?

  4. If God "retaineth not his anger for ever" (Mic 7:18) and "will not always chide" (Ps 103:9), what would it mean for God to sustain conscious torment for eternity? Would that be consistent with these statements?

docs.title: Section C: God's Attitude Toward the Death of the Wicked
docs.text:
1. Read Ezekiel 18:23. "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" What answer does this rhetorical question expect?

  2. Read Ezekiel 33:11. "As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live." God swears by His own life. What does He say He desires for the wicked?

  3. Read 2 Peter 3:9. "Not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." Read also 1 Timothy 2:4. "Who will have all men to be saved." According to these texts, what is God's stated desire for all people?

  4. If God has "no pleasure in the death of the wicked" and is "not willing that any should perish," what would eternal conscious torment — sustained by God's power, without end — say about God's character?

docs.title: Section D: Proportional Justice
docs.text:
1. Read Romans 2:5-6. God "will render to every man according to his deeds." Read also Job 34:11. "The work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways." What standard does God use to determine punishment — the nature of the offended party, or the deeds of the offender?

  2. Read Luke 12:47-48. The servant who knew his lord's will receives "many stripes"; the servant who did not know receives "few stripes." What does this parable teach about whether punishment is uniform or proportional?

  3. Read Matthew 10:15. "It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city." If judgment is "more tolerable" for some than others, what does that require about the nature of punishment?

  4. Read Hebrews 2:2. "Every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward." The Greek word misthapodosia means "a paying back." If punishment is a "just recompense" — a proportional paying back — can finite sins produce an infinite penalty?

docs.title: Section E: The Pattern of Historical Judgments
docs.text:
1. Read the following passages and note what happened in each divine judgment:

    • The flood: Genesis 7:21-23 — "All flesh died... every man... all... were destroyed"
    • Sodom: Genesis 19:24-25 — "The LORD... overthrew those cities"
    • Korah: Numbers 16:31-35 — "They perished... the fire... consumed them"
    • Nadab and Abihu: Leviticus 10:1-2 — "There went out fire... and devoured them, and they died"

    In all of these divine judgments, what is the result — death/destruction or ongoing torment?

  2. Read Psalm 145:17,20. "The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works... The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy." The Hebrew word for "destroy" is shamad — meaning to annihilate, exterminate. According to this text, what does God do with the wicked?

docs.title: Explicit or Inference?
docs.text:
For each statement below, decide: Does the Bible explicitly say this (you can point to a verse), or is it an inference (a conclusion someone draws that no verse directly states)?

A. "God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 18:23; 33:11). - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

B. "Sin against an infinite God deserves infinite punishment." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

C. "God will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:6). - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

D. "God retaineth not his anger for ever" (Mic 7:18). - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

E. "Eternal conscious torment is the just penalty for sin." - [ ] Explicit — the Bible says this - [ ] Inference — someone concluded this

docs.title: Study 18: Matthew 10:28 -- Advanced Study Answer Key
docs.text:
Same-Author Usage and the Fate of the Wicked

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Matthew's Psyche (G5590) Pattern
docs.text:
1. Matthew's 16 uses of psyche -- the 50/50 split.

The even distribution (8 as "life," 8 as "soul") tells us that psyche is not a technical term in Matthew's vocabulary that consistently refers to one thing. It is a flexible word meaning "the living self/person" that English translators render differently depending on context. The 50/50 split makes it impossible to claim that psyche in Matthew exclusively or even primarily means "an immaterial soul." It means "life" just as often.

The 8 "life" occurrences: 2:20 (child's life sought); 6:25 2x (do not worry about your life); 10:39 2x (lose/find life); 16:25 2x (lose/save life); 20:28 (give his life a ransom). The 8 "soul" occurrences: 10:28 2x (kill/destroy the soul); 11:29 (rest for your souls); 12:18 (my soul is well pleased); 16:26 2x (forfeit his soul); 22:37 (love God with all your soul); 26:38 (my soul is sorrowful).

2. Matt 10:28 and 10:39 -- identical word pair, same discourse.

This is the single most significant datum for interpreting Matt 10:28. The identical word pair psyche + apollymi appears in both verses, separated by only 11 verses, within the same continuous discourse (Jesus' commissioning speech to the Twelve, Matt 10:5-42). In 10:39, the pair unambiguously means "lose one's life." No reader of 10:39 understands it as "destroy an immaterial soul." Same-author, same-discourse usage of an identical word pair is the strongest possible linguistic evidence for what the words mean. Matthew's own usage in the immediate context treats psyche as "life/self" and apollymi as "lose/forfeit."

"He that findeth his life [psyche] shall lose [apollymi] it: and he that loseth [apollymi] his life [psyche] for my sake shall find it." -- Matthew 10:39

3. Matt 16:25-26 -- "life" to "soul" in consecutive verses.

The same Greek word psyche transitions from "life" (v.25) to "soul" (v.26) within consecutive verses of the same discourse, with no signal that Matthew intends a different referent. This strongly supports reading psyche as a fluid term for "the living self/person" rather than a technical metaphysical category. If Matthew intended "soul" in v.26 to mean something categorically different from "life" in v.25, he would need to signal that shift. He does not.

*4. Matt 2:20 and 20:28 -- physical life.

In 2:20, those who "sought the young child's psyche" were Herod's agents seeking to physically kill Jesus. In 20:28, Jesus came to "give his psyche a ransom" -- He gave His physical life on the cross. Both usages are unmistakably about physical, bodily life. These inform 10:28 by establishing that when Matthew uses psyche, he frequently means the whole living person's life, not a separable metaphysical component.

docs.title: Section B: Matthew's Apollymi (G622) Pattern
docs.text:
5. Three categories of Matthew's apollymi usage.

(a) God/authority destroying the wicked (judgment context): - 10:28: God "destroys" soul and body in gehenna - 21:41: Vineyard lord will "miserably destroy" the wicked tenants - 22:7: King "destroyed" the murderers and burned their city

In all three, apollymi describes actual destruction/killing. None appends torment vocabulary.

(b) "Lose one's life" usage: - 10:39: "He that findeth his life shall lose [apollymi] it" - 16:25: "Whosoever will save his life shall lose [apollymi] it"

Here apollymi means "forfeit, lose" -- the life is given up or forfeited.

(c) Other uses: - 10:6; 15:24; 18:11: "Lost [apollymi] sheep" -- those on a trajectory toward destruction, whom Jesus came to save - 9:17: Wineskins "perish [apollymi]" -- burst and cease to function (ruin) - 8:25: "Lord, save us: we perish [apollymi]" -- facing death in the storm - 2:13: Herod seeks to "destroy [apollymi]" the child -- kill Him - 12:14: Pharisees plot to "destroy [apollymi]" Jesus -- kill Him - 26:52: "They that take the sword shall perish [apollymi] with the sword" -- die

The semantic range spans from "lose/forfeit" to "ruin" to "destroy/kill." In every judgment or lethal context, the meaning is actual destruction or death.

6. Judgment-context apollymi in Matthew.

In all three judgment-context passages, apollymi means actual destruction: - 10:28: God destroys the whole person in gehenna - 21:41: The tenants are destroyed (killed) as punishment - 22:7: The murderers are destroyed and their city is burned

No judgment-context use of apollymi in Matthew carries a "torment" sense. No passage appends torment vocabulary to the destruction. The pattern is consistent: when Matthew uses apollymi for divine judgment against the wicked, it means actual destruction.

7. The wineskin argument -- Matt 9:17.

The wineskins passage (9:17) demonstrates the "ruin" end of apollymi's semantic range: the wineskins burst, the material persists, but they cease to function as wineskins. This is a valid sense of the word. However, the context is entirely different: household objects in a non-judgment illustration vs. divine eschatological judgment against the wicked. The judgment usages (10:28; 21:41; 22:7) consistently mean actual destruction/killing -- not "ruin while continuing to exist."

Applying the wineskin sense to 10:28 requires selecting the least representative context (physical objects in a domestic illustration) and importing it into the most consequential context (God's final judgment). Same-author usage in the same type of context (judgment) is a more reliable guide than same-author usage in a different type of context (household illustration).

8. The verb shift (apokteino to apollymi) and aorist aspect.

The shift from apokteino (kill outright, used for men's action on the body) to apollymi (destroy fully, used for God's action on soul and body) signals a qualitative difference. Men can only kill the body -- a partial destruction. God can destroy the entire person -- soul and body together. The verb change marks the difference in scope, not a difference in kind (killing vs. torment).

Both verbs are aorist active infinitives. The aorist aspect in Greek is punctiliar -- it views the action as a completed event, a single occurrence, not an ongoing or continuous process. If Jesus intended to describe an ongoing process of torment, the present tense (continuous aspect) would be the natural choice. The aorist describes God's destruction of soul and body as a completed action.

docs.title: Section C: Matthew's Gehenna (G1067) Pattern
docs.text:
9. Vocabulary paired with gehenna in Matthew.

Passage Vocabulary Paired with Gehenna Matt 5:22 Krisis (judgment) -- "in danger of hell fire" Matt 5:29-30 Apollymi (perish) -- one member perishes vs. whole body cast into gehenna Matt 10:28 Apollymi (destroy) -- destroy soul and body in gehenna Matt 18:9 Contrasted with "enter into life" -- life vs. gehenna fire Matt 23:15 "Child of hell" (huios geennes) -- belonging/destination language Matt 23:33 Krisis (judgment/damnation) -- "how can ye escape the damnation of hell?"

No Matthean gehenna passage uses basanizo (torment), basanismos (torment-noun), or any vocabulary describing conscious ongoing existence. Every passage uses destruction or judgment vocabulary. This is not a matter of one or two passages happening to omit torment language -- it is a complete, consistent pattern across all 7 occurrences in a single author who accounts for 58% of all NT gehenna references.

10. The "enter into life" vs. gehenna pattern.

Matthew 18:9 presents the choice as "enter into life" vs. "be cast into hell fire." Mark 9:43, 45, 47 repeat the same pattern: "enter into life" vs. "go into hell." The consistent contrast is life vs. gehenna -- not one kind of existence vs. another. If gehenna involved ongoing conscious existence (even in torment), the contrast with "life" would be incoherent: both outcomes would involve continued existence. The contrast works only if "life" and gehenna represent genuinely opposite outcomes.

11. All 12 NT gehenna occurrences -- torment vocabulary search.

The complete list: Matt 5:22, 29, 30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:15, 33; Mark 9:43, 45, 47; Luke 12:5; James 3:6. Not one of these 12 passages uses basanizo (torment) or basanismos (torment-noun) for human beings in gehenna. This is a complete absence across 4 NT authors (Matthew, Mark, Luke, James). The significance: the claim that gehenna involves eternal conscious torment cannot be sourced from any gehenna passage. It must be imported from passages that use different vocabulary (basanizo) in a different genre (apocalyptic: Rev 14:10-11; 20:10) about different subjects (beast-worshippers, devil/beast/false prophet).

docs.title: Section D: The Synoptic Parallel -- Luke 12:4-5
docs.text:
12. Side-by-side comparison.

Element Matthew 10:28 Luke 12:4-5 What men can do Kill the body Kill the body What men cannot do Kill the soul (psyche) "After that have no more that they can do" What God can do Destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna After killing (apokteino), cast (emballo) into gehenna Vocabulary for God's action Apollymi (destroy) Apokteino (kill) + emballo (cast into) Reference to "soul" Yes -- psyche mentioned twice No -- psyche completely absent

Key differences: (1) Luke omits apollymi entirely, using apokteino instead; (2) Luke omits psyche entirely -- no reference to the "soul" at all; (3) Luke specifies a temporal sequence (kill first, then cast into gehenna). Luke's omission of psyche suggests that the "soul" concept is not essential to the teaching. The point is about God's total authority over human destiny, not about the nature of the soul.

13. Luke's two-step process vs. Matthew's single action.

Luke describes a sequence: meta to apokteinai ("after the killing") + "hath power to cast into gehenna." Killing is complete before the casting into gehenna occurs. This temporal structure makes ongoing conscious torment in gehenna difficult to sustain: the person is already dead before being cast in.

Matthew describes a single comprehensive action: God destroys "both soul and body" in gehenna. The kai...kai construction emphasizes that nothing is left over -- the destruction encompasses the entire person.

Both accounts describe final, total judgment. Neither uses torment vocabulary. They differ in structure (single action vs. two-step process) but converge on the same outcome: God's judgment in gehenna is destructive, not preservative.

14. Vocabulary absent from both accounts.

Despite their vocabulary differences, both Matthew and Luke agree that gehenna does not involve torment. Matthew uses apollymi (destroy); Luke uses apokteino (kill) + emballo (cast into). Neither uses basanizo (torment), basanismos (torment-noun), or any word suggesting ongoing conscious existence. This is particularly significant because both authors had these words available in their vocabulary (Matthew uses basanizo in 8:6 and 8:29 for physical torment and demonic protest; Luke uses it in 8:28 and 16:23-28 in the parable of the rich man). They chose not to use torment vocabulary when describing gehenna.

docs.title: Section E: Greek Grammar and the Phobeo (G5399) Framework
docs.text:
15. The fear-contrast structure.

The logical structure is: do not fear X (men, who can only kill the body); rather, fear Y (God, who can destroy both soul and body in gehenna). The text specifies why God's action is more fearful by describing its scope: God destroys "both soul and body" -- the whole person -- whereas men can only destroy the body. The text does not say "fear God because His torment lasts forever." It says "fear God because He can destroy the entire person." The greater fear is grounded in greater scope and finality, not in duration of suffering.

16. The kai...kai ("both...and") construction.

The correlative kai...kai emphasizes totality: both soul and body. This construction means nothing is excluded from the destruction. After God destroys "both soul and body," there is no remainder -- no surviving component that continues to exist in torment. The emphasis on totality reinforces the completeness of the destruction, not its duration.

17. Aorist aspect and duration.

Both apokteino (kill) and apollymi (destroy) in Matt 10:28 are aorist active infinitives. The aorist aspect views an action as a complete, punctiliar event -- a single occurrence viewed as a whole, not an ongoing or repeated process. If Jesus had intended to describe an ongoing process of destruction or torment, the present infinitive (continuous aspect) would be the expected choice. The aorist indicates that the destruction of soul and body in gehenna is a completed action, not an ongoing one.

This aligns with Luke's temporal sequence (after killing, cast into gehenna) and with the kai...kai totality construction. All three grammatical features point in the same direction: God's judgment in gehenna is a completed, total destruction.

docs.title: Section F: ECT Counterarguments
docs.text:
18. ECT Argument 1 -- Body-soul dualism from "not able to kill the soul."

The text states men cannot kill the psyche. Whether this implies body-soul dualism depends on which of two readings one chooses:

(a) "Psyche as separable conscious soul": The soul is an immaterial entity that survives bodily death. Men can kill the body, but the soul lives on. This reading requires importing body-soul dualism -- a concept the text does not state.

(b) "Psyche as the life/self that only God can end": Men can kill the body, but only God controls the person's ultimate destiny -- their psyche (life/self). This reading follows naturally from Matthew's own usage pattern: psyche = "life" in 50% of uses (E448); the same word pair = "lose life" in 10:39 (E449); Luke omits psyche entirely (E456); "the soul that sins shall die" (E016, Ezek 18:4, 20).

The evidence distribution is heavily weighted against the dualism reading. The FOR evidence consists of one Contextually Clear item (E028 itself, which is ambiguous between the two readings). The AGAINST evidence includes multiple Plain items (E449, E016, E448, N066) that do not require interpretation. The same-author pattern governs the interpretation: psyche in 10:28 carries the same semantic weight as psyche in 10:39, 16:25, and the broader Matthean pattern.

19. ECT Argument 2 -- Apollymi as "ruin" based on wineskins (Matt 9:17).

The wineskin usage demonstrates one end of apollymi's semantic range: ruin (the material persists but the function is lost). The judgment usages demonstrate the other end: actual destruction/killing. The question is which sense applies in Matt 10:28 -- a divine judgment passage.

The FOR evidence for the "ruin" reading consists of one Contextually Clear item (E452 -- wineskins in a non-judgment context). The AGAINST evidence consists of multiple Plain items: judgment apollymi = actual destruction in 21:41 and 22:7 (E451); apollymi is defined as "to destroy fully" (E262); gehenna is paired with destruction vocabulary, never torment vocabulary (E453); judgment apollymi is never followed by torment vocabulary (N067).

The "ruin" reading requires selecting the least representative sense of apollymi (physical objects in a domestic illustration) and applying it to a judgment context where the word consistently means actual destruction. Same-author, same-context-type usage is a more reliable interpretive guide than same-author, different-context-type usage.

20. ECT Argument 3 -- Cessation is "not worse enough" to justify the fear-contrast.

This argument reasons that mere cessation of existence cannot be qualitatively worse than death, so gehenna must involve something beyond death (i.e., ongoing torment) to justify the "fear God more" warning. This reasoning comes from outside the text -- it is a philosophical framework about what constitutes "worse," not an exegetical observation about what the text says.

The text itself specifies what makes God's judgment more fearful: scope (both soul and body, not just the body) and authority (God can do what men cannot). Greater scope and greater finality already account for the greater fear without requiring ongoing torment. Permanent, total, irreversible destruction of the entire person -- including the psyche that men cannot touch -- is qualitatively different from (and worse than) the temporary killing that men can inflict.

This argument is classified as I-C (External Framework): it does not override any explicit statement, but adds a philosophical premise that the text does not contain.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Exercise -- Answers
docs.text:
1. "God can destroy both soul and body in gehenna" (Matt 10:28) - Explicit (E). This directly quotes the verse. The text says exactly this.

2. "Matthew uses the identical word pair psyche + apollymi to mean 'lose one's life' in 10:39, 11 verses after 10:28 in the same discourse" - Explicit (E). This is an observable textual fact. Matt 10:39 uses psyche and apollymi together, and the meaning "lose one's life" is unambiguous in that verse.

3. "No gehenna passage in any NT author pairs gehenna with torment vocabulary" - Necessary Implication (N). This is an observable vocabulary distribution across all 12 NT gehenna passages. Both sides can verify this is what the text contains. No interpretation is required -- it is a factual observation about what vocabulary is present and absent.

4. "Matt 10:28 teaches that the wicked will be destroyed (cease to exist) in gehenna" - Inference (I) -- I-A (Evidence-Extending). This systematizes multiple E/N items (E028: destroy soul and body; E451: judgment apollymi = destruction; E453: gehenna + destruction vocabulary; E449: same word pair = "lose life"; N067: judgment apollymi pattern) into a doctrinal claim. No single verse says "the wicked will cease to exist." All components are text-derived; the inference adds only the systematization. Criteria: #5 (systematizing).

5. "'Not able to kill the soul' implies body-soul dualism" - Inference (I) -- I-B (Competing Evidence). FOR: E028 (men cannot kill the soul -- implies something survives bodily death). AGAINST: E448 (psyche = "life" in 50% of Matthew uses); E449 (same word pair = "lose life" in 10:39); E456 (Luke omits psyche); E016 (the soul that sins shall die); N005 (the soul is mortal). The claim requires choosing between two readings of psyche (separable soul vs. life/self) and importing body-soul dualism. Criteria: #2 (choosing between readings), #1 (adding body-soul dualism).

6. "Apollymi means 'ruin' not 'annihilate' -- soul and body continue in torment" - Inference (I) -- I-B (Competing Evidence). FOR: E452 (wineskins "perish" = ruin in 9:17). AGAINST: E451 (judgment apollymi = actual destruction in 21:41; 22:7); E262 (apollymi = "to destroy fully"); E453 (gehenna + destruction, never + torment); N067 (judgment apollymi consistently = destruction). The claim requires choosing the "ruin" sense (attested in a non-judgment context) over the "destroy" sense (attested in judgment contexts) and adding "continue to exist in ongoing torment" -- something the text does not say. Criteria: #2 (choosing between readings), #1 (adding ongoing torment).

7. "The warning structure implies ongoing conscious suffering -- cessation is not worse enough" - Inference (I) -- I-C (External Framework). The reasoning that cessation is "not worse enough" to justify the fear-contrast comes from outside the text. The text specifies scope (both soul and body) and authority (God can do what men cannot) as the basis for greater fear. The "not worse enough" premise is a philosophical judgment, not an exegetical observation. Criteria: #3 (external philosophical framework).

docs.title: What CAN Be Said / What CANNOT Be Said -- Answers
docs.text:
What CAN be said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies):

  1. The text states God can destroy (apollymi) both soul (psyche) and body (soma) in gehenna (E028, Matt 10:28).

  2. The text states the same word pair (psyche + apollymi) means "lose one's life" in Matt 10:39, 11 verses later in the same discourse (E449, N066).

  3. The text states Matthew uses psyche for both "life" and "soul" in equal proportion; the word carries the sense of "the living self/person" (E448, E450).

  4. The text states the verb changes from apokteino (kill, for men) to apollymi (destroy, for God) in Matt 10:28 (E454).

  5. The text states no gehenna passage in any author pairs gehenna with torment vocabulary (E453, N068).

  6. The text states the soul that sins shall die (E016); the soul is mortal -- it can be destroyed (N005).

  7. The text states Luke's parallel (12:4-5) omits both apollymi and psyche, describing God as killing and casting into gehenna (E456, E457).

  8. The text states both verbs in Matt 10:28 are aorist infinitives -- punctiliar, completed action (E455).

What CANNOT be said (not stated or necessarily implied -- requires adding something):

  1. The text does not state that the soul is immortal or indestructible. Matt 10:28 explicitly says God can destroy the soul.

  2. The text does not state that apollymi means "annihilate" (complete non-existence of all components). The word means "destroy fully" with a semantic range that includes ruin.

  3. The text does not state that apollymi means "ruin while continuing to exist in torment." No gehenna passage appends torment vocabulary.

  4. The text does not state whether the "soul" in 10:28 is a separable conscious entity or the person's life/self. Luke's parallel omits the concept; Matthew's usage pattern supports both readings to varying degrees.

  5. The text does not state that gehenna involves ongoing conscious torment. No gehenna passage uses basanizo or basanismos for human beings.

  6. The text does not state that the wicked will cease to exist. The text says God can destroy them; the duration and nature of that destruction is inferred, not stated.

  7. The text does not state the precise mechanism by which God destroys soul and body in gehenna.

docs.title: Study 18: Matthew 10:28 -- Advanced Study
docs.text:
Same-Author Usage and the Fate of the Wicked

Evidence Tiers

This series uses a three-tier evidence classification to distinguish what Scripture says from what people claim it teaches:

  1. Explicit (E) -- The text directly says this. You can point to a verse and quote it.
  2. Necessary Implication (N) -- No single verse says this word-for-word, but it unavoidably follows from what the text does say. No interpretation is needed -- every reader, regardless of theological position, must agree.
  3. Inference (I) -- Someone claims the Bible teaches this, but no verse says it and no combination of verses forces it. Something must be added beyond what the text contains: a concept, a framework, or a choice between possible readings.

The hierarchy matters: Explicit > Necessary Implication > Inference. An inference cannot override what the text explicitly states.

docs.title: Section A: Matthew's Psyche (G5590) Pattern
docs.text:
1. Matthew uses psyche (G5590) 16 times across 11 verses. Eight occurrences are translated "life" (2:20; 6:25 2x; 10:39 2x; 16:25 2x; 20:28) and eight are translated "soul(s)" (10:28 2x; 11:29; 12:18; 16:26 2x; 22:37; 26:38). Examine this distribution. What does the even 50/50 split between "life" and "soul" tell you about the semantic range of psyche in Matthew's vocabulary?

  2. Read Matthew 10:28 and Matthew 10:39 together. Both are in the same discourse (Jesus' commissioning of the Twelve). Both use the identical word pair psyche + apollymi. In 10:28, the pair is translated "destroy the soul." In 10:39, the same pair is translated "lose his life." What does same-author, same-discourse usage of an identical word pair tell you about what the words mean?

  3. Read Matthew 16:25-26. In verse 25, psyche is translated "life" twice. In verse 26, psyche is translated "soul" twice. This transition occurs in consecutive verses of the same discourse. Does this support reading "soul" as a distinct metaphysical concept, or does it suggest Matthew uses psyche fluidly for "the living self/person"?

  4. Read Matthew 2:20 ("they are dead which sought the young child's life [psyche]") and Matthew 20:28 ("to give his life [psyche] a ransom for many"). In both cases, psyche refers to physical life that can be sought, taken, or given. How do these "life" usages inform the meaning of psyche in 10:28?

docs.title: Section B: Matthew's Apollymi (G622) Pattern
docs.text:
1. Matthew uses apollymi (G622) approximately 18 times across 16 verses. Categorize these uses into three groups: (a) God/authority figures destroying the wicked (10:28; 21:41; 22:7), (b) the "lose one's life" usage (10:39; 16:25), and (c) other uses (lost sheep: 10:6; 15:24; 18:11; wineskins: 9:17; perish in storm: 8:25; etc.). What does each group reveal about the semantic range of apollymi?

  2. Focus on the judgment-context group: Matthew 10:28 (God destroys soul and body in gehenna), Matthew 21:41 (vineyard lord "miserably destroys" wicked tenants), Matthew 22:7 (king "destroyed" murderers and burned their city). When Matthew uses apollymi for divine or royal judgment against the wicked, does it consistently mean actual destruction/killing, or does it carry a "torment" sense in any of these passages?

  3. Read Matthew 9:17. Apollymi is used for wineskins that burst -- they "perish." The wineskins are ruined: the material persists but they cease to function. This is often cited as evidence that apollymi means "ruin, not annihilation." How does this non-judgment usage compare with the judgment usages in 10:28, 21:41, and 22:7? Is the wineskin context (household objects) the same type of context as divine judgment against the wicked?

  4. The verb in Matt 10:28 shifts from apokteino (kill outright, for men's action) to apollymi (destroy, for God's action). Both are aorist active infinitives -- punctiliar aspect, describing completed actions. What does the verb shift signal about the qualitative difference between human killing and divine destroying? What does the aorist aspect indicate about the duration of the action?

docs.title: Section C: Matthew's Gehenna (G1067) Pattern
docs.text:
1. Matthew contains 7 of the 12 total NT gehenna occurrences (58%). Examine the vocabulary paired with gehenna in each Matthean passage:

    Passage Vocabulary Paired with Gehenna Matt 5:22 ___ Matt 5:29-30 ___ Matt 10:28 ___ Matt 18:9 ___ Matt 23:15 ___ Matt 23:33 ___

    Does any Matthean gehenna passage use basanizo (torment), basanismos (torment-noun), or any conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary?

  2. Read Matthew 18:9 alongside Mark 9:43, 45, 47. In all of these passages, what is consistently contrasted with gehenna? What does this "enter into life" vs. gehenna pattern suggest about what gehenna represents?

  3. Extend the search beyond Matthew: examine all 12 NT gehenna occurrences (Matt 5:22, 29-30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:15, 33; Mark 9:43, 45, 47; Luke 12:5; James 3:6). Does any gehenna passage in the entire NT use torment vocabulary (basanizo, basanismos) for human beings? What is the significance of this complete absence?

docs.title: Section D: The Synoptic Parallel -- Luke 12:4-5
docs.text:
1. Compare the two accounts side by side:

    Element Matthew 10:28 Luke 12:4-5 What men can do ___ ___ What men cannot do ___ ___ What God can do ___ ___ Vocabulary for God's action ___ ___ Reference to "soul" ___ ___

    What are the key differences? What does Luke's omission of both apollymi and psyche suggest?

  2. Luke 12:5 uses the construction meta to apokteinai ("after he hath killed") followed by "hath power to cast into gehenna." This is a temporal sequence: killing precedes casting into gehenna. How does this two-step process compare with Matthew's single-action description of God destroying "both soul and body in gehenna"?

  3. Both Matthew and Luke record this teaching, yet they use different vocabulary. Matthew uses apollymi (destroy); Luke uses apokteino (kill) + emballo (cast into). Despite the vocabulary differences, do the two accounts agree or disagree about whether gehenna involves torment? What vocabulary is absent from both accounts?

docs.title: Section E: Greek Grammar and the Phobeo (G5399) Framework
docs.text:
1. The word phobeo (G5399, "fear") appears three times in Matt 10:28 (twice as negated imperative, once as positive imperative). Jesus says: do not fear those who kill the body; rather, fear Him who can destroy soul and body in gehenna. What is the logical structure of the fear-contrast? Does the text specify why God's action is more fearful -- because of duration (ongoing torment) or because of scope (whole person, not just body)?

  2. The correlative kai...kai ("both...and") construction in "both soul and body" emphasizes totality. What does this construction tell you about the scope of God's destruction? Is anything left over after God destroys "both soul and body"?

  3. Both apokteino and apollymi in Matt 10:28 are aorist active infinitives. The aorist aspect in Greek is punctiliar -- it views the action as a completed event, not an ongoing process. If the destruction of soul and body in gehenna is described with punctiliar aspect, what does this suggest about whether the destruction is a completed event or an ongoing process?

docs.title: Section F: ECT Counterarguments
docs.text:
1. ECT Argument 1: "Not able to kill the soul" (Matt 10:28) implies body-soul dualism -- the soul is a separable, conscious entity that survives bodily death. Evaluate this argument against the following evidence:

    • Matthew uses psyche for "life" 8 times and "soul" 8 times (E448)
    • The same word pair (psyche + apollymi) means "lose one's life" in 10:39, same discourse (E449)
    • Luke's parallel omits psyche entirely (E456)
    • Ezekiel 18:4, 20: "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (E016) Does the text require body-soul dualism, or is there an alternative reading consistent with Matthew's usage pattern?

  2. ECT Argument 2: Apollymi means "ruin" not "annihilate," based on the wineskins passage (Matt 9:17) -- the material persists but in a ruined state. Evaluate this against the judgment usages of apollymi in Matthew (10:28; 21:41; 22:7). Which context -- household objects or divine judgment -- is more relevant for determining what apollymi means in a divine judgment passage?

  3. ECT Argument 3: The warning structure of Matt 10:28 (fear God more than men) implies gehenna must involve something worse than death -- and mere cessation would not be qualitatively worse. Where does this reasoning come from -- the text itself, or a philosophical framework about what constitutes "worse"? Does the text specify the nature of the "worse," or could greater scope (whole person vs. body only) and greater finality (permanent vs. temporary) account for the greater fear?

docs.title: Study 18: Matthew 10:28 -- Answer Key
docs.text:
"Destroy Both Soul and Body in Hell" -- What Does Jesus Mean?

A Note on How to Study

Throughout this series, we distinguish between what the Bible explicitly says and what people infer from the Bible. These are not the same thing.

  • Explicit: You can point to a verse and quote it. The text directly says this.
  • Inference: Someone claims the Bible teaches something, but no single verse says it. They have drawn a conclusion -- possibly a good one, possibly not -- but the conclusion itself is not in the text.

In this study, we will examine Matthew 10:28 in detail, paying close attention to how Matthew himself uses the key words in this verse throughout his Gospel. Same-author usage is one of the most reliable tools for determining what a word means in a specific context.

docs.title: Section A: The Verse Itself
docs.text:
1. Read Matthew 10:28. What two things does Jesus contrast in this verse? What can men do, and what can God do?

Jesus contrasts what men can do with what God can do. Men can kill the body but are not able to kill the soul. God is able to destroy both soul and body in gehenna. The contrast is between a limited power (killing the body only) and a total power (destroying the whole person -- soul and body together).

"And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." -- Matthew 10:28

2. What word does Jesus use for what God does to "both soul and body in hell" -- does He say "torment" or "destroy"?

Jesus says "destroy" (apollymi, G622). He does not say "torment" (basanizo). The word apollymi means "to destroy fully" (Strong's). These are two different Greek words with two different meanings. Jesus chose the destruction word, not the torment word.

3. Jesus says men can kill the body but are "not able to kill the soul." Does this verse say the soul is immortal or indestructible? What does it say God can do to the soul?

The verse does not say the soul is immortal or indestructible. It says men cannot kill the soul -- but it immediately adds that God can destroy the soul. If God can destroy it, it is not indestructible. The verse distinguishes between what humans can do (limited) and what God can do (total), not between a mortal body and an immortal soul.

docs.title: Section B: How Matthew Uses "Soul" (Psyche, G5590)
docs.text:
4. Read Matthew 10:39. This verse is only 11 verses after 10:28, in the same discourse. What word is translated "life" here? What does "lose his life" mean in this verse?

The word translated "life" in 10:39 is the same Greek word psyche that is translated "soul" in 10:28. And the word translated "lose" is the same Greek word apollymi that is translated "destroy" in 10:28. So the identical word pair -- psyche + apollymi -- appears in both verses, just 11 verses apart in the same discourse. In 10:39, it means "lose one's life," not "destroy an immaterial soul."

"He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it." -- Matthew 10:39

5. Read Matthew 16:25-26. In verse 25, psyche is translated "life." In verse 26, the same Greek word is translated "soul." What does this tell you about the relationship between "life" and "soul" in Matthew's vocabulary?

The same Greek word (psyche) transitions from "life" to "soul" in consecutive verses of the same discourse. This shows that for Matthew, "life" and "soul" are not two separate concepts -- they are overlapping uses of a single word that means "the living self/person." The English translation changes, but the Greek word does not.

"For whosoever will save his life [psyche] shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life [psyche] for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul [psyche]?" -- Matthew 16:25-26

6. Read Matthew 2:20 and Matthew 6:25. In both verses, psyche is translated "life." What kind of "life" is being discussed -- physical life, or an immaterial soul?

In Matthew 2:20, those who "sought the young child's life [psyche]" were trying to kill Jesus physically -- Herod wanted to destroy the child, not harm an immaterial soul. In Matthew 6:25, "take no thought for your life [psyche]" is about everyday physical needs -- food and drink. In both cases, psyche refers to physical, bodily life.

"Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life." -- Matthew 2:20

7. Looking at all these passages together, does Matthew use psyche to mean "the whole living self/person" or exclusively "an immaterial soul that survives death"?

Matthew uses psyche 16 times across 11 verses. Half (8 occurrences) are translated "life" and half (8 occurrences) are translated "soul(s)." The overall pattern is clear: psyche means "the living self/person" -- one's life, one's whole being. It does not exclusively or even primarily refer to an immaterial soul that survives bodily death. The same word refers to physical life being sought (2:20), worried about (6:25), lost or found (10:39; 16:25), and given as ransom (20:28).

docs.title: Section C: How Matthew Uses "Destroy" (Apollymi, G622)
docs.text:
8. Read Matthew 10:39 again. What does this tell you about the word pair psyche + apollymi in Matthew?

In 10:28, psyche + apollymi = "destroy the soul." In 10:39 (same discourse, 11 verses later), psyche + apollymi = "lose one's life." The same two Greek words, used by the same author in the same speech, carry the meaning of losing/forfeiting one's life -- not tormenting an immaterial soul. Matthew's own usage in the immediate context is the strongest evidence for what these words mean in 10:28.

9. Read Matthew 21:41. In this parable, what does the vineyard lord do to the wicked tenants? What word is used? Does it mean "torment" or "destroy"?

The vineyard lord will "miserably destroy" (apollymi) those wicked men. The word means actual destruction -- the tenants are killed, not tormented. This is the same word Jesus uses in 10:28 for what God does in gehenna.

"They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen." -- Matthew 21:41

10. Read Matthew 22:7. What does the king do to the murderers who rejected his invitation? What word is used?

The king "destroyed" (apollymi) those murderers and burned up their city. Again, the word describes actual destruction -- killing and burning, not ongoing torment.

"But when the king heard thereof, he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city." -- Matthew 22:7

11. Read Matthew 5:29-30. What does Jesus say is better than having your "whole body cast into hell"? What word does He use?

Jesus says it is better for one member to "perish" (apollymi) than for the whole body to be cast into gehenna. The same word -- apollymi -- is paired with gehenna here, just as in 10:28. The consistent pattern: apollymi + gehenna = perishing/destruction, not torment.

"It is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell." -- Matthew 5:29-30

docs.title: Section D: How Matthew Uses "Hell" (Gehenna, G1067)
docs.text:
12. In any of these passages, does Jesus pair gehenna with the word "torment"? What kinds of words does He pair with gehenna instead?

In none of Matthew's 7 gehenna passages does Jesus use the word "torment" (basanizo or basanismos). Instead, He pairs gehenna with destruction and judgment vocabulary:

Passage Vocabulary Paired with Gehenna Matt 5:22 Judgment (krisis) Matt 5:29-30 Perish (apollymi) Matt 10:28 Destroy (apollymi) Matt 18:9 Contrasted with "enter into life" Matt 23:33 Judgment/damnation (krisis)

The pattern is consistent: gehenna is associated with destruction and judgment, never with torment.

13. Read Matthew 18:9. What is the alternative to being "cast into hell fire"? What does the contrast suggest?

The alternative to being cast into gehenna fire is to "enter into life." The contrast is life vs. gehenna -- not one kind of ongoing existence vs. another. This is the same pattern found throughout Scripture: life vs. destruction/perishing, not life vs. torment.

"It is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire." -- Matthew 18:9

docs.title: Section E: The Synoptic Parallel
docs.text:
14. Read Luke 12:4-5. What word does Luke use for what God does -- "destroy" or "kill"? Does Luke mention the "soul" at all?

Luke uses "kill" (apokteino) for God's action, not "destroy" (apollymi). Luke does not mention the "soul" at all. Luke's version reads: "Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell." The concept of the "soul" that men cannot kill is entirely absent from Luke's account of the same teaching.

"Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell." -- Luke 12:4-5

15. Luke 12:5 describes a two-step sequence: God kills, and then has power to cast into gehenna. What does this sequence suggest?

Luke's sequence is: first God kills, then God casts the dead into gehenna. The casting into gehenna happens after the killing. This suggests gehenna is where the already-dead are disposed of, not a place where the living are kept alive in torment. Both accounts (Matthew and Luke) describe gehenna as a place of final, total judgment -- neither uses torment vocabulary.

16. Comparing Matthew 10:28 and Luke 12:4-5, both authors agree on two things about gehenna. What are they?

Both authors agree that: (1) God alone has authority over gehenna -- humans cannot replicate what God does there; and (2) neither author uses torment vocabulary (basanizo, basanismos) to describe what happens in gehenna. Matthew uses "destroy" (apollymi); Luke uses "kill" (apokteino) and "cast into" (emballo). Both describe termination, not ongoing suffering.

docs.title: Explicit or Inference? -- Answers
docs.text:
A. "God is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." - Explicit. Matthew 10:28 directly states this. Jesus uses the word apollymi (to destroy fully).

B. "The soul is immortal and cannot be destroyed." - Inference. No verse says this. Matthew 10:28 explicitly says the opposite -- God can destroy the soul. Ezekiel 18:4, 20 says "the soul that sinneth, it shall die." The claim of an indestructible soul must be imported from outside the text.

C. "In Matthew, the same Greek word psyche is translated both 'life' and 'soul.'" - Explicit. This is an observable textual fact. One can verify it by checking every occurrence of psyche (G5590) in Matthew's Gospel: 8 are translated "life" and 8 are translated "soul(s)."

D. "When Jesus says 'destroy' in Matthew 10:28, He really means 'torment forever.'" - Inference. No verse says apollymi means "torment." No lexicon defines it as torment. Matthew's own judgment usages of apollymi (21:41; 22:7) mean actual destruction. The claim requires adding a meaning the word does not carry and overriding the author's own usage pattern.

E. "'Not able to kill the soul' proves that the soul is a separable, conscious entity that survives bodily death." - Inference. The verse says men cannot kill the psyche. Whether psyche refers to "an immaterial soul that survives death" or "the life/self that only God can end" is an interpretive choice. Matthew's own usage pattern (where psyche = "life" in half of his uses, and the same word pair means "lose one's life" in 10:39) supports the second reading. Luke's parallel omits "soul" entirely, suggesting it is not essential to the point.

docs.title: What the Bible Says vs. What People Say the Bible Teaches
docs.text: The Bible explicitly says... People often claim the Bible teaches... God can destroy both soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28) God torments souls forever in hell The same word (psyche) means "life" and "soul" in Matthew "Soul" refers exclusively to an immaterial, immortal entity The same word pair (psyche + apollymi) means "lose one's life" in 10:39 In 10:28, it means "torment an immaterial soul" Gehenna is paired with destruction vocabulary, never torment vocabulary Gehenna is a place of eternal conscious torment Luke's parallel says God kills and casts into gehenna Gehenna is where the living are kept alive in suffering Men cannot kill the soul; God can destroy it The soul cannot be destroyed by anyone, including God
